201:
Wishing to reject the statement "Pana etaṃ bāhirasamaye" (But this is in the external tradition), he said, "Friends, we alone..." and so forth. In the passage beginning with "Mayaṃ kho," the word "kho" is an emphatic (avadhāraṇa) particle, meaning "We alone prescribe [this]." Then the wanderer (paribbājaka) thought, "This Elder has discarded the external tradition and said, 'We alone.' Seeing what kind of fault do these people prescribe the abandonment of lust and so forth?" Then, wishing to question the Elder, he said, "How is it for you, sirs?" and so forth. The Elder, wishing to answer the wanderer, said, "One who is lustful..." and so forth. In that passage, "attattha" (one's own benefit) refers to one's own welfare, described as the benefit in the present life, the benefit in the future life, and mundane and supramundane benefits. The same method applies to the benefit of others (parattha) and the benefit of both (ubhayattha).

In the terms beginning with "andhakaraṇa" (making blind), lust is called "andhakaraṇa" because it makes one blind by preventing the seeing of things as they really are. It is called "acakkhukaraṇa" because it does not produce the eye of wisdom. It is called "aññāṇakaraṇa" because it does not produce knowledge. It is called "paññānirodhika" (destroying wisdom) because it causes the cessation of these three kinds of wisdom—wisdom of ownership of kamma (kammassakatā-paññā), wisdom of meditative absorption (jhāna-paññā), and wisdom of insight (vipassanā-paññā)—by preventing their occurrence. It is called "vighātapakkhika" (siding with distress) because it leads to the side of affliction known as suffering (dukkha) by yielding undesirable results. It is called "anibbānasaṃvattanika" because it does not lead to the quenching of defilements (Nibbāna). "Friend Ānanda, if such a practice exists, it is indeed fitting and appropriate for your heedfulness; friends, practice heedfulness." Saying this, he rejoiced in the Elder's words, said "Sādhu," and departed. In this sutta, the Noble Path (ariya-magga) mixed with the supramundane is taught. The remaining words in this sutta have clear meanings.

## 2. Ājīvakasuttavaṇṇanā

In the second sutta, regarding the phrase "Householder, in that case...", it is said that the Elder thought: "This householder did not come here with a desire to know; he came only to investigate. I will make this householder himself speak the answer to the question he asked." Having thought thus, and wishing to make the householder himself speak, he said, "In that case" and so forth. In that passage, "tena hi" (in that case) is a term indicating a reason. It means, "Since you ask in this way, I will therefore question you in return on that very matter." "Kesaṃ no" means "By whom is the good Dhamma well-taught?" "Sadhammukkansanā" means exalting and upholding one's own doctrine. "Paradhammāpasādanā" means attacking, disparaging, and belittling the doctrines of others. "Āyatanēva dhammadēsanā" means teaching the Dhamma only on appropriate grounds. "Attho ca vutto" means "The meaning of the question I asked..."
202:
...is clearly shown. "We are of such a nature" refers only to oneself; it is not brought forward to others. There is also a reading "nupanīto."

## 3. Mahānāmasakkasuttavaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, "gilānā vuṭṭhito" means having recovered from illness. "Gelaññā" means because of the state of being ill. "Upasaṅkami" means that after having eaten his morning meal, he approached, taking flowers, perfumes, etc., and being surrounded by a large retinue. "Bāhāyaṃ gahetvā" (taking by the arm) should be understood not as pulling him by the arm, but as rising from his seat, going to Mahānāma, and signaling with his thumb on Mahānāma's right arm to lead him to a suitable place. Then, to that Mahānāma, he taught the virtue, concentration, and wisdom of the seven types of trainees (sekha) by the method beginning with "Mahānāma, the virtue of a trainee also..." and so forth. When teaching the virtue, concentration, and wisdom of the non-trainee (asekha) by way of the fruit of Arahantship above that, he showed: "After trainee-concentration, trainee-insight-knowledge and non-trainee-fruition-knowledge arise; and after trainee-insight-knowledge, non-trainee-fruition-concentration arises." However, the occurrence of the associated concentration and knowledge should be understood as being simultaneous, without before or after.

## 4. Nigaṇṭhasuttavaṇṇanā

In the fourth sutta, "Kūṭāgārasālāyam" refers to the Perfumed Chamber (gandhakuṭi) built with two gables and covered in the hansa-vaṭṭaka style. "Apari-sesaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ paṭijānāti" means claiming all knowledge and vision without leaving even a small remainder. "Satataṃ samitaṃ" means occurring at all times and continuously. "Ñāṇadassanaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ" shows that "Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) is always present before me." "Purāṇānaṃ kammānaṃ" refers to old kammas that were previously accumulated. "Tapasa byantībhāvaṃ" means making an end of cessation through difficult austerities. "Navānaṃ kammānaṃ" refers to new kammas to be accumulated now. "Akaraṇā" means through non-accumulation. By the word "setughātaṃ" (destroying the bridge), he teaches the destruction of the cause. "Kammakkhayā dukkhakkhayo" means the end of suffering through the end of the round of kamma. "Dukkhakkhayā vedanākkhayo" means the end of feeling through the end of the round of suffering. For when the round of suffering is exhausted, the round of feeling is also exhausted. "Vedanākkhayā sabbaṃ dukkhaṃ nijjiṇṇaṃ bhavissati" means that by the end of feeling, the entire suffering of the round will be worn away and destroyed. "Sandiṭṭhikāya" means that which is to be personally realized. "Nijjarāya"...
203:
"For purification" (Visuddhiyā) means for the purification of beings through the practice that wears away defilements, or because of the wearing away of defilements. "Overcoming occurs" (Samatikkamo hoti) means the overcoming of the entire suffering of the round of rebirth. "Venerable Sir, what did the Blessed One say in this practice? Does He prescribe only this practice of wearing away defilements, or another?" is the question.

"Knowing" (Jānatā) means knowing with unobstructed knowledge (anāvaraṇañāṇa). "Seeing" (Passatā) means seeing with the all-seeing eye (samantacakkhu). "For purification" (Visuddhiyā) means for the sake of reaching purification (Nibbāna). "For overcoming" (Samatikkamāya) means for the sake of overcoming. "For cessation" (Atthaṅgamāya) means for the sake of reaching cessation. "For the attainment of the method" (Ñāyassa adhigamāya) means for the sake of attaining the Path along with insight (vipassanā). "For the realization of Nibbāna" (Nibbānassa sacchikiriyāya) means for the sake of realizing Nibbāna, which is unconditioned (apaccayaniibbāna). "Does not perform new kamma" (Navañca kammaṃ na karoti) means not accumulating new kamma. "Old kamma" (Puraṇañca kammaṃ) is kamma accumulated in the past. "Touching and touching, he makes an end" (Phussa phussa byantī karoti) means making an end by repeatedly touching; the meaning is that by repeatedly touching resultant contact (vipākaphassa), he exhausts that kamma. "Visible here and now" (Sandiṭṭhikā) means to be seen by oneself. "Timeless" (Akālikā) means not performing the function of giving results at another time. "Inviting one to come and see" (Ehipassikā) means worthy of being shown as "Come and see." "Worthy of being brought inward" (Opaneyyikā) means worthy of being brought into one's own mind, associated with what should be adhered to. "To be personally known by the wise" (Paccattaṃ veditabbā viññūhi) means to be known by the wise only in their own mental continuums, but difficult for the foolish to know. Thus, two paths and two fruits are spoken of by the power of virtue. For the Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) and Once-returner (Sakadāgāmī) are those who practice to fulfill the virtues. However, by the fulfillment of concentration (samādhisampadā) starting with "Quite secluded from sensual pleasures," three paths and three fruits are spoken of. For the Non-returner (Anāgāmī) noble disciple is said to be one who practices to fulfill concentration. By the words "through the destruction of taints" (āsavānaṃ khayā), etc., the fruit of Arahatship is spoken of. Some teachers, however, say that in this context, virtue and concentration are also intended as those associated with the fruit of Arahatship. That statement is presented separately for the sake of showing the practice according to each individual.

## 5. Nivesakasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fifth sutta, "ministers" (amaccā) means friends with good hearts. "Relatives" (ñātī) means the groups of the mother-in-law and father-in-law. "Kinsmen" (sālohitā) means those with the same blood, such as brothers and sisters. "Unwavering confidence" (aveccappasāde) occurs in the unwavering confidence that arises from knowing the virtues. "Alteration" (aññathattaṃ) means the state of being in another way.
204:
The occurrence of a state in another way (alteration). In the words "of the earth element" (pathavīdhātuyā), etc., there might be an alteration of the earth element which exists in twenty parts in the form of hardness; of the water element which exists in twelve parts in the form of cohesion in liquid; of the fire element which exists in four parts in the form of maturing; and of the air element which exists in six parts in the form of supporting. "But never" (na tveva) shows that while an alteration might occur in these four great elements by their turning into one another, such an alteration would never occur for the noble disciple. Here, "alteration" (aññathattaṃ) refers to the alteration of confidence and the alteration of destination (gati). That [alteration] does not happen to that [noble disciple]. However, the alteration of state (bhāvaññathattaṃ) does occur. For a noble disciple, having been a human, becomes a deva or a brahma. But his confidence does not vanish even in another life, nor does he reach the alteration of destination known as the woeful states (apāya). The Teacher, wishing to show that very meaning, said "Therein, this is the alteration" (tatraidaṃ aññathattaṃ), etc. The rest here is clear in meaning.

## 6. Paṭhamabhava-sutta-vaṇṇanā

In the sixth sutta, "ripening in the sense sphere" (kāmadhātuvepakkaṃ) is kamma that ripens in the sense sphere. "Sense-sphere existence" (kāmabhavo) is the rebirth existence in the sense sphere. "Kamma is the field" (kammaṃ khettaṃ) means wholesome and unwholesome kamma is like a field in the sense of being the place of growth. "Consciousness is the seed" (viñညာဏံ bījaṃ) means the co-nascent volitional consciousness (abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇa) is like a seed in the sense of growing. "Craving is the moisture" (taṇhā sneho) means craving is called water by way of supporting and nourishing. "Of those hindered by ignorance" (avijjānīvaraṇānaṃ) means of those obstructed by ignorance. "Of those fettered by craving" (taṇhāsaṃyojanānaṃ) means of those bound by the bond of craving. "In the low element" (hīnāya dhātuyā) means in the sense sphere. "Consciousness is established" (viññāṇaṃ patiṭṭhitaṃ) means volitional consciousness is established. "In the middle element" (majjhimāya dhātuyā) means in the fine-material sphere. "In the superior element" (paṇītāya dhātuyā) means in the immaterial sphere. The rest here is clear in meaning.

## 7. Dutiyabhava-sutta-vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, "volition" (cetanā) is the volition called kamma. "Aspiration" (patthanā) is also the aspiration called kamma. The rest is just like the previous sutta.

## 8. Sīlabbata-sutta-vaṇṇanā

In the eighth sutta, "habit and practice" (sīlabbataṃ) is just habit (sīla) and practice (vata). "Life" (jīvitaṃ) is the engagement in difficult practices. "Holy life" (brahmacariyaṃ) is living the holy life. "Essence of service" (upaṭṭhānasāraṃ) means having essence by standing close to the object...
205:
Sāraṃ means the sense of being established in the object as: "This Dhamma is excellent, this Dhamma is the ultimate." Saphalaṃ is a question asking whether there is fruit or whether there is increase and growth. "Venerable Sir, in this matter, it should not be answered categorically (one-sidedly)" means, Venerable Sir, a categorical answer should not be given here. Upaṭṭhānasāraṃ sevato means for the person who associates with the Dhamma that is established in the mind as: "This is the essence, the excellent, the ultimate." Aphalaṃ means the absence of the desired benefit. By this much, excluding the monkhood of the Kammavādīs and Kiriyavādīs, all other external sectarian views are included. Saphalaṃ means being together with the desired benefit and increase. By this much, starting from this Dispensation (Sāsana), all the monkhood of the Kammavādīs and Kiriyavādīs is included. "One who is equal to that Venerable Ānanda in wisdom is not easily found"—thus, while answering the question from the stage of a trainee (sekkhabhūmi), it shows that one equal to the wisdom of that Venerable Ānanda is not easily found. In this sutta, the stage of a trainee is discussed.

## 9. Gandhajāta Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the ninth sutta, "He said this" means that after the meal, having returned from the alms-round and performed the duties for the Possessor of Ten Powers (the Buddha), he went to his own place of day-rest. He thought: "In this world, there are fragrances of roots, fragrances of heartwood, and fragrances of flowers. All three of these fragrances go only with the wind, not against the wind. Is there perhaps anything whose fragrance goes even against the wind?" Since he had already secured the boon of the privilege of approaching the Buddha at the time he accepted the eight boons when doubt arose, he immediately rose from his day-rest, went to the Teacher, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place. To dispel the doubt that had arisen, he spoke the words beginning with: "Venerable Sir, there are these three kinds of fragrances."

In those words, gandhajātāni means types of fragrances. Mūlagandho means fragrance based on roots, or the root itself which is endowed with fragrance is called mūlagandha. The fragrance of that root goes with the wind. There is no such thing as the "fragrance of a fragrance." The same method applies to the fragrance of heartwood and the fragrance of flowers. "Ānanda, is there any kind of fragrance...?" In this passage, because of the speaking of virtues such as the taking of refuge, they are called "fragrances" (gandha) because they spread to the various directions like a scent. The person who is the basis of those virtues is called gandhajāta (a kind of fragrance). "Fragrance goes" (gandho gacchati) means it spreads through the speaking of one's virtues. Sīlavā means one who is endowed with the five precepts or the ten precepts. Kalyāṇadhammo means one who has a good nature or beautiful nature because of that very virtue. The meaning of the terms beginning with vigatamalamacchereṇa has been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. Disāsu means in the four directions and in the four...
206:
...intermediate directions. Samaṇabrāhmaṇā means recluses and brahmins who have calmed their evils and removed their evils.

"The fragrance of flowers does not go against the wind" means the fragrance of jasmine (vassika) and other flowers does not go in the direction against the wind. "Neither sandalwood, tagara, nor mallikā" means the fragrance of sandalwood, tagara, and mallikā (jasmine) also does not go against the wind. This is the meaning. Indeed, in the deva world, there is a jasmine called Sumana; on the day it blooms, its fragrance pervades and covers a hundred yojanas. It is said that even that celestial flower is unable to go even a span or a cubit against the wind. "The fragrance of the good goes against the wind" means the fragrance of the virtues such as morality of the wise—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the sons of the Buddha (disciples)—goes against the wind. "The good person wafts in all directions" means the wise good person wafts in all ten directions with the fragrance of virtues such as morality; the meaning is that he pervades all directions with that fragrance.

## 10. Cūḷanikā Sutta Vaṇṇanā

The introduction (nikkhepa) of this tenth sutta is twofold: atthuppattika (arising from an event) and pucchāvasika (arising from a question). If it is asked: Due to what event and whose question was it taught? It was taught due to the event of the Aruṇavatī Sutta and the question of the Elder Ānanda. By whom was the Aruṇavatī Sutta taught? It was taught by two Buddhas: the Blessed One Sikhī and our Teacher. Thirty-one aeons ago from this present aeon, in the city of Aruṇavatī, he was reborn in the womb of Queen Pabhāvatī, the consort of King Aruṇavā. When his knowledge was mature, he departed in the Great Renunciation. The Blessed One Sikhī, having penetrated Omniscient Knowledge at the Bodhi tree and having turned the noble Wheel of Dhamma, was residing near the city of Aruṇavatī. One day, early in the morning, after attending to his physical needs, he set out surrounded by a large community of monks, thinking, "I will enter Aruṇavatī for alms." Standing near the gate-tower of the monastery, he addressed the Chief Disciple named Abhibhū: "Bhikkhu, it is too early to enter Aruṇavatī for alms; let us approach a certain Brahma world."

As he said: "Then, monks, the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, addressed the bhikkhu Abhibhū: 'Come, Brahmin, let us approach a certain Brahma world until it is time for the meal.'"
207:
Monks, at that time, the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, addressed the monk Abhibhū: 'Brahmin, let us go; we shall visit a certain Brahma world until it is time for the meal.' Monks, the monk Abhibhū replied to the Blessed One Sikhī, 'Very well, Bhante.' Then, monks, the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, and the monk Abhibhū went to that certain Brahma world. In that Brahma world, Mahābrahmā, seeing the Blessed One, joyfully welcomed him, prepared a noble seat, and offered it. They also prepared a suitable seat for the Elder. The Blessed One sat on the prepared seat, and the Elder also sat on the seat prepared for him. Mahābrahmā then paid homage to the Blessed One and sat at a respectful distance. 

Then, monks, the Blessed One Sikhī addressed the monk Abhibhū: 'Brahmin, may a Dhamma talk occur to you for the Great Brahma, the Brahma assembly, and the Brahma retinue.' The monk Abhibhū replied, 'Very well, Bhante,' and gave a Dhamma talk to the Great Brahma, the Brahma assembly, and the Brahma retinue. While the Elder was preaching the Dhamma, the host of Brahmas complained: 'For a long time we have had the coming of the Teacher to the Brahma world, yet this monk, setting aside the Teacher, takes it upon himself to give a Dhamma talk.' 

The Blessed One, knowing the dissatisfaction of those Brahmas, said to the monk Abhibhū: 'Brahmin, the Brahma, the Brahma assembly, and the Brahma retinue are complaining about you. Therefore, Brahmin, stir them up even more exceedingly.' The Elder, accepting the Teacher's word, performed various kinds of psychic miracles and, making the thousandfold world system known by his voice, recited the two verses beginning with 'Ārambhatha nikkamatha' (Exert yourselves, go forth). 

How did the Elder make the thousandfold world system known? First, he entered the blue kasina (nīlakasiṇa) and pervaded all places with darkness. Then, when beings thought, 'What is this darkness?', he showed them light. To the beings who were investigating, 'What is this light?', he showed himself. Devas and humans in the thousandfold universe stood with palms joined, paying homage only to the Elder. The Elder thought, 'May the great multitude hear the sound of my preaching the Dhamma'...
208:
He recited these verses. All the devas and humans, being eager to hear, heard the sound as if the Elder were sitting in the midst of the assembly preaching the Dhamma. The meaning also became clear to them. 

Then the Blessed One Sikhī, together with the Elder Abhibhū, returned to the city of Aruṇavatī. After wandering for alms and returning from the alms round after the meal, he asked the community of monks: 'Monks, did you hear the verses being recited by the monk Abhibhū while he was standing in the Brahma world?' Those monks replied, 'Yes, Bhante,' and to show that they had heard, they recited those same two verses. The Teacher gave his approval, saying 'Sādhu, Sādhu,' and concluded the teaching. Thus, this sutta was first taught by the Blessed One Sikhī thirty-one aeons ago. 

Our Blessed One, having attained omniscience and turned the noble Wheel of Dhamma, was staying at Jetavana Monastery near Sāvatthī. On the full moon day of the month of Nayon, he addressed the monks and began this Aruṇavatī Sutta. The Elder Ānanda, standing and fanning him, learned the entire sutta from beginning to end without missing even a single syllable. The next day, after returning from the alms round and performing his duties for the Blessed One, the Possessor of the Ten Powers, the Elder Ānanda went to his place for the day's rest. After performing his duties for his resident and attending pupils and after they had departed, he sat reflecting on the Aruṇavatī Sutta taught the previous day. Then the entire sutta appeared clearly to him. 

He thought: 'Yesterday the Teacher said that the chief disciple of the Blessed One Sikhī, while standing in the Brahma world, dispelled the darkness within a thousand universes, showed the radiance of his body, and made his voice heard while preaching the Dhamma. If such is the scope of a disciple, how far could the Blessed One, who has fulfilled the ten perfections and attained omniscience, make his voice known?' To dispel the doubt that had arisen, he immediately approached the Blessed One and asked about that matter. To show this matter, it is said: 'Atha kho āyasmā Ānando' (Then the Venerable Ānanda...). 

In that text, 'sammukhā' means 'this was heard by me directly (face-to-face),' not by hearsay, nor through a succession of messengers; this is the intended meaning. 'Kīvatakaṃ pahoti sarena viññāpetuṃ' means 'To what extent is one able to dispel the darkness with the radiance of the body and make it known by voice?' [The Buddha replied:] 'Ānanda, that monk Abhibhū was a disciple; immeasurable...'
209: "Tathāgatā"—the Blessed One spoke this word with this intention: "Ānanda, what do you say? That Elder Abhibhū was merely a disciple established in partial knowledge. But the Tathāgatas, having fulfilled the ten perfections and attained omniscience, are immeasurable. Why do you speak like this, as if taking a little dust on the tip of a fingernail and comparing it with the dust of the great earth? The domain of disciples is one thing, the domain of Buddhas is another. The range of disciples is one thing, the range of Buddhas is another. The power of disciples is one thing, the power of Buddhas is another." Thus, the Blessed One, having spoken of his immeasurable nature with this intention, remained silent. The Venerable Ānanda asked a second time. The Blessed One, wishing to show [the same], said: "Ānanda, why do you speak like this, as if taking the hole of a door-bolt and comparing it with the infinite sky; as if taking a small cātaka bird and comparing it with a king of Garuḍas that is a hundred and fifty yojanas in size; as if taking water with an elephant's trunk and comparing it with the great Ganges river; as if taking water in a pit four cubits deep and comparing it with the seven great lakes; as if taking a poor man who receives only a measure of rice and comparing him with a Cakkavatti king; as if taking a dust-spirit (pamsupisāca) and comparing him with Sakka, the king of devas; as if taking the glow of a firefly and comparing it with the light of the sun?" Wishing to show for the second time his immeasurable nature, he remained silent. Then the Elder thought: "The Teacher has been asked by me but has not yet spoken. Now, I will request him for the third time and cause him to roar the Buddha's lion's roar." He requested for the third time. To show this, the passage beginning with "Tatiyampi kho" was spoken. Then the Blessed One, wishing to answer the Elder, said: "Have you heard, Ānanda," and so on. The Elder thought: "The Teacher said to me only this much, 'Ānanda, have you heard of the thousandfold minor world-system (sahassī cūḷanikā lokadhātu)?' and then became silent. Now he will roar the Buddha's lion's roar." Wishing to request the Blessed One, he spoke the words beginning with "Etassa Bhagavā kālo." The Blessed One also spoke the words beginning with "Ānanda, in that case," to give a detailed explanation to the Venerable Ānanda. In that Pali, "yāvatā" means as far as the place extends. "Candimasūriyā" means the moon and the sun. "Pariharanti" means they move about. "Disā bhanti" means they illuminate all directions. "Virocanā" means being radiant. By this much, a single world-system (cakkavāḷa) is defined and shown. Now, wishing to show it by multiplying it a thousand times, he said "tāva sahassadhā loko." "Tasmiṃ sahassadhā loke" means in that thousandfold world-system. Sahassaṃ...
210: "Cātumahārājikānaṃ" means a thousand realms of the Cātumahārājikā devas. Since there are four Great Kings in each world-system, it is said there are four thousand Great Kings. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all places. "Cūḷanikā" means a small world-system. This is the domain (visaya) of the disciples. Why is this minor world-system brought up? It is to show the extent of the middle-sized world-system. "Yāvatā" means as far as the place extends. "Tāva sahassadhā" means by that thousandfold part. "Dwisahassī majjhimikā lokadhātu" is the world-system with the extent of a million kotis of world-systems, calculated by multiplying these thousand world-systems by a thousand. This is not the domain of disciples, but the domain of Buddhas alone. It is shown that even in such a place, the Tathāgatas can dispel the darkness, display the radiance of their bodies, and make themselves known by their voice. By this much, the "field of birth" (jātikhetta) of the Buddhas is shown. This is because this extent of space trembles on the day the Bodhisattas, in their final existence, pass away from the deva realm and take conception in their mother's womb, on the day of their birth, the day of their great renunciation, the day they attain enlightenment, the day they preach the Dhammacakka, the day they relinquish the life-force, and the day of their Parinibbāna. "Tisahassī mahāsahassī" refers to the world-system counted by a thousand for the third time starting from a thousand. Because it is calculated by making a thousandfold of a thousand world-systems, and because it is counted by great thousands, it is called "Mahāsahassī" (Great Thousandfold). By this much, the world with the extent of a hundred thousand kotis of world-systems is shown. If the Blessed One wishes, he can dispel the darkness in such a place, display the radiance of his body, and make himself known by his voice. However, the Elder Gaṇakaputta Tissa said: "The extent of the Tisahassī Mahāsahassī world-system is not like this. This is a place where the teachers' recitation was confused or words were omitted; only the area with the extent of ten thousand kotis of world-systems is called the Tisahassī Mahāsahassī world-system." By this much, the Blessed One shows the "field of authority" (āṇākhetta). This is because within this range, the authority of the Āṭānāṭiya Paritta, Isigili Paritta, Dhajagga Paritta, Bojjhaṅga Paritta, Khandha Paritta, Mora Paritta, Metta Paritta, and Ratana Paritta prevails. "Yāvatā pana ākaṅkheyya" means as far as the place he might wish for. By these words...
211:
He shows the field of scope (visayakkhetta). Indeed, there is no limit or boundary to the field of scope of the Buddhas. Regarding this absence of limit, they cite this analogy: If one were to fill one hundred thousand crores of universes (cakkavāḷas) up to the Brahma realm with mustard seeds, and if a person were to travel through the eastern direction dropping one mustard seed in each universe, all those mustard seeds would be exhausted, but the universes in the eastern direction would not come to an end. The same principle applies to the south and other directions. In that field of scope, there is nothing that is not within the range (avisaya) of the Buddhas.

When this was said, the Elder Ānanda thought: "The Blessed One said, 'Ānanda, if the Tathāgata so desires, he can make his voice heard throughout the great trichiliocosm (tisahassī-mahāsahassī-lokadhātu), or as far as he desires.' However, this world is uneven, and the universes are infinite. While the sun is rising in one place, it is at the zenith in another, and setting in another. While it is the first watch of the night in one place, it is the middle watch in another, and the last watch in another. Furthermore, beings are preoccupied with their duties, preoccupied with play, and preoccupied with food; thus, for various reasons, they are distracted and heedless. How then will the Blessed One make them understand with his voice?"

Having thought thus, in order to cut off his doubt, he asked the Tathāgata, "How, then, [does this happen]?" and so forth. Then the Teacher, answering him, said, "Here, Ānanda, the Tathāgata..." and so forth. In that passage, "he would pervade it with radiance" means he would pervade it with the radiance of his body. But what would he do while pervading it? In the place where the sun is visible, he would make it set by his own psychic power. In the place where it is not visible, he would make it rise and place it in the middle (at the zenith). Then, in the place where the sun was visible, people would think, "The sun was just visible, and now it has set; is this the magic of the Nāgas, or is it some kind of magic of the bhūtas, yakkhas, or devatās?" In the place where the sun was not visible, people would think, "The sun had just set, and now it has risen again; is this some kind of magic of the Nāgas, bhūtas, yakkhas, or devatās?" Then, while those people are reflecting on the light and darkness and searching for the cause, saying, "Due to what reason is this happening?", the Teacher, [entering] the blue kasina (nīlakasiṇa)...
212:
The Blessed One would enter [the blue kasina] and spread a dense darkness. Why would he spread it? It is for the purpose of causing a sense of awe (saṃvega) in those beings who are preoccupied with various duties. Then, knowing that they have become awestruck, he would enter the white kasina attainment (odātakasiṇa-samāpatti) and, emitting pure and dense Buddha-rays, he would make the entire world a single mass of light in an instant, like the time when a thousand moons and a thousand suns rise simultaneously. And he does this by emitting radiance from a portion of his body only as large as a sesame seed. If a person were to make the earth of a universe the lamp-bowl, the water of the great ocean the oil, and Mount Sineru the wick, and having placed it on the summit of another Mount Sineru, were to light it, he would create light only within a single universe. Beyond that, he would not be able to illuminate even a span's distance. The Tathāgata, however, by emitting radiance from a portion of his body the size of a sesame seed, can make the great trichiliocosm (or even beyond that) a single mass of light. Such is the greatness of the Buddha's qualities.

"They would perceive that light" means that upon seeing that light, they would think, "The person who made the sun set and rise again, and who dispersed the dense darkness, is now standing here having created this light; oh, what an extraordinary man!" and they would sit down paying homage with joined palms. "He would make the sound heard" means he would make the sound of the Dhamma discourse heard. If a person were to make the mountain of a universe the drum, the great earth the drum-skin, and Mount Sineru the drumstick, and having placed it on the summit of another Mount Sineru, were to beat it, he would make that sound heard only within a single universe; he would not be able to make it pass even a span beyond that. The Tathāgata, however, sitting upon his seat or couch, can make his voice heard throughout the great trichiliocosm or even beyond. Such is the great power of the Tathāgatas. Thus, with these words, the Blessed One shows only the field of scope (visayakkhetta).

Upon hearing this lion's roar of the Buddha (buddhasīhanāda), a powerful joy (pīti) arose within the Elder Ānanda. Moved by the force of that joy and wishing to make an inspired utterance (udāna), he said, "It is a gain for me!" and so forth. In that passage, "My teacher is of such great power" means, "The attainment of such a teacher of great power is a gain for me and is well-attained." Or it means, "That I have the opportunity to carry the bowl and robes of such a teacher, to massage his feet and back, to offer water for washing his face and for bathing, to sweep the precinct of the Perfumed Chamber (gandhakuṭi), to ask questions when doubt arises, and to hear the sweet Dhamma—this is a great gain for me and is well-attained." It was with the understanding of having such a powerful Buddha and the privilege of serving him that he said, "Lābhā vata me" and so forth. Here, it should be understood that the Buddha's perfections, such as creating light and making his voice heard, are of immense power. Udāyī refers to the Elder Kāḷudāyī. That Elder had previously held a grudge against the Elder Ānanda, who was the attendant. Therefore, now seeing an opportunity at the end of the Buddha's lion-like speech, he wished to humble the Elder Ānanda, as if extinguishing a bright lamp or striking the tip of a bird's beak, and said, "Stop, friend [Ānanda]," and so forth. When the Elder Udāyī spoke thus, the Blessed One...
213:
"Hearing the sweet Dhamma... all these are gains for me and well-attained benefits," he said with this intention. In this context, the greatness of the Buddha's powers (iddhī), characterized by turning darkness into light and making sounds audible, should be understood as his possession of great psychic power (mahiddhikata). His great majesty (mahānubhāvata) should be understood through the pervasiveness of those very powers. Udāyī refers to the Elder Kāḷudāyī. It is said that he previously bore a grudge against the Elder Ānanda, who was the attendant. Therefore, having found an opportunity at the conclusion of this lion's roar of the Buddha, he spoke thus, wishing to destroy the Elder's devotion, like one extinguishing a bright lamp flame, like one striking the snout of a wandering ox, or like one overturning a platter filled with food.

When this was said, the Buddha—meaning, when this was said by the Elder Udāyī, the Buddha, like a well-wishing man standing in a safe place who repeatedly says, "Come this way, come this way," to a man standing and trembling on the edge of a precipice—likewise, wishing to restrain the Elder Udāyī from those words, said, "Do not say so, Udāyī; do not say so, Udāyī." In that statement, "hi" is a mere particle; it means "Do not speak thus." Mahārajjaṃ refers to the sovereignty of a universal monarch (cakkavatti). Did not the Teacher make the benefits of the devotion arising from the Dhamma teaching of a single disciple immeasurable? Why then does he limit the benefits of the devotion arising from this lion's roar of the Buddha? It is because of the extent of the noble disciple's (ariya-sāvaka) existence (attabhāva). For even a stream-enterer (sotāpanna) of dull wisdom obtains existence in the worlds of gods and humans seven times at most; therefore, wishing to define his destination (gati), the Buddha spoke thus. Diṭṭheva dhamme means while remaining in this very present existence. Parinibbāyissati means he will attain final Nibbāna through the Nibbāna that is free from any remaining conditions. Thus, crowning the discourse with Nibbāna, he concluded this Sīhanāda Sutta.

## The Third Chapter: Ānanda Chapter (Ānandavagga)

## (9) 4. The Chapter on Recluses (Samanavagga)

## 1. Commentary on the Samana Sutta

In the first sutta of the fourth chapter, samaniyāni means the possessions of a recluse. Samanakaraṇīyāni means the duties to be performed by a recluse. In the terms such as adhisīlasikkhāsamādānaṃ, samādānaṃ means undertaking or taking up. The undertaking and fulfilling of the training in higher virtue is called adhisīlasikkhāsamādāna.
214:
Undertaking the training in higher virtue (samādāna) means fulfilling it. The same method should be understood for the remaining two terms (undertaking the training in higher mind and higher wisdom). Here, the distinction between virtue (sīla) and higher virtue (adhisīla), mind (citta) and higher mind (adhicitta), wisdom (paññā) and higher wisdom (adhipaññā) should be understood. Among these, the five precepts are called virtue; in relation to them, the ten precepts are called higher virtue. In relation to those, the fourfold purification virtue (catupārisuddhisīla) is called higher virtue. Alternatively, all mundane (lokiya) virtue is called virtue, while supramundane (lokuttara) virtue is called higher virtue. Because it is to be trained in, it is called training (sikkhā).

The sense-sphere mind (kāmāvacara-citta) is called mind; in relation to it, the fine-material sphere mind (rūpāvacara-citta) is called higher mind. In relation to that, the immaterial sphere mind (arūpāvacara-citta) is also called higher mind. Alternatively, all mundane mind is just mind, while supramundane mind is higher mind. The same method applies to wisdom. Therefore (tasmā) means because these three duties of a recluse (samanakaraṇīya) exist, therefore. Intense (tibbo) means thick or strong desire. Desire (chando) means the wholesome desire (kusalachanda) characterized by the wish to act. Thus, in this sutta, the three trainings—both mundane and supramundane—are taught.

## 2. Commentary on the Gadrabha Sutta

In the second sutta, "piṭṭhito piṭṭhito" means from behind, from behind. "Ahampi dammo ahampi dammo" refers to the donkey following along while saying, "I too am a tamed ox." "Seyyathāpi gunnaṃ" means as it is with cows. For cows may be black, red, white, or other colors, but a donkey has no such color. Just as with the color, the sound and the footprints are also of a different nature. The remaining words have clear meanings. In this sutta also, the three trainings are taught in a mixed (mundane and supramundane) manner.

## 3. Commentary on the Khetta Sutta

In the third sutta, "paṭikacceva" means from the very beginning. "Sukaṭṭhaṃ karoti" means he plows well with a plow. "Sumatikataṃ" means well-leveled or well-prepared by means of intelligence. "Kālena" means at the proper time for sowing. The remaining words are clear. In this sutta also, the three trainings are taught in a mixed manner.
215:
## 4. Vajjiputtasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fourth sutta, 'Vajjiputtako' refers to the son of the Vajji royal family. 'Diyaḍḍhasikkhāpadasataṃ' refers to the one hundred training rules with fifty more (one hundred and fifty training rules). This was said in reference to the training rules prescribed at the time that monk was present. That monk was truly endowed with honesty, was of an upright nature, without crookedness, and not bent like a plow-handle. Therefore, he thought, "Will I be able to keep this many training rules or not?" and informed the Blessed One. 'Sakkoma'haṃ' means "I am able." That monk spoke thus, thinking, "For one who trains in this many training rules, it is not a heavy burden to train in the three trainings."

Then, the Blessed One, like one who binds a hundred bundles of grass and places them on the head of someone who cannot even carry fifty bundles, desired to give the other two trainings on top of the one training rule that the monk could not even practice. Thus, He spoke the words beginning with "Tasmātiha tvaṃ bhikkhu."

It is heard that a delicate countryman named Uttara lived at the Lohapāsāda monastery. Then, the young monks said, "Uttara, the fire hall is leaking; please provide suitable grass [for thatching]." He went to the forest to get grass, and after binding the grass he had cut into bundles, they asked, "Uttara, will you be able to take fifty bundles?" He replied, "I will not be able." When asked, "Will you be able to take eighty?" he said, "Venerable sirs, I will not be able." When asked, "Will you be able to take a hundred bundles?" he replied, "Yes, venerable sirs, I will take them." The young monks bound a hundred bundles and placed them on his head. He carried them, groaning as he went, and dropped them near the fire hall. Then the monks asked, "Uttara, are you exhausted?" He replied, "Yes, venerable sirs, the young monks have deceived me; they told me to carry fifty bundles when I could not even carry this hundred." The monks said, "Yes, Uttara, they have indeed deceived you." The fulfillment of this analogy should be understood in this way. In this sutta as well, only the three trainings, which are a mixture of mundane and supramundane, are taught.

## 5. Sekhasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fifth sutta, 'ujumaggānusārino' means a person (paṭipannaka) who practices following the Noble Path, which is called the straight path. 'Khayasmiṃ paṭhamaṃ ñāṇaṃ' means the first Path Knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) arises first. The Path is called 'khaya' (destruction) because it exhausts the defilements.
216:
The knowledge associated with the Path that exhausts those defilements is called 'khaya-ñāṇa' (knowledge in the destruction [of taints]). 'Tato aññā anantarā' means that immediately after that fourth Path Knowledge, another arises, meaning the Knowledge of the Fruition of Arahantship (arahatta-phala-ñāṇa) arises. 'Aññāvimuttassa' refers to one who is liberated through the liberation of the Fruition of Arahantship. 'Ñāṇaṃ ve hoti' refers to the arising of Reviewing Knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa). Thus, in both the sutta and the verses, the seven types of trainees (sekha) are taught. At the end, however, the Arahant (khīṇāsava) is shown.

## 6. Paṭhamasikkhāsutta-vaṇṇanā

In the sixth sutta, 'attakāmā' refers to those who desire their own welfare. 'Yatthetaṃ sabbaṃ samodhānaṃ gacchati' means the training rules in which all these one hundred and fifty training rules are included. 'Paripūrakārī hoti' means one who practices completely. 'Mattaso kārī' means one who practices to a certain extent; it means one cannot do everything in its entirety. 'Khuddānukhuddakāni' refers to the remaining training rules excluding the four Pārājikas. In that exclusion, Saṅghādisesa is called 'khuddaka' (minor), and Thullaccaya is called 'anukhuddaka' (lesser). Or, Thullaccaya is called 'khuddaka', and Pācittiya is called 'anukhuddaka'. Or, Pācittiya is called 'khuddaka', and Pāṭidesanī, Dukkaṭa, and Dubbhāsita are called 'anukhuddaka'. However, the teachers who preserve this Aṅguttara Nikāya say, "Excluding the four Pārājikas, all the remaining training rules are called minor and lesser rules (khuddānukhuddaka)."

Regarding the phrase 'tāni āpajjatipī vuṭṭhātipī', first, an Arahant (khīṇāsava) does not commit worldly faults (loka-vajja), but only commits prescribed faults (paṇṇatti-vajja). In committing them, they may do so by body, speech, or mind. Committing by body refers to rules such as Kuṭikāra and Sahaseyya. Committing by speech refers to rules such as Sañcaritta and Padasodhamma. Committing by mind refers to the rule of Rūpiyapaṭiggahaṇa (receiving money). The same principle applies to trainees (sekha).

"Monks, I have not taught that for a Noble Person (ariya-puggala) there is inability in committing such an offense or in rising from it." 'Ādibrahmacariyakāni' refers to the four great moral training rules which are the beginning of the holy life of the Path. 'Brahmacariyasāruppāni' means those same four training rules are suitable and appropriate for the fourfold Noble Path. 'Tattha' means in those training rules. 'Dhuvasīlo' means having constant virtue. 'Ṭhitasīlo' means having established virtue. 'Sotāpanno' means one who, by the Path called the 'Stream'...
217:
He is one who has attained the fruit. Avinipātadhamma means having the nature of not falling into the four lower realms. Niyata means being fixed by the certainty of the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga). Sambodhiparāyaṇa means having enlightenment, which is the three higher paths, as one's destination (resort).

Tanuttā means the state of being thin. For a Once-returner (sakadāgāmī), defilements such as lust (rāga) and others are thin like a layer of cloud or a fly's wing; they are not thick. Orambhāgiya refers to the things (dhamma) that belong to the lower part (the sensual realm). Saṃyojana means fetters. Parikkhaya means due to complete exhaustion (cutting off). 'He is opapātika' means he is one who is spontaneously reborn (in the Brahma realm). 'One who attains Nibbāna in that realm' (tatra parinibbāyī) means one who has the nature of attaining Nibbāna in the higher realm itself without descending to a lower realm. Anāvattidhamma means one who has the nature of not returning (to the lower sensual realm) by way of birth or destination (yoni-gati).

In the phrases such as padesaṃ padesakārī, the 'one who fulfills a part' (padesakārī) refers to the Stream-enterer, the Once-returner, and the Non-returner; such a person fulfills only a part (of virtue, etc.). The 'one who fulfills completely' (paripūrakārī) refers to the Arahant; such a person fulfills (virtue, etc.) completely. Avañjhāni means they are not in vain, they are fruitful, and they have the increase of benefit. In this discourse as well, the three trainings are taught in a mixed manner.

## 7. Dutiya-sikkhāsutta-vaṇṇanā

In the seventh discourse, kolaṃkola means one who goes from family to family (from life to life). Here, by the word kula, 'existence' (bhava) is intended; therefore, in the phrase 'two or three families,' the meaning should be understood as two or three existences. This kolaṃkola person runs through two or three existences, or at the most, up to six existences. Therefore, the distinction should be noted as two, three, four, five, or six existences. Ekabījī means 'one-seeded' because such a person has the seed of rebirth for only one existence.

In the terms such as uddhaṃsota, there is one who has the stream of craving that leads upwards and reaches the Akaniṭṭha realm; there is one who has the stream of craving that leads upwards but does not reach the Akaniṭṭha realm; there is one who does not have the stream of craving that leads upwards but reaches the Akaniṭṭha realm; and there is one who neither has the stream of craving that leads upwards nor reaches the Akaniṭṭha realm. Among them, the one who attains the fruit of non-returning in this world, is reborn in realms such as Aviha, stays there for the full lifespan, and then is reborn successively in higher and higher realms until reaching the Akaniṭṭha realm, is called an uddhaṃsota akaniṭṭhagāmī. However, the one who is reborn in realms such as Aviha, does not attain Nibbāna there, and without reaching the Akaniṭṭha realm, attains Nibbāna in a higher Brahma realm, is called one who is uddhaṃsota but not an akaniṭṭhagāmī. From here...
218:
...passing away, he is reborn only in the Akaniṭṭha realm; this person is called an uddhaṃsota akaniṭṭhagāmī. But the one who is reborn in any of the four realms starting with Aviha and attains Nibbāna right there is called neither an uddhaṃsota nor an akaniṭṭhagāmī.

One who, being born anywhere, attains Arahantship with exertion (saṅkhāra) and effort (payoga) is called a sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī. One who attains it without exertion and effort is called an asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī. One who is reborn in the Aviha realms where the lifespan is a thousand aeons, and after passing the middle of the lifespan, which is the five-hundredth aeon, attains Arahantship, is called an upahacca-parinibbāyī. The same method applies to the Atappa and other realms. Antarā-parinibbāyī refers to one who attains Nibbāna without passing the middle of the lifespan; such a person is of three types. First, among those reborn in the Aviha realms with a lifespan of a thousand aeons, some attain Arahantship on the very day of rebirth. If they do not attain it on the day of rebirth, they attain it at the end of the first hundred aeons; this person is called the first antarā-parinibbāyī. Another person, being unable to do so, attains it at the end of two hundred aeons; this is the second antarā-parinibbāyī. Another person, being even more unable, attains it at the end of four hundred aeons; this is the third antarā-parinibbāyī. The rest of the Atappa and other realms follow the same method as stated.

Standing at this point, twenty-four Stream-enterers, twelve Once-returners, forty-eight Non-returners, and twelve Arahants should be explained. In this Dispensation, there are two burdens: the burden of faith (saddhādhura) and the burden of wisdom (paññādhura). There are four modes of practice, such as the painful practice with slow intuition (dukkha-paṭipadā dandhābhiññā). Among them, one person applies himself through the burden of faith, attains the fruit of stream-entry, is reborn for only one more existence, and makes an end of the suffering of the round; this person is an ekabījī. He is of four types by way of the modes of practice. Just as this one who applies himself through faith is of four types, so too the one who applies himself through the burden of wisdom is of four types; thus, there are eight ekabījī Stream-enterers. Similarly, there are eight kolaṃkola and eight sattakkhattuparama; thus, they are called the twenty-four Stream-enterers. Among the three liberations (vimokkha), those who reach the stage of Once-returner through the emptiness liberation (suññata-vimokkha) are four by way of the four modes of practice. Similarly, there are four who reach it through the signless liberation (animitta-vimokkha) and four through the undirected liberation (appaṇihita-vimokkha); thus, these Once-returners are twelve. In the Aviha realms, there are five Non-returners: three antarā-parinibbāyī, one upahacca-parinibbāyī, and one uddhaṃsota akaniṭṭhagāmī. These five become ten by way of five asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī and five sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī. In the Atappa and other realms, there are also ten each. In the Akaniṭṭha realm, however, the uddhaṃsota...
219:
In the Akaniṭṭha realm, there are no Uddhaṃsota individuals; therefore, in that realm, there are 4 individuals who attain final Nibbāna with exertion (Sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī) and 4 individuals who attain final Nibbāna without exertion (Asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī), making a total of 8. Thus, there are 48 types of Non-returners (Anāgāmī). Just as there are 12 types of Once-returners (Sakadāgāmī), it should be understood that there are likewise 12 types of Arahants. In this sutta as well, only the three trainings (sikkhā) mixed with mundane and supramundane aspects are taught.

## 8. Tatiya-sikkhā-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the eighth sutta, the phrase "taṃ vā pana anabhisambhavaṃ appaṭivijjhanti" means not reaching that Fruition of Arahantship and not penetrating it. In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all places. In this sutta as well, only the three trainings mixed with mundane and supramundane aspects are taught. The ninth sutta has an obvious meaning. In this sutta as well, only the three trainings mixed with mundane and supramundane aspects are taught.

## 10. Dutiya-sikkhattaya-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, in the passage "āsavānaṃ khayā" (through the destruction of taints), the Path of Arahantship is called the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā). However, the Fruition of Arahantship should not and cannot be called "training" (sikkhā) because it arises for a person who has already completed the training.

"Yathā pure tathā pacchā" (as before, so after) means that just as one trains in the three trainings initially, one trains in the same way later. The same method applies to the second phrase. "Yathā adho tathā uddhaṃ" (as below, so above) means that just as one contemplates the lower part of the body by way of foulness (asubha), one similarly pervades and contemplates the upper part of the body. The same method applies to the second phrase. "Yathā divā tathā rattiṃ" (as by day, so by night) means that just as one practices the three trainings during the day, one similarly practices them at night. "Abhibhuyya disā sabbā" (overcoming all directions) means overcoming all directions by way of the object of meditation. "Appamāṇa-samādhinā" (by immeasurable concentration) means by the concentration associated with the Path of Arahantship.

"Sekha" (trainee) refers to a person who is still practicing along with the tasks to be done. "Paṭipadaṃ" refers to the person who practices. "Saṃsuddhacāriyaṃ" refers to a person with well-purified conduct, with perfectly pure virtue. "Sambuddhaṃ" refers to a person who has penetrated the Four Noble Truths. "Dhīraṃ paṭipadantaguṃ" refers to a person who is steadfast by way of being firm in the aggregates (khandha) and firm in the sense bases (āyatana), endowed with fortitude, and who has reached Nibbāna, the end of the practice. "Viññāṇassa" (of consciousness) refers to the consciousness called the final death-consciousness (cuti-citta). "Taṇhākkhayavimuttino" refers to the Arahant who is endowed with the liberation of the Fruition of Arahantship, known as liberation through the destruction of craving. "Pajjotasseva nibbānaṃ" means like the extinguishing of a lamp. "Vimokkho hoti cetaso" means the liberation of the mind, the state of non-occurrence, takes place. For the Arahant who is liberated through the destruction of craving...
221:
## (10) 5. Loṇakapallavagga

## 1. Commentary on the Accāyika Sutta

In the Accāyika Sutta, the first in the fifth chapter, *accāyikāni* means very urgent matters. *Karaṇīyāni* means duties that must definitely be performed. In fact, a matter that does not necessarily have to be done is called *kicca* (business/task). A matter that must definitely be done is called *karaṇīya* (duty). *Sīghaṃ sīghaṃ* means quickly (with speed). In the phrase "*tassa kho taṃ*", *taṃ* is merely a particle. "*Na tthi sā iddhi vā ānubhāvo vā*" means that there is no such power or influence that can cause sprouting on that very day. *Uttarasve* means on the third day. *Utupariṇāminī* means having the transformation of the obtained season. *Jāyanti* means that on the third day, white sprouts appear; when seven days are reached, green sprouts appear. *Gabbhīnīpi honti* means that after reaching one and a half months, they become "pregnant" (the ears of grain emerge). *Paccanti* means that after reaching three months, they ripen.

Now, although the Buddhas have no need for householders or crops, they bring forth various similes to demonstrate persons or meanings in the Dispensation that are comparable to those householders and crops. Therefore, to show the meaning for which this simile was brought, He said, "*Evameva kho*" and so on. This statement is clear in its meaning. As for training (*sikkhā*), in this sutta as well, it is taught as a mixture of mundane and supramundane.

## 2. Commentary on the Paviveka Sutta

In the second sutta, *cīvarapavivekaṃ* means seclusion from the defilements that arise on account of robes. The same method should be understood for the remaining two: *piṇḍapātapaviveka* and *senāsanapaviveka*. *Sāṇāni* are cloths woven from hemp. *Masāṇāni* are mixed cloths. *Chavadussāni* are cloths discarded from corpses, or garments made by stitching together *eraka* grass and so on. *Paṃsukūlāni* are rags discarded on the ground. *Tirīṭāni* are garments made from tree bark. *Ajināni* are antelope skins. *Ajinakkhipaṃ* is that same antelope skin split down the middle; it is also said to be an antelope skin with the hooves attached. *Kusacīraṃ* is a garment made by stitching together *kusa* grass. The same applies to bark-fiber robes (*vākacīra*) and wood-shaving robes (*phalakacīra*). *Kesakambalaṃ* is a blanket made of human hair. *Vālakambalaṃ* is a blanket made of horse-tail hair and so on. *Ulūkapakkhikaṃ* is a garment made by stitching together owl feathers.
222:
*Sākabhakkhā* means one who habitually eats fresh vegetables. *Sāmākabhakkhā* means one who habitually eats millet grain. Among the words beginning with *nīvāra*, *nīvāra* refers to a type of grain that grows spontaneously in the forest. *Daddula* is the scrapings discarded by leather-workers after scraping skins. *Haṭa* refers to resin, or moss, or the sap of trees such as the *kaṇikāra*. *Kaṇa* is rice bran (or broken rice). *Ācāma* is the burnt rice crust sticking to the rice pot. They take and eat that rice from the place where it was discarded; it is also called rice-scum. *Piññāka* (sesame cake) and so on are clear enough. *Pavattaphalabhojī* means one who habitually eats fruit that has fallen naturally. *Bhusāgāra* is a threshing floor.

*Sīlavā* means one endowed with the fourfold purification virtue. *Dussīlyañcassa pahīnaṃ hoti* means that the five types of immorality have been abandoned. *Sammādiṭṭhiko* means one who has right view. *Micçhādiṭṭhi* is wrong view. *Āsavā* refers to the four taints. *Aggappatto* means one who has reached the summit of virtue. *Sārappatto* means one who has reached the essence of virtue. *Suddho* means one who is perfectly pure. *Sāre patiṭṭhito* means one who is established in the essence of virtue, concentration, and wisdom.

*Seyyathāpi* means "just as if" or "for example". *Sampannaṃ* means being full of completely ripe sali rice. *Saṅgharāpeyya* means he would have it gathered. *Ubbahāpeyya* means he would have it carried to the threshing floor. *Bhusikaṃ* is chaff. *Koṭṭāpeyya* means he would have it put into a mortar and pounded with pestles. *Aggappattāni* means reaching the state of the best rice. The same method applies to words like *sārappatta* and so on. The remaining words are clear. Here, the statement "immorality is abandoned and wrong view is abandoned" should be understood as referring to the state of having abandoned them through the Path of Stream-entry.

## 3. Commentary on the Sarada Sutta

In the third sutta, *viddhe* means when the clouds have cleared and moved far away. *Deve* means in the sky. *Abhivihacca* means having dispelled. *Yato* means at which time. *Virajaṃ* is so called because it is free from the dust of lust and so on. Because it is free from those stains, it is called *vītamalaṃ* (stainless). *Dhammacakkhuṃ* is the eye of the Path of Stream-entry that perceives the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. *Na tthi taṃ saṃyojanaṃ* means that for that person, those two types of fetters no longer exist; or it is said they do not exist because the remaining fetters are unable to bring one back to this sensual realm again. In this sutta, the "Non-returner through Jhana" (*jhānānāgāmī*) is discussed.

## 4. Commentary on the Parisa Sutta

In the fourth sutta, *na bāhulikā honti* means they are not those who practice to increase the four requisites. *Na sāthalikā* means they do not practice the three trainings laxly. In the word *okkamanne*, the five hindrances are called *okkamana* because of their nature to cause one to fall down. They have laid down the burden regarding those five hindrances that cause the three trainings to fall away. *Pavivekepubbaṅgamā* means they are led by the three kinds of seclusion: physical seclusion, mental seclusion, and seclusion from the substrata of existence. *Vīriyaṃ āraddhaṃ* means they arouse and exert two types of energy. *Appattassa* is for the sake of attaining the extraordinary states not yet reached, namely Jhana, Insight, Path, and Fruition. The same applies to the remaining two terms. *Anugatiṃ āpajjati* means that pupils such as co-residents (*saddhivihārika*) and apprentices (*antevāsika*) follow the actions performed by their teachers and preceptors, reaching a state of following whatever behaviors they see in their teachers and preceptors. *Ayaṃ vuccati bhikkhave aggavatī parisā* means, "Monks, this assembly is called the foremost assembly."
223:
The five hindrances (nīvaraṇas) are called 'okkamana' (descending) because they have the nature of causing one to descend; in these hindrances, the burden has been laid down. They are the precursors in the three types of seclusion (viveka), namely: physical seclusion (kāya-viveka), mental seclusion (citta-viveka), and seclusion from the substrata of existence (upadhi-viveka). They also exert and uphold the two types of energy (viriya). They strive to attain the extraordinary Dhamma that has not yet been attained, known as jhāna, insight (vipassanā), the Path (magga), and the Fruition (phala). In the remaining two phrases, the method should be understood in this same way. 'Later generations' (pacchimā janatā) refers to resident pupils, students, and so forth. They follow the example of the actions performed by their teachers and preceptors. When that group of disciples follows the example of whatever actions they have seen in their teachers and preceptors, it is called 'following the example of what is seen' (diṭṭhānu-gatiṃ āpajjanti). Monks, this assembly is called an assembly of foremost persons (aggavatī parisā).

'Having become quarrelsome, having become contentious' means having developed quarrels and strife. In this context, 'bhaṇḍana' (quarrel) refers to the preliminary stage of strife (verbal quarreling), while 'kalaha' (strife) refers to the transgression by way of physical contact, such as using the hands. 'Having fallen into disputes' means having arrived at opposing views. Harsh words are called 'mouth-weapons' (mukhasatti) because they pierce and destroy virtues; they live piercing one another with those mouth-weapons. 'Harmonious, rejoicing together, blending like milk and water' means being united, having equal joy, and being as one like milk and water. They look at each other with peaceful eyes of loving-kindness. The fivefold joy (pīti) arises. Both the mental body (nāma-kāya) and the physical body (rūpa-kāya) become free from distress. Having a tranquil body, one experiences the happiness of both body and mind. The mind becomes well-concentrated on the object.

'With large raindrops' means with great drops of rain. In the phrase 'mountain clefts, rifts, and gullies' (pabbata-kandara-padara-sākhā), 'kandara' (cleft) refers to a mountain region split or broken by water, which is also called 'nitamba' (mountain slope) or 'nadikuñja' (river-bend). 'Padara' (rift) refers to a place where the earth is cracked when it has not rained for eight months. 'Sākhā' (gullies) refers to small channels flowing into small pools. 'Kusobbha' refers to small pits or puddles. 'Mahāsobbha' refers to large pits or pools. 'Kunnadi' refers to small rivers. 'Mahānadi' refers to great rivers such as the Ganges and the Yamuna.
224:
## 5-7. Commentary on the First Ājānīya Sutta, etc.
97-99. In the fifth sutta, 'by factors' (aṅgehi) means by the factors of virtue. 'Worthy of a king' (rājāraha) means worthy of and suitable for a king. 'A king's possession' (rājabhogga) means being an object of use for a king. 'A limb of a king' (rañño aṅgaṃ) means it is designated as a 'limb' because it is comparable to the king's own limbs, such as hands and feet. 'Endowed with beauty' (vaṇṇasampanno) means endowed with physical beauty. 'Endowed with strength' (balasampanno) means endowed with physical strength. 'Worthy of offerings' (āhuneyyo) means worthy of receiving almsfood known as 'āhuti'. 'Worthy of hospitality' (pāhuneyyo) means suitable for food prepared for guests. 'Worthy of gifts' (dakkhiṇeyyo) means suitable for the offering (dakkhiṇā) known as a gift of faith, given by way of relinquishing the ten types of gift-objects. 'Worthy of reverential salutation' (añjalikaraṇīyo) means suitable for receiving the raising of joined palms. 'An unsurpassed field of merit for the world' (anuttaraṃ puṇṇakkhettaṃ lokassa) means a place where the seeds of merit of the entire world grow without equal.

'Endowed with beauty' (vaṇṇasampanno) [in a spiritual sense] means endowed with the beauty of virtue. 'Endowed with strength' (balasampanno) means endowed with the strength of energy (viriya). 'Endowed with speed' (javasampanno) means endowed with the speed of wisdom (ñāṇa). 'Possessing power' (thāmavā) means one who is endowed with the power of wisdom. 'Of firm endeavor' (daḷhaparakkamo) means of steadfast endeavor. 'One who has not laid down the burden' (anikkhittadhuro) means one whose burden is not set down, whose burden is upheld; it refers to one who practices with the resolve: 'I shall not lay down the burden of energy until I have reached the highest fruit, Arahantship.' In this fifth sutta, the Path of Stream-entry is described by way of the Four Noble Truths, and the endowment with the speed of wisdom is described by way of the Path of Stream-entry. In the sixth sutta, the three higher Paths and the three higher Fruitions are described, and the endowment with the speed of wisdom is described by way of those three Paths and Fruitions. In the seventh sutta, the Fruition of Arahantship is described, and the task of the Path is described by way of the Fruition of Arahantship itself. The Fruition may also be called 'speed' (java) because it arises with the speed of the impulsion (javana).

## 8. Commentary on the Potthaka Sutta
In the eighth sutta, 'new' (nava) is said in reference to its manufacture. 'Potthaka' refers to cloth made of bark. 'Medium' (majjhimo) means of medium use. 'Old' (jiṇṇo) means worn out by use. 'Wiping the pot' (ukkhaliparimajjanaṃ) means wiping the rice pot. 'Immoral' (dussīlo) means devoid of virtue. 'Ugliness' (dubbaṇṇatā) means being unattractive due to the absence of the beauty of virtue. 'Following the example of what is seen' (diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjanti) means they imitate the actions performed by that person. 'Not of great fruit' (na mahapphalaṃ) means not of great fruit by way of the resultant fruit. 'Not of great benefit' (na mahānisaṃsaṃ) means not of great benefit by way of the resultant benefit.
225:
Appagghatāya means because of having little value in terms of the value of the result. Kāsikaṃ vatthaṃ refers to cloth made by twisting three cotton threads together, and that cloth is produced only in the Kāsī region. The remaining words are clear. In this sutta, virtue (sīla) mixed with mundane and supramundane is spoken of.

## 9. Loṇakapalla Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the ninth sutta, yathā yathāyaṃ should be analyzed as yathā yathā ayaṃ. Tathā tathā taṃ means that kamma in such and such a manner. The meaning is this: If someone says, "In whatever way a person performs kamma, in that same way he experiences its result. Because it is not possible to prevent the result of a performed kamma, however much kamma he performs, he must experience the result of that much kamma."

Evaṃ santaṃ means "if this were so." Brahmacariyavāso na hoti means that because the kamma to be experienced in the next life (upapajjavedanīya kamma) performed before the development of the Path must inevitably be experienced, even if the holy life (brahmacariya) is lived, it is as if it were not lived. Okāso na paññāyati sammā dukkhassa antakiriyāya means that if this were so, because that person is both accumulating kamma and experiencing results, by that method, no opportunity is seen for making a complete end of the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭadukkha).

Yathā yathā vedanīyaṃ means in whatever manner it is to be experienced. Tathā tathāssa vipākaṃ paṭisaṃvediyati means in that same manner he experiences its result. The meaning is this: Among the seven impulsive moments (javana), the kamma in the first javana, if conditions are present, gets its turn to ripen and becomes kamma to be experienced in the present life (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya kamma); if conditions are absent, it is called lapsed kamma (ahosikamma). The kamma in the seventh javana, if conditions are present, becomes kamma to be experienced in the next life (upapajjavedanīya kamma); if conditions are absent, it is called lapsed kamma. The kamma in the middle five javanas becomes kamma to be experienced in subsequent lives (aparāpariyavedanīya kamma) as long as the round of rebirths continues. Among these manners, in whatever manner kamma is to be experienced, this man performs that kamma; in that same manner he experiences its result. In the Commentary, only kamma that has obtained its turn to ripen is called yathāvedanīya kamma. "Monks, if this were so, the living of the holy life is possible" means that because there is the possibility of kamma that can be exhausted by the Path which makes an end of kamma, it is called living (vāsa); such a statement is well-spoken.
226:
Hoti is the meaning. Okāso paññāyati sammā dukkhassa antakiriyāya means: because if this were so, through the cessation of the volitional consciousness (abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇa) by means of various Paths, the suffering of the round of rebirths does not arise in future lives; therefore, the opportunity for making a complete end of suffering is clearly manifest.

Now, wishing to show the nature of kamma whose result is to be experienced in such a manner, he said, "Monks, here a certain person," and so on. In that statement, appamattakaṃ means small, slight, or inferior. Tādisaṃyeva means just like that. Diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṃ means it is called so when it gets its turn to ripen in the very life in which that kamma was performed. Nāṇupi khāyati means it is not manifest even slightly in the second existence (attabhāva); it means it does not give even a tiny result in the second existence. Bahudeva means "how much more then would it give a great result?" By the terms such as abhāvitakāyo, an ordinary person (puthujjana) who is devoid of physical development (kāyabhāvanā) and who goes along the round of rebirths is shown. Paritto means one with little virtue. Appātumo: ātuma refers to the self or body (attabhāva); although that body is large, because of the smallness of virtue, he is just appātumo (one with a small self). Appadukkhavihārī means one who dwells in suffering even due to a small evil.

By the terms such as bhāvitakāyo, the Arahant is shown. That Arahant is called bhāvitakāyo because his body is developed through physical development known as contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā). Or, he is bhāvitakāyo because of the growth of the form-body (rūpakāya). Bhāvitasīlo means one with developed virtue. The same method should be understood for the remaining two terms. Or, he is called bhāvitakāyo through development occurring at the five sense-doors. By this term bhāvitakāyo, virtue of restraint of the senses (indriyasaṃvarasīla) is meant, and by the term bhāvitasīlo, the remaining three types of virtue are meant. Aparitto means one who does not have little virtue. Mahatto means although the body is small, because of the greatness of virtue, he is called mahatto (great-souled). Appamāṇavihārī is just a name for the Arahant. That Arahant is called appamāṇavihārī because of the absence of lust (rāga), etc., which make limits.

Paritte means small. Udakamallake means in a water-cup. Orabbhiko means a sheep-owner. Urabbhaghātako means a butcher. Jāpetuṃ vā means to cause loss through loss of property. Although there is a variant reading jhāpetuṃ, it has this same meaning. Yathāpaccayaṃ vā kātuṃ means to do as one wishes. Urabbhadhanaṃ means wealth equal to the value of a sheep. If he wishes, he gives; if he does not wish, by the neck...
228:
"Bhikkhus, there is that occasion"—in this text, 'occasion' (samaya) refers to the time of obtaining these five suitable factors (sappāya): suitable weather, suitable food, suitable lodging, a suitable person, and hearing the Dhamma. "That mind" refers to that insight-mind (vipassanā-citta) at that time. "It stands well only within oneself" means it stands only in oneself. Here, what occurs within oneself is called 'internal' (ajjhatta). The internal object (gocarajjhatta) is also appropriate. It means that having abandoned various diverse objects, it stands only in the single object of Nibbāna. "Sannisīdati" means it settles down well. "Ekodihoti" means it becomes one-pointed. "Samādhiyati" means it is well-placed. In the terms beginning with "santo," it is 'peaceful' (santa) because of the stilling of opposing defilements. It is 'sublime' (paṇīta) in the sense of being non-distressing. It is 'obtained by stilling' (paṭippassaddhaladdho) because it is obtained through the stilling of defilements. It is 'attained to the state of singleness' (ekodibhāvādhigato) because it has reached the state of one-pointedness. It is not 'restrained by forceful suppression' (sasaṅkhāraniggayhavāritagato) because it arises at the end of cutting off defilements and not by suppressing and restraining defilements with effort. By this much, this bhikkhu is said to have escaped the round and reached Arahantship.

Now, wishing to show the practice for direct knowledge of one who is an Arahant, he said the words beginning with "yassa yassa ca." In that text, "abhiññā sacchikaraṇīyassa" refers to that which is to be realized by knowing with direct knowledge. "Sati satiāyatane" means when there is a cause, whether it be the cause known as a past cause or the cause consisting of the basis of direct knowledge such as jhāna which is to be obtained now. In detail, however, this discussion on direct knowledge should be understood in the manner already stated in the Visuddhimagga. Here, the words beginning with "āsavānaṃ khayā" (through the destruction of taints) should be understood as being spoken by way of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti).

## 11. Nimittasuttavaṇṇanā

In the eleventh Sutta also, 'higher mind' (adhicitta) is just the mind of serenity and insight. "Tīṇi nimittāni" means three causes. "Kālena kālaṃ" means from time to time, meaning at the appropriate time. In the words beginning with "the sign of concentration (samādhinimitta) should be attended to from time to time," it means that having noted each appropriate time, one-pointedness should be attended to at the time suitable for one-pointedness. For here, one-pointedness (ekaggatā) is called the 'sign of concentration.' The definition of the term there is: concentration itself is the sign, thus 'sign of concentration.' In the other two terms also, this is the method. 'Exertion' (paggaho) is a name for energy (vīriya), and 'equanimity' (upekkhā) is a name for the state of neutrality (majjhattabhāva).
229:
Therefore, at the time suitable for exerting energy, energy should be attended to; at the time suitable for neutrality, one should stand in the state of neutrality. "That mind has a cause for it to become lazy" means there exists a cause by which that mind might stand in a state of laziness. In the other cases also, this is the method. In the passage "upekkhānimittaṃyeva manasi kareyya," the meaning is that one should look on with equanimity at the speed of knowledge (ñāṇajava). "Āsavānaṃ khayāya" means for the sake of the fruit of Arahantship.

"Ukkaṃ bandheyya" means he should prepare the furnace. "Ālimpeyya" means he should put coals in that furnace, light the fire, and by blowing with a tube, make the fire burn. "Ukkāmukhe pakkhipeyya" means having moved the coals aside, he should place it on top of the coals or place it in a crucible (mūsā). "Ajjhupekkhati" means he observes whether it is cooked or uncooked.

"Sammā samādhiyati āsavānaṃ khayāya" means the mind is well-placed for the sake of the fruit of Arahantship. By this sequence of words, the bhikkhu who has developed insight and reached Arahantship is shown. Now, wishing to show the sequence of direct knowledge of that Arahant, he said the words beginning with "yassa yassa ca." That should be understood in the manner already stated below.
