## 3. Tatiyapaṇṇāsakaṃ
## (11) 1. Sambodhavagga
## 1. Pubbevasambodhasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the Tatiyapaṇṇāsaka, the phrase "Pubbeva sambodhā" means at the very beginning of realizing the Four Noble Truths, occurring only after the attainment of the Noble Path (Ariya Magga). "Anabhisambuddhassa" refers to one who has not yet penetrated and realized the Four Noble Truths. "Bodhisattasseva sato" refers to being a creature who will awaken, a person striving to attain Supreme Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi), or one who is attached to the Noble Path known as Supreme Enlightenment.

Indeed, from the time the aspiration for Buddhahood was fulfilled through the meeting of the eight factors at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, the Tathāgata became attached to Supreme Enlightenment. Because he came without relinquishing the supreme effort to attain that Supreme Enlightenment, thinking, "I must reach this Supreme Enlightenment," he is called a "Bodhisatta."

"Ko nu kho" means "What indeed?" "Loko" refers to the world of formations (saṅkhāraloka). "Assādo" refers to the aspect of gratification or sweetness. "Ādīnavo" refers to the aspect of danger or that which is not to be delighted in. "Tassa mayhaṃ" means "to me who was such a Bodhisatta." "Chandāragavinaya chandāragappahāna" means that by depending on Nibbāna, desire and lust (chandarāga) come to an end and are abandoned. Therefore, Nibbāna is called the "removal of desire and lust" and the "abandoning of desire and lust." "Idaṃ lokanissaraṇaṃ" means this Nibbāna is called "escape from the world" (lokanissaraṇa) because it is the exit from the world of formations. "Yāvakīvaṃ" means "for as long as." "Abbaññāsiṃ" means "I knew through the superior knowledge of the Noble Path." By both terms "Ñāṇañca pana me dassanaṃ," the knowledge of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇāñāṇa) is meant. The remaining words in this sutta are clear.

## 2. Paṭhama-assādasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, "Assādapariyesanaṃ acariṃ" means "I wandered for the purpose of seeking gratification (pleasure)." From when? Starting from the time of being the hermit Sumedha. "Paññāya" means through the Path-wisdom (maggapaññā) together with insight (vipassanā). "Sudiṭṭho" means well-penetrated and known. In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all instances. The third sutta is entirely clear.
231:
## 4. Samaṇabrāhmaṇasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, "Sāmaññattha" refers to the four Noble Fruits (Ariya Phala). The other term (brahmaññattha) is a synonym for that same Sāmaññattha. Alternatively, Sāmaññattha refers to the four Paths (Magga), and Brahmaññattha refers to the four Fruits (Phala). In all four of these suttas, only the world of aggregates (khandhaloka) is taught.

## 5. Ruṇṇasutta-vaṇṇanā
The fifth sutta was set forth (taught) because a specific incident arose. What was the incident? It was due to the improper conduct of the group of six monks (chabbaggiya). Those monks were wandering about singing, dancing, and laughing. The monks reported this to the Buddha, the Possessor of Ten Powers (Dasabala). The Teacher summoned those monks and began (taught) this sutta for the purpose of admonishing them.

In that sutta, "Ruṇṇa" means weeping. "Ummattaka" refers to the behavior of a madman. "Komāraka" refers to actions that should be done by children. "Dantavidamsakahasita" means laughing loudly while showing the teeth and clapping the hands. "Setughāto gīte" indicates, "Let there be the destruction of the causes (of defilements) in your singing; abandon singing that is accompanied by such causes." The same principle applies to dancing. "Alaṃ" means it is very proper. In the phrase "Dhammappamoditānaṃ sataṃ," the word "Dhamma" refers to a cause; it refers to the (smiling) of virtuous people who are joyful due to some righteous cause. "Sitaṃ sitamattāya" means when there is a reason to smile, whatever smile you make, it is only proper for you, dear sons, to smile just enough to show the front teeth and display a pleasant manner.

## 6. Atittisutta-vaṇṇanā
In the sixth sutta, "Soppassa" refers to sleeping. "No satisfaction in indulging" means that however much one indulges, one still desires it; there is no such thing as satisfaction. The same principle applies to the remaining two terms. If the water in the great ocean were liquor, and a drunkard were reborn as a fish there, that fish would never find satisfaction whether swimming or sleeping in that ocean. In this sutta, only the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) is taught.

## 7. အရက္ခိတသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ
In the seventh sutta, "Avassuta" means being wet (with defilements). "Not a good death" means it is not a good death because it is a condition for rebirth in the lower realms (apāya). "Kālakiriyā" is a synonym for that death. In the bright side (sukkapakkha), it is a good death because it is a condition for rebirth in the celestial realm...
232:
It is the attainment of good kamma. That good kamma, which is free from the rot of defilements, is indeed suitable only for the three noble disciples, starting with the Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna). The remaining words in this sutta are clear.

## 8. Vyāpanna Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the eighth sutta, 'vyāpanna' refers to that which exists having abandoned its natural state. The rest is as explained in the previous sutta.

## 9. Paṭhama Nidāna Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, 'nidānāni' means causes. 'Kammānaṃ samudayāya' means for the purpose of accumulating kammas that lead to the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa). 'Lobhapakataṃ' means that which is done through greed. 'Sāvajjaṃ' means that which is blameworthy. 'Taṃ kammaṃ kammasamudayāya saṃvattati' means that kamma leads to the arising and accumulation of other kammas that lead to the round of rebirth. 'Na taṃ kammaṃ kammanirodhāya' means that kamma does not lead to the cessation of kammas that lead to the round of rebirth. In the wholesome side (sukkapakkha), 'kammānaṃ samudayāya' means for the purpose of the arising of kammas that lead away from the round of rebirth (vivaṭṭa). In this way, the entire meaning should be understood.

## 10. Dutiya Nidāna Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, 'kammānaṃ' refers only to kammas leading to the round of rebirth. 'Chandarāgaṭṭhāniye' means occurring in things that are causes for lustful desire (chandarāga). 'Ārabbha' means depending on, intending, or because of. 'Chando' means the desire of craving. 'Yo cetaso sārāgo' means whatever nature of attachment or clinging of the mind exists; the Buddha says that such attachment is a 'fetter' (saṃyojana) or a 'bond' (bandhana). In the wholesome side, 'kammānaṃ' refers to kammas leading away from the round of rebirth. 'Tadabhinivatteti' means it brings about that future result. Or, when that result (vipāka) is known and understood, at that time it brings about both the causes of that lustful desire and that result. By this word, Insight (Vipassanā) is shown. By the word 'tadabhinivattetvā', the Path (Magga) is shown. By the word 'cetasā abhinivijjhitvā', the Path is also shown. 'Paññāya ativijjha passati' means one sees by piercing through defilements with Path-wisdom along with Insight. Thus, the meaning should be understood in all respects. In this sutta, the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) and the ending of the round (vivaṭṭa) are taught.

## Sambodhavaggo Paṭhamo.
233:
## (12) 2. Āpāyika Vagga

## 1. Āpāyika Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the second chapter, they are called 'āpāyika' because they will go to the planes of misery (apāya). They are called 'nerayika' because they will go to hell (niraya). "Without abandoning this" means without giving up these three evil states, such as the false claim of leading a holy life. "One who claims to lead a holy life" refers to one who pretends to be a person leading a holy life, or one who, without abandoning their appearance, claims, "I too am one who leads a holy life." "Destroys" (anuddhaṃseti) means to abuse, threaten, and accuse. "There is no fault in sensual pleasures" means there is no fault for one who indulges in objective sensuality (vatthukāma) with defiled sensuality (kilesakāma). "The state of being fit to drink" means the state of being fit to be drunk or consumed; it is the state of being fit to be consumed just as a thirsty person drinks water with a mind free from hesitation. In this sutta, only the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) is taught.

## 2. Dullabha Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, "one who is grateful and appreciative" refers to a person who, knowing the deed done by another, thinking "this person has done me a favor," makes it known and performs a return favor.

## 3. Appameyya Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, it is called 'suppameyya' because it is easily measured. It is called 'duppameyya' because it is difficult to measure. It is called 'appameyya' because it is impossible to measure. "One who hoists the banner of pride" means one who has pride like a tall reed (naḷa), meaning one who lives hoisting up empty, essence-less pride. "Frivolous" (capala) means one endowed with frivolous behavior such as decorating the alms-bowl. "Rough-mouthed" (mukhara) means one who has harsh speech. "One with scattered speech" means one whose speech is unrestrained. "Unconcentrated" means one devoid of one-pointedness of mind. "One with a wandering mind" means one whose mind is unstable, like an unstable cow or an unstable wild deer. "One who does not guard the faculties" means one whose faculties are wide open. The remaining words in this sutta are clear.

## 4. Āneñja Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, "relishes that jhāna" means relishing that Ākāsānañcāyatana jhāna. "Desires that jhāna" means longing for that very jhāna. "Attains joy through that jhāna" means reaching gladness through that jhāna. "One who stands in that jhāna" means one who abides in that jhāna. "One who is inclined toward that jhāna" means one who is solely bent toward that jhāna. "One who dwells frequently in that jhāna" means one who spends much time with that jhāna. "Enters into association with" means reaching a state of being together, referring to being reborn in that celestial realm.
234:
The meaning is: regarding the phrase 'goes to hell' etc., it is said with reference to going to that hellish realm by way of aparāpariya-kamma (kamma to be experienced in a subsequent life), as one is not yet liberated from hell and so forth. This is because for a person born in the realm of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana), there is no unwholesome kamma stronger than access concentration (upacāra-jhāna) that could cause rebirth in the lower realms in the immediately following life. 'A disciple of the Blessed One' refers to any one of the individuals: a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna), a Once-returner (sakadāgāmi), or a Non-returner (anāgāmi). 'In that very existence' means in that very formless realm (arūpa-bhava). 'Attains final Nibbāna' means attaining final Nibbāna through the Nibbāna without conditions (appaccaya-parinibbāna). 'Adhippayāsa' means excessive effort. The remaining points here should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. In this sutta, the upappatti-jhāna (rebirth-producing jhāna) is taught for the worldling (puthujjana), while for the noble disciple (ariya-sāvaka), both that upappatti-jhāna and the vipassanā-pādaka-jhāna (jhāna as a basis for insight) are taught.

## 5. Vipattisampadāsutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, 'sīla-vipatti' refers to the state of failure in virtue. The same method applies to the remaining two. The phrase 'there is no gift given' is said with reference to the absence of fruit from the gift given. A great offering associated with much effort is called 'yiṭṭha'. 'Huta' refers to the requisites respectfully given to beloved guests. Both yiṭṭha and huta are rejected with reference only to the absence of fruit. 'Sukata-dukkaṭānaṃ' means the meaning of wholesome deeds well done and unwholesome deeds poorly done. 'Phalaṃ vipāko' means that whatever is called 'fruit' (phala) or 'result' (vipāka), he says that such a result does not exist.

'This world does not exist' means that for a being staying in the world beyond, this present world does not exist. 'The world beyond does not exist' means that for a being staying in this present world, the world beyond does not exist. It shows the meaning that all beings are annihilated right in their respective places of birth. 'There is no mother, there is no father' is said by way of the absence of fruit from right conduct or wrong conduct towards those parents. 'There are no spontaneously born (opapātika) beings' means there are no such things as beings who are born after passing away. 'Sampadā' means fulfillment. 'Sīla-sampadā' means the state of fulfillment and non-deficiency of virtue. The same method applies to the remaining two. The phrase 'there is a gift given' etc. should be understood by the method opposite to what was stated.

## 6. Apaṇṇakasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the sixth sutta, 'apaṇṇaka maṇi' refers to a die with six sides. 'Sugati sagga' refers to any one of the heavenly worlds such as the Cātumahārājika. In this sutta, both virtue (sīla) and right view (sammādiṭṭhi) are taught in combination. The seventh sutta is quite clear in its meaning.
235: ## 8. Paṭhamasoceyyasutta-vaṇṇanā In the eighth sutta, 'soceyyāni' means states of purity. 'Kāya-soceyya' means purity in the body-door. In the remaining two terms (vacī-soceyya and mano-soceyya), the method is the same. In these four successive suttas, the practice for laypeople (agārika-paṭipadā) is taught. This practice is also suitable for those who are Sekhas (trainees), such as Sotāpannas and Sakadāgāmīs. ## 9. Dutiyasoceyyasutta-vaṇṇanā In the ninth sutta, 'ajjhattaṃ' means states arising within one's own continuity. 'Kāmacchanda' refers to the hindrance of sensual desire (kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa). In the case of hindrances such as ill-will (byāpāda) and others, the method is the same. The remaining meanings in this sutta are just as explained below. In the verse, however, 'kāya-suci' means purity in the body-door or being pure by body. In the remaining two terms, the method is the same. 'Ninhātapāpakaṃ' refers to one who stands having washed away and cleansed all evils. Through this sutta and the verse, only the Arahant (khīṇāsava) is spoken of. ## 10. Moneyyasutta-vaṇṇanā In the tenth sutta, 'moneyyāni' means states of a sage (muni-bhāva). 'Kāya-moneyya' means the state of a sage, a good state, or a wise state in the body-door. In the remaining two terms, the method is the same. 'Monks, this is called kāya-moneyya' refers to the abandoning of the three bodily misconducts as kāya-moneyya. Alternatively, the three bodily good conducts are also called kāya-moneyya. Similarly, knowledge (ñāṇa) taking the physical body as object, full understanding (pariññā) of the body, the path (magga) associated with full understanding, the abandoning of desire and lust (chandarāga) for the body, and the attainment of the fourth jhāna where bodily formations (kāya-saṅkhāra) cease are all called kāya-moneyya. The same applies to vacī-moneyya (verbal sagehood). The distinction here is: just as the fourth jhāna attainment is kāya-moneyya, in vacī-moneyya, the second jhāna attainment where verbal formations (vacī-saṅkhāra) cease should be known as vacī-moneyya. For mano-moneyya (mental sagehood), knowing the meaning in this same way, the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (saññāvedayitanirodha-samāpatti) where mental formations (citta-saṅkhāra) cease should be known as mano-moneyya. 'Kāya-muni' means a noble and pure sage in the body-door, or a sage by body. In the remaining two terms, the method is the same. 'Sabbappahāyī' refers to an Arahant who has abandoned everything. This is because an Arahant has abandoned all defilements. ## The Second Chapter, Āpāyika-vagga.
236:
## (13) 3. Kusināravagga
## 1. Kusinārasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the third vagga, 'Kusinārāyaṃ' means in the city of that name. 'Baliharaṇe vanasaṇḍe' means in the jungle thicket of that name. It is called 'Baliharaṇa' because offerings (bali) are brought there for the purpose of feeding spirits (bhūtas). 'Ākaṅkhamāno' means if one desires. 'Sahatthā' means with one's own hand. 'Sampavāreti' means to cause one to refuse by saying 'Enough, enough' both by word and by gesture of the hands. The phrase 'Sādhu vata māyaṃ' should be resolved as 'Sādhu vata maṃ ayaṃ'. (It means: 'It is indeed good that this householder satisfies and causes me to refuse with these excellent foods.')

'Gathito' means being bound by the sap of craving. 'Mucchito' means being infatuated by the very infatuation of craving. 'Ajjhopanno' means being swallowed and obsessed by craving. 'Anissaraṇapañño': one who eats after abandoning and pulling oneself out of desire and lust (from the round of rebirths) is called 'one who has the wisdom of deliverance' (nissaraṇapañño). This monk, however, is not like that; because he eats with strong desire and lust, he is called 'one who lacks the wisdom of deliverance' (anissaraṇapañño). The 'bright side' (sukkapakkha) should be understood as the opposite of what was said. It should be understood that in this sutta, thoughts of renunciation (nekkhamma-vitakka) and so forth are taught in a mixed manner.

## 2. Bhaṇḍanasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, 'pajahiṃsu' means they abandon. 'Bahulamakaṃsu' means they did frequently. In this sutta also, the three types of thoughts are taught in a mixed manner.

## 3. Gotamakacetiyasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, 'Gotamake cetiye' means at the abode of the yakkha named Gotamaka. Indeed, for the first twenty years after his enlightenment, the Blessed One mostly stayed in shrines (deva-temples), such as sometimes at the Cāpāla shrine, sometimes at the Sārandada shrine, sometimes at the Bahuputta shrine, and sometimes at the Gotamaka shrine. At this time, he was staying at the site of the Gotamaka yakkha's abode, depending on the city of Vesālī. Therefore, it is said, 'Gotamake cetiye'. 'Etadavoca' refers to the utterance of this sutta beginning with 'Abhiññāyāhaṃ'.

It should be understood that the Blessed One taught this sutta because of a specific occasion (atthuppatti). What was that occasion? It was due to the occasion of the Mūlapariyāya Sutta. In detail: many monks who had been ordained from Brahmin families, relying on the words of the Buddha they had learned, developed conceit regarding their knowledge, thinking, 'When the Sammāsambuddha teaches, he will only teach what we already know, not what we do not know.' With this attitude of not wanting to acknowledge [new knowledge], they went to the hall for hearing the Dhamma. When the monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, the Teacher had those monks summoned, made them give a verbal acknowledgement, and then taught the Mūlapariyāya Sutta. Those monks...
237:
...relying on the words of the Buddha they had learned, developed conceit regarding their knowledge, thinking, 'When the Sammāsambuddha teaches, he will only teach what we already know, not what we do not know,' and thus did not go to the place of hearing the Dhamma. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One. The Teacher had those monks summoned, took their verbal acknowledgement, and taught the Mūlapariyāya Sutta. Those monks did not see (understand) the 'coming' or the 'going' (the structure and depth) of the discourse. Not seeing it, they thought, 'The Sammāsambuddha says, "My speech leads to deliverance from the round of rebirths," but he only says whatever comes to his mouth (whatever occurs to him).' The Teacher, knowing their thoughts, began (taught) this sutta.

In that sutta, 'Abhiññāya' means having known, penetrated, and realized directly these five aggregates, twelve bases, eighteen elements, twenty-two faculties, four truths, nine causes, seven contacts, seven feelings, seven volitions, seven perceptions, and seven consciousnesses; and likewise, having known, penetrated, and realized directly those various dhammas through the method beginning with 'these are the four foundations of mindfulness.' 'Sanidānaṃ' means I teach only with a cause (reason), not without a cause. 'Sappāṭihāriyaṃ' means I teach only with the refutation of opposing views, not without the refutation of opposing views. 'Alañca pana vo' means it is indeed fit for you. 'Tuṭṭhiyā' means it is indeed fit for you to be joyful, reflecting on the qualities of the Triple Gem: 'The Blessed One is the Sammāsambuddha, the Dhamma is well-expounded (svākkhāta), the Saṅgha is well-practiced (suppaṭipanna).' In the remaining two phrases, the method is the same.

'Akampittha' means it shook in six ways. This kind of earthquake also occurred at the Bodhimaṇḍa. It is heard that when the Bodhisatta ascended the Bodhimaṇḍa from the southern direction, the southern part seemed to reach down to Avīci, while the northern part seemed to rise and strike the peak of existence (bhavagga). When he went to the west, the western part seemed to reach Avīci, while the eastern part seemed to rise and strike the peak of existence. When he went to the north, the northern part seemed to reach Avīci, while the southern part seemed to rise and strike the peak of existence. When he went to the east, the eastern part seemed to reach Avīci, while the western part seemed to rise and strike the peak of existence. The Bodhi tree also seemed once to reach Avīci and once to rise and strike the peak of existence. On that day too, the great earth, a thousand world-systems in extent, shook in these six ways.
238:
## 4. Bharandukālāmasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, 'kevalakappaṃ' means 'entire'. 'Anvāhiṇḍanto' means 'wandering about'. Regarding the phrase 'did not see', for what reason did they not see? It is said that this Bharandu Kālāma (also referred to as Bhadanta Kālasāma in the Nissaya) wandered about eating the excellent alms-food of the Sakyans. Knowing that a Dhamma discourse would arise when he reached that person's dwelling place, the Blessed One made a determination so that no other lodging would be apparent. Therefore, he was not seen.

'Purāṇasabrahmacārī' means a former fellow-practitioner. It is said that he had been in that very hermitage during the time of Āḷāra Kālāma; it is in reference to this that it is said. 'Santharaṃ paññāpehi' means 'spread the bedding that should be spread'. 'Santharaṃ paññāpetvā' means having spread the coverlet on a suitable small couch. In the phrase 'kāmānaṃ pariññaṃ paññāpeti', 'pariññā' means 'transcending'; therefore, he prescribes the first jhāna as the transcending of sensual pleasures. 'Na rūpānaṃ pariññaṃ' means he does not prescribe the formless attainments (arūpāvacara samāpatti) as the transcending of forms. 'Na vedanānaṃ pariññaṃ' means he does not prescribe Nibbāna as the transcending of feelings. 'Niṭṭhā' means destination or completion. 'Udāhu puthū' means 'or else, various'.

## 5. Hatthakasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, in the phrase 'abhikkantāya rattiyā', the word 'abhikkant' is found in the senses of exhaustion (passing), excellence, beauty, and great joy, among others. Among these, it is found in the sense of exhaustion in such passages as: "Venerable Sir, the night has passed (abhikkantā), the first watch is gone, the Saṅgha of monks has been sitting for a long time; Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha to the monks." It is found in the sense of excellence in such passages as: "This person is more excellent (abhikkantataro) and more sublime than these four persons."

It is found in the sense of beauty in such verses as: "Who is this who worships my feet, shining with power and glory, illuminating all directions with such beautiful (abhikkantena) color?" It is found in the sense of great joy in such passages as: "Venerable Gotama, it is excellent (abhikkantaṃ)!" In this sutta, however, it should be taken in the sense of excellence. Therefore, 'abhikkantāya rattiyā' means in the desirable, lovely, and pleasing night. In the phrase 'abhikkantavaṇṇā', the word 'abhikkanta' is used in the sense of a very beautiful color, while the word 'vaṇṇa' is found in the senses of complexion, praise, caste, cause, shape, measure, visual object, and so on. Among these, it is found in the sense of complexion in such passages as: "The Blessed One has a golden complexion (suvaṇṇavaṇṇo)."
239:
In such passages as "The Blessed One...", the word 'vaṇṇa' is evident in the sense of complexion. In such passages as "Householder, when did you compose these praises (vaṇṇā) of the ascetic Gotama?", it is evident in the sense of praise. In such passages as "Venerable Gotama, there are these four castes (vaṇṇā)", it is evident in the sense of caste. In such passages as "That being so, for what reason (vaṇṇena) is he not called a composer?", it is evident in the sense of cause. In such passages as "Having created the form (vaṇṇam) of a great elephant king", it is evident in the sense of shape. In such passages as "There are three sizes (vaṇṇā) of alms-bowls", it is evident in the sense of measure. In such passages as "Color (vaṇṇo), smell, taste, nutritive essence", it is evident in the sense of visual object. In this context, the word 'vaṇṇa' should be understood in the sense of complexion. Therefore, 'abhikkantavaṇṇā' means those with very beautiful complexions, desirable complexions, and pleasing complexions.

In the term 'kevalakappaṃ', the word 'kevala' exists in many senses such as without remainder, many, unmixed, not exceeding (mere), firm, and detached. This is true; the sense of 'without remainder' is found in such passages as "The entirely (kevala) complete and pure holy life." The sense of 'many' is found in such passages as "Many (kevalakappā) people of Anga and Magadha will come taking much food." The sense of 'unmixed' is found in such passages as "The arising of this entire (kevalassa) mass of suffering [unmixed with happiness] occurs." The sense of 'not exceeding' (mere) is found in such passages as "This venerable one has mere (kevalaṃ) faith without excess." The sense of 'firm' is found in such passages as "The co-resident of Venerable Anuruddha named Bāhiya stands firmly (kevalakappaṃ) for the schism of the Saṅgha." The sense of 'detached' is found in such passages as "One who is detached (kevalī), who has lived the life, is called a supreme man." In this context, however, the sense of 'without remainder' is intended.

This word 'kappa' also exists in many senses such as belief, usage, time, designation, cutting, conception, hint, and the state of being all-around. This is true; the sense of 'belief' is found in such passages as "This word of the Venerable Gotama is to be believed (okappanīyam)." The sense of 'usage' is found in such passages as "Monks, I allow you to enjoy fruit with five types of ascetic usage (kappa)." The sense of 'time' is found in such passages as "He dwells for a constant time (niccakappaṃ)." The sense of 'name/designation' is found in such passages as "The Venerable Kappa (asked) thus."
240:
(The word kappa) occurs in the sense of designation (paññatti). In passages such as "alankato kappitakesamassū," it occurs in the sense of cutting (chedana). In passages such as "kappati dvaṅgulakappo," it occurs in the sense of variation or option (vikappa). In passages such as "atthi kappo nipajjituṃ," it occurs in the sense of a pretext or reason (lesa). In passages such as "kevalakappaṃ veḷuvanaṃ obhāsetvā," the sense of "entirety" or "all-around" (samantabhāva) is intended. Here too, the sense of "entirety" of that word kappa is intended. Therefore, in the passage "kevalakappaṃ jetavanaṃ," it means the entire Jetavana monastery without remainder.

Obhāsetvā means having pervaded with light. Vālukāya means in a fine heap of sand. Na saṇṭhāti means it does not remain or stand. Regarding the term oḷārikaṃ (the commentator explains in detail): when a Brahma deity stands on the earth, it is appropriate for their physical form to be created as coarse, or the earth itself should be created as coarse. Therefore, it is said "oḷārikaṃ" (coarse). By the word dhamma, it shows the words of the Buddha previously learned. Nappavattino ahesuṃ means that words rooted in recitation indeed declined. Appaṭivāno means unrelenting or not turning back.

Dassanassa means seeing with eye-consciousness. Upaṭṭhānassa means serving with the four requisites. Adhisīlaṃ refers to the ten precepts. Those ten precepts are called "higher virtue" (adhisīla) in comparison to the five precepts. Avihaṃ gato shows that one has been reborn in the Aviha Brahma world.

## ၆။ Kaṭuviyasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the sixth sutta, goyogapilakkhasmiṃ means near the Pilakkha tree (wavy-leaf fig) located at the place where cows are sold. Rittassādaṃ means having empty enjoyment due to the absence of jhanic bliss. Bāhirassādaṃ means having external enjoyment due to the power of sensual pleasures. Kaṭuviyaṃ refers to something loathsome (ucchiṭṭha) like refuse or spit. Āmagandhena means with a foul smell, which is called anger. Avassutaṃ means moist or wet. Makkhikā refers to the flies of defilements. Nānupatissanti means they will not rise and follow. Nānvāssavissanti means they will not follow and bite. Saṃvegamāpādi means one has become a stream-enterer.

Kaṭuviyakato means made like refuse. Ārakā hoti means stays far away. Vighātasseva bhāgavā means having a share only of suffering. Careti means goes or walks. Dummedho means an unwise person. In this sutta, only the round of suffering (vaṭṭa) is discussed; however, in the verses, both the round and the ending of the round (vivaṭṭa or Nibbāna) are discussed. In the seventh sutta, only the round of suffering is discussed.
241:
## ၈။ Dutiya-anuruddhasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the eighth sutta, "this is in your conceit" (idaṃ te mānasmiṃ) means this is your conceit that has increased in nine ways. "This is in your restlessness" (idaṃ te uddhaccasmiṃ) means this is your restlessness (uddhacca), which is the state of agitation of the mind. "This is in your remorse" (idaṃ te kukkuccasmiṃ) means this is your remorse (kukkucca).

## ၉။ Paṭicchannasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, āvahanti means they enter (the round of suffering). "Being concealed, it leads" (paṭicchanno āvahati) means it departs only while being concealed. "Being revealed, it shines" (vivaṭo virocati)—in this passage, four types of openness (vivaṭatā) should be understood: openness on one side, openness on both sides, openness by oneself in meaning, and openness in all meanings. Among these four, openness on one side refers to the uncommon training rules (asādhāraṇa-sikkhāpada). Openness on both sides refers to the common training rules (sādhāraṇa-sikkhāpada). Openness by oneself in meaning refers to the attained qualities of the Dhamma. Openness in all meanings refers to the words of the Buddha, which are the three Pitakas.

## ၁၀။ Lekhasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, abhiṇhaṃ means repeatedly, without interval, and constantly. Āgāḷhena means firmly and harshly. Pharusena means with harsh speech. It means even when spoken to firmly and harshly. Amanāpena means in a way that does not adhere to or increase in the mind. "It just fits" (sandhiyatimeva) means it is just joined. "It is just consistent" (saṃsandatimeva) means it is just continuous. "It is just joyful" (sammodatimeva) means it just reaches the state of unity. In all other remaining parts, the meaning is clear.

## Kusināravaggo tatiyo.
## (၁၄) ၄။ Yodhājīvavaggo
## ၁။ Yodhājīvasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the fourth chapter, one is called a warrior (yodhājīva) because one lives by means of fighting. "Rājāraha" means one who is worthy of a king. "Rājabhogga" means one who is a king's possession or utility. "Reckoned only as a limb" (aṅganteva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati) means one is reckoned as a limb because of being necessarily desired, like a hand or a foot. "One who can shoot to a distance" (dūre pātī hoti) means in water...
242:
He causes the arrow to fall at a distance of eight *usabhas* on land, or even further than that. Indeed, a soldier of King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi Abhaya caused an arrow to fall at a distance of nine *usabhas*, while in his final birth, the Bodhisatta could cause an arrow to fall at a distance of one *yojana*. 'Akkhana-vedhī' refers to an archer who can shoot without missing, or it means one capable of shooting even through a flash of lightning. 'Mahato kāyassa padāletā' means one capable of piercing through a hundred wooden planks bound together, a hundred buffalo hides, an iron plate one inch thick, an *asana* wood plank four inches thick, a fig wood plank one span thick, or a sand-cart lengthwise. The passage beginning with 'Yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ' has been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*. The phrase 'Netaṃ mama' etc., is spoken by way of abandoning craving (*taṇhā*), conceit (*māna*), and wrong view (*diṭṭhi*). 'Sammapaññāya passati' means seeing with the wisdom of the Path together with insight (*vipassanā*) through the right cause. 'Padāleti' means breaking through by means of the Path of Arahantship.

## 2. Parisā Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, 'ukkācitavinītā' refers to an assembly that is disciplined without questioning, which is difficult to discipline. 'Paṭipucchāvinītā' refers to an assembly that is disciplined through questioning, which is easy to discipline. 'Yāvatāvinītā' means an assembly disciplined by the power of measure, or disciplined by knowing the measure. In the Pali 'yāvatajjhā', however, it means 'up to the inclination' (*ajjhāsaya*), implying an assembly disciplined by knowing their inclination. The third sutta has a clear meaning.

## 4. Uppāda Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, 'dhammaṭṭhitatā' means the state of being established by nature. 'Dhammaniyāmatā' means the certainty of nature. 'Sabbe saṅkhārā' refers to the formations occurring in the four planes. 'Aniccā' (impermanent) is so called because of the sense of non-existence after having arisen. 'Dukkhā' (suffering) is so called because of the sense of constant oppression. 'Anattā' (non-self) is so called because of the sense of not following one's will. Thus, in this sutta, the three characteristics are taught in combination.

## 5. Kesakambala Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, in the phrase 'tantāvutānaṃ vatthānaṃ', the genitive case expresses the sense of the nominative; it means clothes woven by looms. 'Kesakambalo' is a blanket woven from human hair.

...woven blanket. 'Puthusamaṇabrāhmaṇavādānaṃ'—this phrase also has the genitive case in the sense of the nominative. 'Paṭikiṭṭho' means the lowest or the most inferior. 'Moghapuriso' means a man who is empty of the jhānas, paths, and fruits. 'Paṭibāhati' means he forbids or hinders. 'Khippaṃ uḍḍeyya' means one should set a fish-trap (*kumina*). The sixth and seventh suttas have clear meanings.

## 8. Assakhaluṅka Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the eighth sutta, 'assakhaluṅko' means a young horse (colt). 'I say this regarding the speed of this horse' means I say that the knowledge of these Four Noble Truths is the speed (swiftness) of the intellect of that man who is like a colt. 'I say this regarding the beauty of this horse' means I say that the knowledge of this Abhidhamma is the beauty of that person's virtue. 'I say this regarding the height and girth of this horse' means I say that the obtaining of these four requisites is that person's state of being tall and well-proportioned.

## 9. Assaparassa Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, 'assaparasse' means another horse among horses. 'Purisaparasse' means individuals among men who are like horses; it means successive men. In this sutta, the three paths and fruits are taught. Therein, it should be understood that this person is endowed with the speed of knowledge through the three paths.

## 10. Assājānīya Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, 'bhadre' means good horses. 'Assājānīye' refers to horses that know what is a cause and what is not. The same method applies to thoroughbred men (*purisājānīya*). In this sutta, the fruit of Arahantship is taught. Therein, it should be understood that this person is endowed with the speed of knowledge through the Path of Arahantship.

## 11. Paṭhama Moranivāpa Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the eleventh sutta, 'accantanitṭho' means one whose end is Nibbāna which transcends the end, or one whose end is the stable Nibbāna. The rest is the same.

## 12. Dutiya Moranivāpa Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the twelfth sutta, 'iddhipāṭihāriyena' means by the miracle of psychic power that accomplishes its purpose. 'Ādesanāpāṭihāriyena' means by the miracle of instruction, which involves speaking and repeatedly speaking by pointing out and advising.

## 13. Tatiya Moranivāpa Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the thirteenth sutta, the Third Moranivāpa Sutta, 'sammādiṭṭhiyā' means by Right View for the purpose of attaining the attainment of the fruit (*phala-samāpatti*). 'Sammāñāṇena' means by the knowledge of the fruit. 'Sammāvimuttiyā' means by the remaining states of the attainment of the fruit. In all these three suttas, only the Arahant is spoken of.

## 10. Pubbaṇha Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, among the terms beginning with 'sunakkhattaṃ', on whatever day the three states of good conduct are fulfilled, that day is called one that has obtained the conjunction of a good constellation; for that reason, it is said that for him it is always a 'good constellation' (*sunakkhatta*). That very day is called one in which a blessing has been performed; for that reason, it is said that for him it is always a 'good blessing' (*sumangala*). His dawn is also always a 'good dawn' (*suppabhāta*); his rising from bed is also a 'good rising' (*suhuṭṭhita*); the moment is also a 'good moment' (*sukkhana*); the instant is also a 'good instant' (*sumuhutta*). Herein, the duration of ten finger-snaps is called a *khaṇa*; ten *khaṇas* make a *laya*; ten *layas* make a *khaṇalaya*; ten times that is a *muhutta*; ten times that is a *khaṇamuhutta*—this is how the division should be understood. 'Suyitṭhaṃ brahmacārīsū' means on whatever day the three good conducts are fulfilled, then the gift given to those of noble conduct is called 'well-offered' (*suyitṭha*).

157-163. Hereafter, 'harsh practice' (āgāḷhā paṭipadā) refers to a harsh practice characterized by firm grasping through the power of harsh greed. 'Scorched' (nijjhāmā) means well-burnt, heated, or glowing through the power of the practice of self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga). 'Middle' (majjhimā) refers to the practice that is neither too harsh nor too scorched, existing in the middle. 'Naked ascetic' (acelaka) refers to one who is without clothes, being naked. 'Loose in conduct' (muttācāra) refers to one whose conduct is unrestrained; in matters such as defecation, he is devoid of the conduct of worldly gentlemen and performs defecation, urination, chewing, and eating while only standing.

'Hand-licker' (hatthāpale khana) refers to one who, when the meal in his hand is finished, licks his hand with his tongue. Even after defecating, he licks his hand, perceiving the hand as a stick. He is called 'not one who comes when called' (na-ehibhadantika) because he does not come even when told, 'Come, venerable sir,' to receive alms. He is called 'not one who stands when told' (na-tiṭṭhabhadantika) because he does not stand even when told, 'Then please stand, venerable sir.' It is said that he does not do both of these things, thinking, 'This would be following the words of the donor.'

'Brought' (abhihaṭa) refers to alms food that is taken and brought before it reaches him. 'Prepared specifically' (uddissakata) refers to alms food announced as, 'This is prepared specifically for you.' 'Invitation' (nimantana) refers to alms food invited by saying, 'Please enter such a family, street, or village,' which he neither enjoys nor accepts. 'Not from the mouth of a pot' (na kumbhimukhā) means he does not accept alms food offered by taking it out of a pot. 'Not from the mouth of a basket' (na kaḷopimukhā) means he does not accept from a kaḷopī, which is either a pot or a basket. Why? Because he thinks, 'The pots and baskets receive a blow from the ladle because of me.' 'Not across a threshold' (na eḷakamantaraṃ) means he does not accept alms food offered across a threshold. Why? Because he thinks, 'This threshold is placed in between because of me.' The same method applies to sticks and pestles.
246:
'Of two' (dvinnaṃ) means that when two people are eating, if one of them stands up to offer alms, he does not accept it. Why? Because it becomes an interruption to the mouthful. In the passages beginning with 'not from a pregnant woman' (na gabbhiniyā), he does not accept alms from a pregnant woman because the child in the womb would suffer. He does not accept from a nursing mother because it would be an interruption to the child's milk. He does not accept from a woman who has gone to a man because it would be an interruption to their pleasure. 'Not from announced meals' (na saṅkittīsu) refers to meals prepared by announcing and collecting. It is said that during a time of famine, the disciples of the naked ascetics collect rice and so forth from various places for the sake of the naked ascetics and cook a meal; a high-level naked ascetic does not accept that. 'Not where there is [a dog]' (na yattha sā) means that in a place where a dog is present, waiting with the hope of 'I will get a morsel of food,' he does not accept the food brought without giving it to that dog. Why? Because it would be an interruption to the food that the dog should receive.

'Moving in swarms' (saṇḍasaṇḍacārinī) refers to moving in groups or swarms. If people, upon seeing a naked ascetic, enter the kitchen to offer alms, and while they are entering, flies resting on pots (kaḷopimukha) and so forth fly up and move in swarms, he does not accept the alms food brought from there. Why? Because he thinks, 'An interruption to the flies' search for food has occurred because of me.' 'Husk-water' (thusodaka) refers to sovīraka medicinal liquid made from all kinds of grain. In this context, only the drinking of alcohol is blameworthy, but this ascetic perceives all medicinal liquids as blameworthy. 'One-houser' (ekāgārika) refers to one who returns after receiving alms from only one house. 'One-mouthfuler' (ekālopika) refers to one who subsists on only one mouthful. The same method should be understood for 'two-houser' and so forth. In the phrase 'even from one bowl' (ekissāpi dattiyā), 'dattiyā' refers to a small bowl in which the first portion of alms is placed. 'Once-a-day-er' (ekāhika) means every other day; 'half-monther' (addhamāsika) means every half-month. 'Eating meals in turns' (pariyāyabhattabhojana) refers to eating meals according to a schedule; eating meals brought according to a turn of days, such as a one-day turn, a two-day turn, a seven-day turn, or a half-month turn. Terms like 'vegetable-eater' (sākabhakkha) have the same meaning as previously stated.

'Standing-upright-er' (ubbaṭṭhaka) refers to one who always stands. 'Devoted to the exertion of crouching' (ukkuṭikappadhānamanuyutta) refers to one devoted to the energy of crouching; even when moving, he goes by jumping and jumping while remaining in a crouching position. 'Thorn-bed-dweller' (kaṇṭakāpassayika) refers to one who drives iron thorns or natural thorns into the ground, spreads a skin over them, and performs standing, walking, and so forth upon them.
247:
"Seyya" means performing the act of sleeping even in that [place where the hide is spread]. "Sāyatatiyakaṃ" refers to one who descends into the water for the third time in the evening. One lives devoted to the practice of descending into the water three times a day—in the morning, at noon, and in the evening—with the thought, "I shall wash away evil."

"Kāye kāyānupassī" and so forth should be understood in the same manner as already explained in the commentary on the Ekanipāta. "Bhikkhus, this practice is called the Middle Way (majjhimā paṭipadā)" means: Bhikkhus, this practice should be known as the "Middle Way" because it does not approach the two extremes of devotion to sensual pleasure and devotion to self-mortification, or because it is liberated from the extremes of eternalism and annihilationism.

## 1. Commentary on the Anubuddhasutta

In the first sutta of the Catukkanipāta, "ananubodhā" means through not knowing or not understanding. "Appaṭivedhā" means through not penetrating or not realizing. "Dīghamaddhānaṃ" means for a long time. "Sandhāvitaṃ" means having hurried along by way of passing from one birth to another. "Saṃsaritaṃ" means having wandered by way of repeatedly coming and going. "Mamañceva tumhākañca" means both I and you [have hurried and wandered]. Alternatively, in the phrase "sandhāvitaṃ saṃsaritaṃ," the meaning should be understood as: the hurrying and wandering of myself and you has occurred. "Ariyassa" refers to the faultless [virtue, etc.]. These three things—virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā)—should be understood only as those associated with the Path and Fruit. By the name "vimutti" (liberation), only the Fruit (phala) is indicated. "Bhavataṇhā" is craving for existences. "Bhavanetti" is the rope of existence. This is a name for craving itself. Because that craving binds beings by the neck like oxen and leads them to various existences, it is called "bhavanetti."

"Anuttarā" means supramundane. "Dukkhassantakaro" means one who makes an end to the suffering of the round of rebirth. "Cakkhumā" means one endowed with the five eyes. "Parinibbuto" means extinguished through the extinguishment of defilements (kilesa-parinibbāna). This was the Buddha's first parinibbāna at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). Later, however, he attained parinibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu) between the twin Sāla trees; thus, he concluded the teaching according to the sequence of events.

## 2. Commentary on the Papatitasutta

In the second sutta, "papatito" means one who has fallen or slipped. "Appapatito" means one who has not fallen but is firmly established. Therein, the multitude of worldlings is called "fallen." Those such as Stream-enterers (sotāpanna) are called "fallen" at the moment defilements arise. The one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava, the Arahant) is called "entirely established."
250:
"Cutā patanti" means those who pass away are said to fall. "Patitā" means those who fall are said to pass away. The meaning is: because they pass away, they fall; and because they fall, they pass away. "Giddhā" refers to those who are lustful with passion. "Punāgatā" means those who have come again to birth, again to aging, again to sickness, and again to death. "Kataṃ kiccaṃ" means the task to be done by the four paths has been completed. "Rataṃ rammaṃ" means delighting in the collection of qualities worthy of delight. "Sukhenānvāgataṃ sukhaṃ" means the successive reaching or obtaining of one happiness through another. The meaning is: reaching divine happiness through human happiness, insight happiness through jhāna happiness, path happiness through insight happiness, fruit happiness through path happiness, and Nibbāna happiness through fruit happiness.

## 3. Commentary on the Paṭhamakhatasutta

The third sutta should be understood just as stated in the commentary on the Dukanipāta. In the verses, "nindiya" refers to a person worthy of blame. "Nindati" means he blames. "Pasamsiyo" is a person worthy of praise. One who acts in this way is said to accumulate misfortune (kali) with that mouth. And through that misfortune, he does not obtain happiness. The loss (parājaya) of all one's wealth along with oneself is only a small misfortune (kali). But if one should corrupt the mind toward those who have gone well (sugata), this corruption of mind is a much greater misfortune than that [loss of wealth]. Now, showing the nature of that greater misfortune, he said "sataṃ sahassānaṃ" and so forth. Therein, "sataṃ sahassānaṃ" is one hundred thousand by the Nirabbuda count. "Chattiṃsati" is another thirty-six Nirabbudas. "Pañca ca" is five Abbudas by the Abbuda count. It means that one who blames the Noble Ones (ariya) is reborn in hell, and the lifespan there is of this much duration.

## 4. Commentary on the Dutiyakhatasutta

In the fourth sutta, regarding "mātari pitari ca" and so forth, Mittavindaka is one who practiced wrongly toward his mother; Ajātasattu is one who practiced wrongly toward his father; Devadatta is one who practiced wrongly toward the Tathāgata; and Kokālika is one who practiced wrongly toward the disciples of the Tathāgata. "Bahuñca" means much demerit indeed. "Pasavati" means he obtains. Through that unrighteous conduct (adhammacariya) known as wrong practice, after passing away from here, he goes to a state of deprivation; that is, he is reborn in one of the states of deprivation such as hell. In the case of the "white side" (merit), the method is the same.
251: ## 5. Anusotasutta-vaṇṇanā In the fifth sutta, one is called 'anusotagāmī' because of going along with the stream of saṃsāra. Appassutasutta-vaṇṇanā In the sixth sutta, 'anupapanno' means one who has not approached. Regarding 'suttaṃ' and so forth, the decision should be known thus: the Ubhatovibhaṅga, Niddesa, Khandhaka, Parivāra, Suttanipāta, Maṅgala Sutta, Ratana Sutta, Nālaka Sutta, Tuvaṭaka Sutta, and other words of the Tathāgata named Sutta are to be known as 'Suttaṃ'. Pure verses in the Dhammapada, Theragāthā, Therīgāthā, and Suttanipāta that do not have the name 'Sutta' are to be known as 'Gāthā'.

Words of the Buddha not mixed with other limbs are to be known as Veyyākaraṇa. Pure verses in the Dhammapada, Theragāthā, Therīgāthā, and Suttanipāta that do not have the name 'Sutta' are to be known as 'Gāthā'. The eighty-two suttas consisting of verses associated with knowledge accompanied by joy are to be known as 'Udāna'. The one hundred and ten suttas beginning with 'Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā' (Thus was it said by the Blessed One) are to be known as 'Itivuttaka'. The five hundred and fifty birth stories beginning with the Apaṇṇaka Jātaka are to be known as 'Jātaka'. All suttas associated with wonderful and marvelous qualities, beginning with 'Monks, these four wonderful and marvelous qualities are found in Ānanda,' are to be known as 'Abbhutadhamma'. All suttas such as the Cūḷavedalla Sutta, Mahāvedalla Sutta, Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta, Sakkapañha Sutta, Saṅkhārabhājanīya Sutta, and Mahāpuṇṇama Sutta, which were asked after repeatedly gaining wisdom and satisfaction, are to be known as 'Vedalla'.

'Na attham aññāya na dhammam aññāya' means not knowing the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) and the Pali Text (Pāḷi). 'Dhammānudhammapaṭipanno' means not practicing the preliminary practice along with virtue, which is the appropriate practice for the nine supramundane states (lokuttara dhamma). In this way, the meaning should be understood in all sections (vāra). Here, in the first section, a person of little learning and poor virtue is described; in the second, a person of little learning who is an Arahant; in the third, a person of much learning and poor virtue; and in the fourth, a person of much learning who is an Arahant.

'Sīlesu asamāhito' means one who does not fulfill the virtues. 'Sīlato ca sutena ca' means they censure that person saying, 'This person is immoral and has little learning,' both in terms of virtue and in terms of learning. Because that person has performed the task of learning through that learning, their learning is said to be successful; therefore, it is said, 'Tassa sampajjate sutaṃ'. 'Nāssa sampajjate' means it is not successful because the task of learning has not been performed. 'Dhammadharaṃ' means being the foundation of the heard scriptures (pariyatti). 'Sappaññaṃ' means having good wisdom. In the phrase 'Nekkhaṃ jambonadasseva', 'Jambonada' refers to gold of pure quality. It means like a 'nikkha' (gold coin) of that Jambonada gold, or like a gold ingot weighing five suvaṇṇas.

## 8. Vesārajjasuttavaṇṇanā
In the eighth discourse, regarding the word "vesārajjāni," the state opposite to timidity (sārajja) is called intrepidity (vesārajja). This name refers to the knowledge accompanied by joy that arises in one who reviews the absence of timidity in four areas. "Āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ" means the noble position, the most excellent position. Alternatively, the previous Buddhas, such as Vipassī and others, are called "āsabha"; thus, it means the position (or domain) of those Buddhas. In another way, a bull that is the leader of a hundred cows is called an "usabha"; a bull that is the leader of a thousand cows is called a "vasabha." Or, a bull that is the leader of a hundred pens is an "usabha," and a leader of a thousand pens is a "vasabha." A bull that is superior to all cattle, capable of enduring all dangers, white and inspiring in appearance, capable of bearing heavy loads, and unshaken even by the sound of a hundred thunderclaps is called a "nisabha." In this context, it is that "nisabha" which is intended by the term "usabha." Indeed, this name "usabha" is a synonym for that "nisabha." Because it belongs to such an "usabha," it is called "āsabha." "Ṭhānaṃ" refers to standing firmly, pressing the earth with four legs. This Omniscient Knowledge is also called "āsabha" because it is like that of a "nisabha usabha." Just as the bull-elephant known as "nisabha" stands in an immovable position, pressing the earth with four legs, similarly, the Blessed One stands in an immovable position in the world with its devas, pressing the earth of the eight assemblies with the four legs of the Knowledge of Intrepidity, such that no enemy or adversary can shake Him. While standing thus, He claims that supreme position, approaches it, and does not renounce it but bears it within Himself. Therefore, it is said: "He claims the supreme position (āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti)."

"Parisāsu" means in the eight assemblies. "Sīhanādaṃ nadati" means He roars a noble roar, a fearless roar; or He roars a roar similar to that of a lion. This meaning should be understood through the Sīhanāda Sutta. Alternatively, just as a lion is called "sīha" because of its ability to endure (sahana) and to strike down (hanana) enemies, similarly, the Blessed One is called "sīha" because He endures worldly conditions (lokadhamma) and strikes down the doctrines of others. The voice of the Blessed One, who is thus called a lion, is the "lion's roar" (sīhanāda). In that context, just as a lion king, endowed with the strength of a lion, roars the lion's roar everywhere with intrepidity and without hair-standing-on-end, so too the lion-like Blessed One, endowed with the Tathāgata powers, roars the lion's roar—endowed with the elegance of various methods of teaching such as "Such is form"—in the eight assemblies with intrepidity and without hair-standing-on-end. Therefore, it is said: "He roars the lion's roar in the assemblies (parisāsu sīhanādaṃ nadati)."
254:
In the phrase "brahmacakkaṃ pavatteti," "brahma" means noble, excellent, or pure. As for the word "cakka" (wheel):

"It is seen in the sense of prosperity (sampatti), a mark (lakkhaṇa), a chariot part (rathanga), a posture (iriyāpatha), giving (dāna), a gem-wheel, the wheel of Dhamma, and the chest-wheel (uracakka), etc. Here, it is understood as the Wheel of Dhamma (dhammacakka), and that wheel should be explained in two ways."

In sentences such as "Bhikkhus, there are these four wheels, possessed of which devas and humans..." (A.N. 4.31), this word "cakka" is evident in the sense of prosperity (sampatti). In the phrase "Wheels appeared on the soles of the feet" (D.N. 2.35), it is in the sense of a mark (lakkhaṇa). In "The wheel follows the hoof of the ox" (Dhp. 1), it is in the sense of a chariot part (rathanga). In "There are four wheels and nine gates" (S.N. 1.29), it is in the sense of posture (iriyāpatha). In "Give, enjoy, be not negligent, set the wheel (of giving) in motion for all beings" (Jā. 1.7.149), it is in the sense of giving (dāna). In "The divine gem-wheel appeared" (D.N. 2.243), it is in the sense of a gem-wheel (ratanacakka). In "The wheel set in motion by me" (Sn. 562), it is in the sense of the Wheel of Dhamma (dhammacakka). In "The wheel revolves on the head of the person struck by desire" (Jā. 1.1.104), it is in the sense of a chest-wheel (uracakka/razor-wheel). In "If one were to cut flesh with a wheel-weapon sharp as a razor" (D.N. 1.166), it is in the sense of a weapon-wheel (paharaṇacakka). In "The thunderbolt-circle" (D.N. 3.61), it is in the sense of a thunderbolt-circle (asanimaṇ္ဍala). Here, however, this word "cakka" is intended in the sense of the Wheel of Dhamma (dhammacakka).

That Wheel of Dhamma is of two kinds: the knowledge of penetration (paṭivedha-ñāṇa) and the knowledge of teaching (desanā-ñāṇa). Between these two, the knowledge of penetration is that which is infused with wisdom and brings the Noble Fruit to oneself. The knowledge of teaching is that which is infused with compassion and brings the Noble Fruit to disciples. Among these, the knowledge of penetration is of two types: arising (uppajjamāna) and arisen (uppanna). It is called "arising" from the Great Renunciation until the Path of Arahantship, and "arisen" at the moment of the Fruit. Alternatively, it is "arising" from the Tusita heaven until the Path of Arahantship at the seat of the Great Enlightenment, and "arisen" at the moment of the Fruit. Or, it is "arising" from the time of Buddha Dīpaṅkara until the Path of Arahantship at the seat of Enlightenment, and "arisen" at the moment of the Fruit. The knowledge of teaching is also of two types: setting in motion (pavattāmāna) and set in motion (pavatta). It is called "setting in motion" until the Path of Stream-entry of the Venerable Aññāsi Koṇḍañña, and "set in motion" at the moment of the Fruit. Between these two, the knowledge of penetration is supramundane (lokuttara), while the knowledge of teaching is mundane (lokiya). Both of these knowledges are unique to the Buddhas and are their own innate (born of the breast) knowledge.

## Sammāsambuddhassa te paṭijānato
"To you who claim: 'I am a Perfectly Enlightened One, all dhammas have been fully realized by me.'" "Anabhisambuddhā" means (you have not fully realized) these (specific dhammas).
255:
In the phrase "These certain dhammas are not fully awakened to by you," "therein indeed" (tatra vata) refers to the dhammas shown as "not fully awakened to." "With a reasoned speech" (sahadhammena) means with a speech accompanied by a root cause. In the phrase "This is a sign" (nimitta), both the person and the dhamma are intended as the "sign." The meaning here is: "I do not see that person who will challenge me. I do not see that dhamma which, having been shown, will challenge me by saying, 'This certain dhamma is not fully awakened to by you.'"

"Reached the state of safety" (khemappatta) means having reached security. The remaining two terms are synonyms for this "khemappatta." All of this is said with reference to the Knowledge of Self-Confidence (vesārajja-ñāṇa). Indeed, for the Buddha, the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala), who sees neither a person who would challenge Him nor a cause for challenge—namely, an unawakened dhamma—by saying "This certain dhamma is not fully awakened to by you," there arises a very powerful joy as He reflects, "Being truly a Buddha by nature, I declare 'I am a Buddha.'" The knowledge associated with that joy is called "Vesārajja." With reference to that knowledge, it is said, "Reached the state of safety," and so on. In this way, the meaning should be understood everywhere.

In the phrase "obstructive dhammas" (antarāyikā dhammā), they are called "obstructive" because they create obstacles. In terms of meaning, these are the seven classes of offenses (āpatti) committed intentionally. Indeed, an offense committed intentionally, even if it is only a minor offense like a dukkaṭa (wrongdoing) or dubbhāsita (wrong speech), can create an obstacle to the Paths and Fruits. However, in this context, sexual intercourse (methunadhamma) is intended. Indeed, for anyone who indulges in sexual intercourse, an obstacle to the Paths and Fruits undoubtedly arises.

"For what purpose" (yassa atthāya) means for the purpose of the destruction of lust (rāgakkhaya), etc. "The Dhamma is taught" (dhammo desito) means the Dhamma such as the meditation on foulness (asubhabhāvanā), etc., is taught. "Therein indeed me" (tatra vata maṃ) means "me" in that dhamma which does not lead out of suffering (aniyyanika). The remaining meaning should be understood in the same manner as already stated.

"Vādapatha" (paths of speech) refers to the views themselves. "Puthū" means many. "Sitā" means bound or prepared all around. Alternatively, "puthussitā" means those that have reached a state of being many, or they are called "puthussitā" because they are constructed by many people. "Which they rely upon" means they rely upon that cause which is a view even now. "They do not exist" means those paths of speech do not arise, they break up, and they vanish. The name "Dhammacakka" (Wheel of Dhamma) is a name for both the knowledge of teaching (desanā-ñāṇa) and the knowledge of penetration (paṭivedha-ñāṇa). Among these two, the knowledge of teaching is mundane (lokiya), and the knowledge of penetration is supramundane (lokuttara). "Kevalī" means one who is possessed of all qualities. "Tādisaṃ" means of such a nature.
256:
## 9. Taṇhuppādasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, they are called "uppādā" (arising) because craving arises in those requisites such as robes, etc. What arises? Craving arises. Because they are the root causes for the arising of craving, they are called "taṇhuppādā"; it means the bases or causes of craving. "Cīvara-hetu" (because of robes) means craving arises because of robes, thinking, "Where shall I get a pleasant robe?" In the phrase "itibhavābhavathetu," the word "iti" is an indeclinable used in the sense of illustration (nidassana). The meaning is that just as craving arises because of robes, etc., so it also arises because of existence and non-existence (or various types of existence). Regarding "bhavābhava," in this context, it particularly refers to superior things like ghee, fresh butter, etc. Some also say it refers to the most excellent and less excellent existences among the successful existences (sampatti-bhava).

"Taṇhā-dutiyo" (craving as a companion) means that this being, wandering in the round of rebirth (saṃsāra) whose beginning is unknown, does not wander alone, but wanders only by obtaining craving as a companion. Therefore, it is said "taṇhā-dutiyo." In the phrase "itthabhāva-aññathābhāvaṃ," "itthabhāva" refers to this present existence (attabhāva), and "aññathābhāva" refers to a future existence. Alternatively, another existence of this kind is called "itthabhāva," and an existence not of this kind is called "aññathābhāva." That "saṃsāra" consisting of "itthabhāva" and "aññathābhāva" is the succession of the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), and sense bases (āyatana). "Nātivattati" means it cannot be transcended. "Evamādīnavaṃ ñatvā" means having known the danger in the aggregates of the past, future, and present in this way. "Taṇhaṃ dukkhassa sambhavaṃ" means having known craving thus: "This craving is the natural cause from which the suffering of the round arises." By this much, the state of this monk having developed insight and reached Arahantship is shown. Now, wishing to praise that one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), He said "vītataṇho" (free from craving), and so on. Therein, "anādāno" means being without clinging through grasping. "Sato bhikkhu paribbaje" means the khīṇāsava monk, who has reached the fullness of mindfulness and clear comprehension, should live and wander mindfully and with clear comprehension. Thus, having explained the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) in the sutta, the round and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) are explained in the verses.

## 10. Yogasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, they are called "yoga" (yokes) because they yoke one to the suffering of the round. Among "kāmayoga" (yoke of sensuality), etc., lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure is "kāmayoga." Desire and lust for the realms of fine-material and immaterial existence is "bhavayoga" (yoke of existence); likewise, attachment to meditative absorption (jhāna) is also "bhavayoga." Lust accompanied by the eternalist view and the sixty-two types of views are "diṭṭhiyoga" (yoke of views). Ignorance regarding the Four Noble Truths is "avijjāyoga" (yoke of ignorance). Alternatively, it is "kāmayoga" because it yokes one to sensual pleasures; "bhavayoga" because it yokes one to existences...
257:
It is called the bond of existence (bhavayoga) because it yokes one to existence. It is called the bond of views (diᙩᙩhiyoga) because it yokes one to views. It is called the bond of ignorance (avijjāyoga) because it yokes one to ignorance; these are merely designations for the states mentioned below. Now, wishing to show them in detail, the Blessed One said: "And how, bhikkhus, (is there the bond of sensual pleasure?)" and so forth. In that passage, 'samudaya' means arising by way of production. 'Atthaᅅgama' means destruction by way of passing away. 'Assāda' means the state of being pleasant (gratification). 'Adĩnava' means the fault of being unpleasant (danger). 'Nissaraᅇa' means the state of having escaped (from the round of suffering). 'Kāmesu' means in the objects of sensual pleasure. 'Kāmarāga' is the lust that arises based on the cords of sensual pleasure. In the remaining terms, the method is the same. 'Anuseti' means it occurs (underlies). "This, bhikkhus, is called the bond of sensual pleasure" means, bhikkhus, this is called the cause of yoking, the cause of binding to the cords of sensual pleasure; thus the meaning should be understood in all instances.

'Phassāyatanānaᅃ' means of the eye and so forth, which are the causes of eye-contact and so forth. 'Avijjā aāᅇaᅃ' is ignorance, which is called non-knowing because it is the opposite of knowledge. In the phrase "Thus is the bond of sensual pleasure," the word 'iti' (thus) should also be applied to the four bonds as "Thus is the bond of sensual pleasure, thus is the bond of existence."

'Saᅃyutta' means surrounded. 'Pāpakehi' means by low states. 'Akusalehi' means by unwholesome states born of lack of skill. 'Saᅃkilesikehi' means by states that cause defilement, meaning those that spoil the clarity of a clear mind. 'Ponobbhavikehi' means by states that produce a new existence again. 'Sadarathehi' means by states accompanied by distress. 'Dukkhavipākehi' means by states that produce suffering at the time of fruition. 'Āyatiᅃ jātijarāmaraᅇikehi' means by states that produce birth, aging, and death repeatedly in the future. Therefore, "he is said to be one not secure from the bonds (ayogakkhemĩ)" means that because a person whose bonds are not abandoned is associated with those unwholesome states, and because he has not attained Nibbāna, which is the security from the four bonds, he is called 'not secure from the bonds'.

'Visaᅃyoga' means the causes of disconnection. 'Kāmayogavisaᅃyoga' means the cause of disconnection from the bond of sensual pleasure. In the remaining terms, the method is the same. Among them, the meditation on foulness (asubha-jhāna) is the disconnection from the bond of sensual pleasure; the path of non-returning (anāgāmimagga) attained by making that meditation a basis is certainly called the disconnection from the bond of sensual pleasure. The path of arahantship (arahattamagga) is called the disconnection from the bond of existence. The path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga)...
258:
The path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga) is called the disconnection from the bond of views (diᙩᙩhiyogavisaᅃyoga). The path of arahantship (arahattamagga) is called the disconnection from the bond of ignorance (avijjāyogavisaᅃyoga). Now, wishing to show those natures of the bond of sensual pleasure, the bond of existence, and so forth in detail, the Blessed One said: "And which, bhikkhus," and so forth. The meaning of that should be understood by the method already mentioned.

"Bhava-yogena cũbhayaᅃ" means those who are yoked to the bond of existence, and those who are yoked to both the bond of sensual pleasure and the bond of existence to a slightly greater degree, meaning those endowed with any of the bonds. "Purakkhatā" means placed in front or surrounded. "Kāme pariāya" means having fully understood the two kinds of sensual pleasure. "Bhava-yogaca sabbaso" means having fully understood the bond of existence in its entirety. "Samũhacca" means having uprooted from the root. "Virājayaᅃ" means while causing to fade away or having caused to fade away. If it is said "causing to fade away" (virājento), the Path (magga) is spoken of; if it is said "having caused to fade away" (virājetvā), the Fruit (phala) is spoken of. "Muni" refers to the sage who has destroyed the taints (khĩᅇāsava-muni). Thus, in this sutta and in the verses, only the round of rebirth (vaᙩᙩa) and the cessation of the round (vivaᙩᙩa) are discussed.

## The First Chapter: Bhaᅇᅁagāma (Bhaᅇᅁagāmavaggo Paᙩhamo).

## 2. The Walking Chapter (Caravaggo)

## 1. Commentary on the Walking Sutta (Carasutta-vaᅇᅇanā)

In the first sutta of the second chapter, "adhivāseti" means one places the mind upon it and lets it dwell. "Nappajahati" means one does not abandon. "Na vinodeti" means one does not dispel. "Na byantĩkaroti" means one does not make an end, a limited circumference (does not eliminate to the end). "Na anabhāvaᅃ gameti" means one does not lead it to non-existence again, to non-growth or destruction. "Carampi" means even while walking. "Anātāpĩ" means being without effort (unenergetic). "Anottāpĩ" means being without fear of blame. "Satataᅃ" means always. "Samitaᅃ" means without interval (continuously). Having known the meaning in all places thus, the meaning in the bright side (sukkapakkha) should be understood by the opposite of the method mentioned.

In the verses, "gehanissitaᅃ" means dependent on defilements. "Mohaneyyesu" means in the objects that produce delusion. "Abhabbo" means being one who is not a fit vessel (unworthy). "Phuᙩᙩhuᅃ sambodhimuttamaᅃ" means to touch the supreme knowledge known as the path of arahantship.
259:
## 2. Sīlasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the second sutta, *sampannasīlā* means those with perfected virtue. *Sampannapātimokkhā* means those with perfected Pātimokkha. *Pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutā* means being closed off (restrained) by the virtue of the restraint of the Pātimokkha; it means "dwell being endowed with it." *Ācāragocarasampannā* means "be those who are endowed with and have attained both proper conduct (*ācāra*) and proper resort (*gocara*)." *Aṇumattesu vajjesu* means "in faults of the smallest measure (atomic size)." *Bhayadassāvino* means those who habitually see those minute faults as danger. *Samādāya sikkhatha sikkhāpadesu* means "having undertaken (taken up) the training rules in all groups of training, practice them."

With this much of the Dhamma teaching, "*Sampannasīlānaṃ... pe... sikkhāpadesu*," having encouraged them to undertake the three trainings and having spoken in praise of the qualities attained, the Buddha now says "*Kimassa*" and so forth, wishing to show what should be done further. In that passage, *kimassa* means "how should it be?"

*Yataṃ care* means in whatever manner a person practicing is restrained (or free from hindrances), in that manner should he practice. This method should be understood in all places. *Acce* means "should sit" (or "should stay"). *Yatamenam pasāraye* means whatever limb, large or small, one extends, one should extend it having made it restrained (well-guarded). *Uddhaṃ* means above; *tiriyaṃ* means in the middle; *apācīnaṃ* means below. By this much of the extent, the five aggregates of the past, present, and future are taught. The word *yāvatā* is a word denoting a limit. *Jagato gati* is the completion (arising) of the world of beings. *Samavekkhitā ca dhammānaṃ udayabbayaṃ* means well-contemplating the arising and passing away of those five aggregate phenomena which are distinguished as past and so forth in the entire world. It is said, "One who sees the arising of the five aggregates sees twenty-five characteristics; one who sees the passing away sees twenty-five characteristics"; thus, it is well-contemplated (or seen) through these fifty characteristics.

*Cetosamathasāmīci* means the practice appropriate for the tranquility of the mind (*samatha*). *Sikkhamānaṃ* means practicing, fulfilling. *Pahitatto* means one with a mind sent forth (towards Nibbāna). *Āhu* means "they say." The remaining words here are clear. In this sutta, after teaching virtue in a mixed way (mundane and supramundane), the Arahant is described in the verses.
260:
## 3. Padhānasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, *sammappadhāna* means good efforts, noble energies. *Sammappadhānā* means those with perfected energy. *Māradheyyābhibhūtā* means those who stand having overcome and transcended the realm of Māra, which is the round of rebirth in the three planes. Those Arahants are called *asita*, meaning those without the dependence of craving. *Jātimaraṇabhayassa* means the fear that arises because of birth and death, or the fear which is birth and death itself. *Pāragū* means those who have reached the other shore, Nibbāna. Those Arahants are called *tusita*, meaning those who are joyful. *Jetvā māraṃ savāhaniṃ* means those who stand having conquered Māra along with his army. Those Arahants are called *aneja*, meaning they are steady and unmoved because they lack the agitation known as craving (*ejā*). *Namucibala* means the army of Māra. *Upātivattā* means those who have transcended. Those Arahants are called *sukhita*, meaning they are happy with supramundane bliss. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"Happy indeed are the Arahants; craving is not found in them. The conceit 'I am' is utterly cut off; the net of delusion is burst asunder."

## 4. Saṃvarasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fourth sutta, *padhānāni* means energies. *Saṃvarappadhāna* is the energy that arises in one who restrains the eye and so forth. *Pahānappadhāna* is the energy that arises in one who abandons sensual thoughts and so forth. *Bhāvanappadhāna* is the energy that arises in one who develops the factors of enlightenment. *Anurakkhaṇappadhāna* is the energy that arises in one who guards the sign of concentration (*samādhinimitta*).

In the terms such as *vivekanissita*, the three terms *viveka*, *virāga*, and *nirodha* are all names for Nibbāna. Nibbāna is called *viveka* (seclusion) because it is secluded from acquisitions (*upadhi*); it is called *virāga* (fading away) because lust and so forth fade away in dependence on it; it is called *nirodha* (cessation) because they cease. Therefore, in terms such as *vivekanissita*, it means depending on Nibbāna either by way of the object or by way of attainment.

In the term *vossaggapariṇāmi*, there are two kinds of relinquishment (*vossagga*): relinquishment as giving up (*pariccāga-vossagga*) and relinquishment as entering into (*pakkhandana-vossagga*). Therein, insight (*vipassanā*) is called relinquishment as giving up because it gives up lust in the defilements and the aggregates by way of abandonment of specific factors (*tadaṅga*). The path (*magga*) is called relinquishment as entering into because it enters into Nibbāna by way of the object. Therefore, *vossaggapariṇāmi* means that the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, developed in such a way, inclines toward the abandoning of defilements and entering into Nibbāna; it means one develops that enlightenment factor of mindfulness having reached the state of insight or the state of the path. The same method applies to the remaining terms. *Nimitta* refers to the concentration itself obtained through the perception of bones (*aṭṭhikasaññā*) and so forth, which is called *samādhinimitta*. *Anurakkhati* means guarding by cleansing lust, hatred, and delusion, which are enemies of concentration.
261:
The developed factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (sati-sambojjhaṅga) inclines towards the relinquishment of defilements and entering into Nibbāna. It reaches the state of insight (vipassanā) and the state of the path (magga), and thus one develops that factor of enlightenment of mindfulness; this is the meaning here. The same method applies to the remaining terms. "Bhaddakaṃ" refers to that which is obtained. The sign of concentration (samādhi-nimitta) refers to the concentration itself obtained through the power of the perception of bones (aṭṭhika-saññā) and so forth. "Anurakkhati" (guards) means guarding by cleansing greed, hatred, and delusion, which are obstacles to concentration. Although only the five perceptions such as the perception of bones are mentioned here, the ten kinds of foulness (asubha) should be explained in detail in this context. The detailed explanation of those foulness subjects has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga. In the verse, only the energy (viriya) that accomplishes restraint (saṃvara) and so forth is mentioned. "Khayaṃ dukkhassa pāpuṇeti" means one should reach the fruit of arahantship (arahatta-phala), which is the end of suffering.

## 5. Paññatti-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, "agga-paññattiyo" refers to those who are designated as the supreme. "Attabhāvīnaṃ" means among those who possess an individual existence (attabhāva). "Yadidaṃ rāhu asurindo" means that this Rāhu, the Lord of Asuras, is the supreme. In this context, it is said that Rāhu, the Lord of Asuras, is four thousand eight hundred yojanas in height. The span between his two arms is one thousand two hundred yojanas. The breadth of his palms and the soles of his feet is three hundred yojanas. His finger joints are fifty yojanas, the space between his eyebrows is fifty yojanas, his forehead is three hundred yojanas, and his head is nine hundred yojanas.

Among those who enjoy sensual pleasures, this king named Mandhātā is the supreme among those who enjoy both celestial and human sensual pleasures. This King Mandhātā was born among humans who had an incalculable (asaṅkheyya) lifespan, and by causing a rain of gold and silver to fall whenever he wished, he enjoyed human sensual pleasures for a long time. In the celestial realm, he enjoyed refined sensual pleasures for the duration of the lifespans of thirty-six Sakka kings, and thus became the supreme among those who enjoy sensual pleasures. "Ādhipateyyānaṃ" means among those who exercise lordship or leadership. The Tathāgata is said to be the supreme, the most excellent, and the peerless by virtue of his mundane and supramundane qualities.

(The Buddha is the supreme) among those who shine with the success of celestial prosperity and with fame, which is known as having a retinue. (The Buddha is the supreme) in the upper, middle, and lower regions, and as far as the extent of the world's existence. It means as far as the entire extent of the world's manifestation.
262:
## 6. Sokhumma-sutta-vaṇṇanā

In the sixth sutta, "sokhummāni" refers to the knowledges that penetrate the subtle characteristics such as impermanence. "Rūpa-sokhummena samannāgato hotīti" means being endowed with the knowledge that grasps the fine and subtle characteristics of form (rūpa). "Paramena" means with the supreme (knowledge). "Tena ca rūpa-sokhummena" means with that knowledge that grasps the subtle characteristics until reaching the state of conformity (anuloma). "Na samanupassatīti" means one does not see it simply because of its non-existence. "Na patthetīti" means one does not long for it simply because of its non-existence.
