The same method applies to the subtlety of feeling (vedanā) and so forth.

"Rūpa-sokhummataṃ ñatvā" means knowing the state of subtlety through the knowledge that grasps the fine and subtle characteristics of the aggregate of form (rūpa-kkhandha). "Vedanānañca sambhavaṃ" means also knowing the arising of the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-kkhandha). "Saññā yato samudetīti" means knowing the cause from which the aggregate of perception (saññā-kkhandha) arises. "Atthaṃ gacchati yattha cāti" means knowing the place (Nibbāna) where it ceases. "Saṅkhāre parato ñatvā" means knowing the aggregate of formations (saṅkhāra-kkhandha) as alien (parato), as something external to oneself, because of its nature of breaking down due to impermanence. By this term, the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) is taught. By the phrase "dukkhato no ca attato," the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā) and the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā) are shown. "Santo" means one who is peaceful due to the peacefulness of the defilements. "Santipade rato" means one who delights in Nibbāna. Thus, in the sutta, insight (vipassanā) is taught in four places, and in the verses, the supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara-dhamma) is also taught.

## 7. Paṭhama-agati-sutta-vaṇṇanā

17-19. In the seventh sutta, "agati-gamanāni" are not the paths that should be followed. "Chandāgatiṃ gacchatīti" means one goes to a wrong course through desire (chanda) or favoritism; one does what should not be done. The same method applies to the remaining suttas. "Chandā dosā bhayā mohā" means through desire, hatred, fear, and delusion. "Ativattatīti" means one transcends. The eighth sutta is clear in its meaning. In the ninth sutta, it is taught by both methods according to the capacity of those individuals who are capable of realizing the Four Noble Truths.

## 10. Bhattuddesaka-sutta-vaṇṇanā

In the tenth sutta, "bhattuddesako" refers to the one who assigns meals by tickets (salāka-bhatta) and so forth. "Kāmesu asaṃyatā" refers to those who are unrestrained in the objects of sensual pleasure (vatthu-kāma) by means of the defilements of sensual pleasure (kilesa-kāma).
263:
Such a person is also called the dregs of the assembly (parisākasata). 'By the recluse' (samaṇena) means by the Buddha-recluse. Such a person is called the cream of the assembly (parisāmaṇḍa) because of their purity.

## The Second Chapter: Cara Vagga is finished.

## 3. Uruvela Vagga

## 1. Commentary on the First Uruvela Sutta

In the first sutta of the third chapter, regarding the word 'Uruvelāyaṃ', Uruvelā means a great heap or a great mound of sand. Alternatively, 'uru' is said to mean sand, and 'velā' means a boundary. The sand brought because of transgressing the boundary is called Uruvelā; this is how the meaning should be understood here.

In detail: In the past, before the Buddhas had arisen, ten thousand young men of good family went forth as ascetics and lived in that region. One day, they gathered and made this agreement: 'Bodily actions and verbal actions are evident to others, but mental actions are not. Therefore, if anyone thinks a sensual thought, a thought of ill-will, or a thought of cruelty, there is no other accuser for him. Let him accuse himself, and bringing sand in a bowl, let him pour it in this place; let this be his penalty.'

From then on, whoever thought such a thought would pour sand there with a bowl. In this way, a great mound of sand gradually formed. Later generations of people enclosed that place and made it a site for a shrine (cetiya). With reference to that shrine site, it is said: 'Uruvelā means a great heap, a great mound of sand.' With the same reference, it is also said: 'Alternatively, uru means sand, velā means boundary; the sand brought because of transgressing the boundary is called Uruvelā.'

'On the bank of the river Nerañjarā' shows that he was staying on the bank of the Nerañjarā river, depending on the village of Uruvelā. 'At the Ajapāla Banyan tree' means that goatherds used to sit and stand in the shade of that banyan tree. Therefore, that banyan tree became known as the Ajapāla Banyan tree. It means 'under that banyan tree'. 'Newly awakened' (paṭhamābhisambuddho) means having first realized the Four Noble Truths. 'Arose' (udapādi) means this thought arose in the fifth week (sattāha). Why did it arise? It arose because it is the practice of all Buddhas and because of past cultivation. To demonstrate this point of past cultivation, the Tittira Jātaka should be cited.
264:
Goatherds used to sit and stand in the shade of that banyan tree. Therefore, that banyan tree came to be known as the Ajapāla Banyan tree. It means 'under that banyan tree'. 'Newly awakened' (paṭhamābhisambuddho) means having first become a Buddha by knowing the Four Noble Truths. 'Arose' (udapādi) means this thought (vitakka) arose in the fifth week. Why did it arise? It arose because it is the practice of all Buddhas and because of past cultivation. Between these two, the Tittira Jātaka is brought forward to show the past cultivation.

In detail: While an elephant, a monkey, and a partridge (tittira) were living in a certain place, they thought, 'Whoever among us is the eldest, let us live showing respect to him.' Looking at a banyan tree and investigating, 'Who among us is the eldest?', they realized the partridge was the eldest. They showed the partridge the respect due to an elder, lived together in harmony and joy, and were reborn in heaven. Knowing that reason, the deity residing in the tree spoke this verse:

'Those humans who are skilled in the Dhamma,
And show respect to the elders,
Are praiseworthy in this very life,
And reach a happy destination in the life to come.'

Thus, even when born in the rootless animal realm, the Tathāgata delighted in living with respect; why would he not delight in it now that he has become a Buddha? (He certainly does). 'Without respect' (agāravo) means being devoid of respect for others besides himself, not placing anyone in a position of reverence. 'Without deference' (appatisso) means being devoid of obeying the authority of one who should be respected, not placing anyone in the position of a senior. In this context, 'a recluse or a brahmin' (samaṇaṃ vā brāhmaṇaṃ vā) refers only to those recluses and brahmins who have calmed and warded off evil. 'Having honored and respected' (sakkattvā garuṃ katvā) means bringing about honor and reverence.

'In the world with its devas' (sadevake loke) and so on: it is called 'sadevaka' because it is together with devas. Although Mara and Brahma are included by taking 'devas', Mara, known as Vasavatti, exercises power over all; Brahma is of great majesty—with one finger he can spread light over a thousand world systems, with two fingers over two thousand, and with ten fingers over ten thousand world systems. 'With its Maras and its Brahmas' (samārake sabrahmake) is mentioned separately so that they may not say, 'This one is more perfect in virtue than the Buddha.' Similarly, recluses are learned, virtuous, and wise through the power of one Nikāya and so on; brahmins are also learned and wise through the power of the science of sites (vatthuvijjā) and so on. 'With its recluses and brahmins' (sasamaṇabrāhmaṇiyā pajāya) is mentioned so that they may not say, 'These are more perfect than the Buddha.'

The term 'with its devas and humans' (sadevemanussāya) is used to include again the devas and humans already mentioned, to show them without exception. Alternatively, the first three terms are spoken by way of the world of locations (okāsaloka), and the last two terms are spoken by way of the world of beings (sattaloka). 'One more perfect in virtue' (sīlasampannataraṃ) means a person who is especially superior in virtue. In this sutta, the four qualities starting with virtue are spoken of in terms of the mundane and the supramundane. Since the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimuttiñāṇadassana) is reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa), it is only mundane. 'Not seeing' (apassanto) means that our Buddha, from Avīci to the peak of existence, does not see anyone superior to himself in virtue and so on, and thus [thought], 'I shall live [respecting]...'
265:
The phrase "among the generation of recluses and brahmins" is spoken so that it cannot be said that there are recluses or brahmins who are more fully endowed with virtue and so forth than this Blessed One. The phrase "with devas and humans" is spoken by including those devas and humans already mentioned, for the purpose of showing them without exception. Alternatively, the first three terms are spoken in terms of the world (okāsaloka), while the last two are spoken in terms of beings (sattaloka). "Sīlasampannataraṃ" means a person who is more fully endowed with virtue, or more excellent in virtue. In this sutta, although the four qualities beginning with virtue are spoken of as both mundane and supramundane, the "knowledge and vision of liberation" (vimuttiñāṇadassana) is purely mundane. This is because it is only reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇāñāṇa).

"Appeared" means: This Blessed One, seeing no one superior to himself in virtue and so forth from Avīci to the peak of existence (bhavagga), thought, "I shall live honoring and depending on the ninefold supramundane Dhamma (nava-lokuttara-dhamma) that I myself have realized." The Blessed One reflected on the reason, the meaning, the benefit, and the distinction. At that time, the Brahma [Sahampati] thought, "I shall go and arouse effort in that Blessed One," and he appeared clearly before the Blessed One; the meaning is that he stood in his presence.

In this context of "vihariṃsu viharanti ca" (they lived and they live), if someone should say, "Because of the plural word 'viharanti', there are many Buddhas in the present as well," they should be refuted with the words: "Venerable sir, the Blessed One is even now the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha)."

One should demonstrate the absence of other Buddhas through suttas such as: "I have no teacher, no one like me exists; in the world with its devas, I have no counterpart." Therefore (since all Buddhas revere the True Dhamma), "one who desires greatness" means one who wishes for the state of being great. "One who remembers the dispensation of the Buddhas" means one who recalls the instruction of the Buddhas.

"When" means at which time. "Endowed with greatness" means endowed with the four types of greatness: greatness of seniority (rattaññu-mahatta), greatness of abundance (vepulla-mahatta), greatness of the holy life (brahmacariya-mahatta), and greatness of foremost gains (lābhagga-mahatta). "Then I also had respect for the Saṅgha" means: At what time did the Blessed One show respect to the Saṅgha? It was at the time of the offering of a pair of cloths by Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī. For at that time, the Blessed One, in saying regarding the pair of cloths brought for him, "Gotamī, give it to the Saṅgha; when it is given to the Saṅgha, I will be honored and the Saṅgha will be too," was indeed showing respect to the Saṅgha.
266:
## 2. Commentary on the Second Uruvela Sutta

In the second sutta, "sambahulā" means many people. "Brahmāṇā" means the brahmins who came together with the Huhukka brahmin. "Jiṇṇā" means those decayed by old age. "VuḍḎhā" means those aged in years. "Mahallakā" means those who are elders by birth. "Addhagatā" means those who have passed through the three stages of life. "Sutametaṃ" means "we have heard this word." "Tayidaṃ bho gotama tatheva" means "Venerable Gotama, that matter which we have heard is exactly so." "Tayidaṃ bho gotama na sampannameva" means "that failure to perform such acts as salutation is indeed improper."

In the terms beginning with "akālavādī": one is an "akālavādī" because one speaks at the wrong time. One is an "abhūtavādī" because one speaks what is not a fact or what does not exist. One is an "anatthavādī" because one speaks what is unbeneficial and does not speak what is beneficial. One is an "adhammavādī" because one speaks what is not Dhamma and does not speak Dhamma. One is an "avinayavādī" because one speaks what is not Vinaya and does not speak Vinaya. "Anidhānavatiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā" means one who speaks words not worth treasuring in the heart. "Akālena" means at a time unsuitable for speaking. "Anapadesaṃ" means without a reason to cite, not speaking in a way that includes the cause. "Apariyantavatiṃ" means without limit, not speaking by showing the boundaries. "Anatthasaṃhitaṃ" means not speaking in connection with mundane or supramundane benefits. "Bālo thero'tveva saṅkhaṃ gacchati" means he is reckoned only as a foolish elder.

The terms beginning with "kālavādī" should be understood by way of the opposite of the meanings already mentioned. "Paṇḍito thero'tveva saṅkhaṃ gacchati" means he is reckoned as "wise" because he is endowed with wisdom, and as an "elder" because he has attained the state of stability.

"Bahussuto hoti" means that the doctrine (pariyatti) heard by that person is abundant. The meaning is that the ninefold dispensation of the Teacher (navaṅga satthusāsana) has been learned by way of the Pali, the connection (anusandhi), and the sequence. "Sutadharo" means one who is a container for the doctrine heard. If a person learns from this side but it escapes from the other side, not remaining like water in a broken pot, and is unable to preach or teach even a single sutta or Jātaka in the midst of an assembly, such a person is not called a "sutadharo." If the word of the Buddha learned by a person remains just as it was when learned, and does not vanish even if he does not recite it for ten or twenty years, such a person is called a "sutadharo." "Sutasannicayo" means one who has accumulated and collected the doctrine heard. For such a person, the doctrine heard is accumulated in the casket of the heart, like an inscription on stone, or like lion's fat placed in a golden vessel...
267:
The presence of learning in the heart is called 'sutasannicaya' (one who accumulates what is heard). 'Dhātā' means retaining the learned teachings through mastery. For some, the learned word of the Buddha is not stable and wavers due to lack of mastery. When asked, "Recite such-and-such a Sutta or Jātaka," they say, "I will know after reciting, comparing, and inquiring." For others, the learned Dhamma is mastered and flows like the stream of the subconscious (bhavaṅga). When asked, "Recite such-and-such a Sutta or Jātaka," they can immediately bring it forth and recite that very Sutta or Jātaka. Referring to such a person, it is said 'dhātā'.

'Vacasā paricitā' means having recited by word of mouth in terms of ten Suttas, ten Vaggas, or ten sets of fifty (Paṇṇāsa). 'Manasānupekkhitā' means having repeatedly reflected with the mind. To one who contemplates with the mind the word of the Buddha recited by mouth, it becomes clear in various places. It appears to wisdom just as forms appear to one who stands having lit a great lamp. Referring to such a person, this is said. 'Diṭṭhiyā suppaṭividdhā' means having well-penetrated and understood with wisdom both in terms of meaning and reason.

In the word 'ābhicetasikānaṃ', 'abhiceto' refers to the exalted, pure mind or higher mind (adhicitta). Those states born in that exalted higher mind or depending on that higher mind are called 'ābhicetasika'. 'Diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānaṃ' means those that are happy dwellings in the present life. 'Diṭṭhadhamma' refers to the present existence (attabhāva). This name, 'happy dwellings in the present life', is a designation for the jhānas of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara). Meditators who sit having attained those jhānas experience the unsoiled bliss of renunciation (nekkhamma) in this very existence. Therefore, they are called 'diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārāni'.

'Nikāmalābhī' means one who obtains as desired, one who obtains by the power of one's own will, meaning one who is able to attain [the jhāna] at any desired moment. 'Akicchalābhī' means one who is able to attain [the jhāna] by discarding the opposing hindrances (nīvaraṇa) with ease. 'Akasiralābhī' means one who obtains the abundant jhānas without trouble, meaning one who is able to emerge [from them] according to the determined time. Some persons merely obtain the jhāna but are unable to attain it at any desired moment. Some are able to attain it as desired but discard the obstructive states with difficulty. Some can attain it as desired and discard the obstructive states without difficulty, yet are unable to emerge exactly at the determined time like a water-clock. When a person possesses these three types of perfection, they are called 'akicchalābhī akasiralābhī'. The words beginning with 'āsavānaṃ khayā' have the same meaning as previously stated. Thus, in this Sutta, when speaking of virtue, learning (bāhusacca), and jhāna, it refers only to the virtue, learning, and the jhānas used by an Arahant. 'Āsavānaṃ...'
268:
By the words beginning with "āsavānaṃ khayā," the fruition of Arahantship (arahattaphala) is spoken of. Here, it should be understood that the function of the path (magga) is revealed by its fruit.

"Uddhatena" means with a mind accompanied by restlessness. "Samphaṃ" means frivolous talk. "Asamāhitasankappo" means one whose thoughts are not fixed (not concentrated) on a good object. "Mago" means one who is like a wild deer. "Āရာ" means one who is far away. "Thāvareyyamhā" means from the permanent state (Nibbāna). "Pāpadiṭṭhi" means one with evil views. "Anādaro" means one who is disrespectful. "Sutavā" means one endowed with learning. "Paṭibhānavā" means one endowed with the two types of analytical clarity (paṭibhāna). "Paññāyatthaṃ vipassatī" means seeing through the meaning of the Four Truths with path-wisdom accompanied by insight (vipassanā). "Pāragū sabbadhammānaṃ" means one who has reached the further shore of all phenomena such as the aggregates (khandha). One is a "pāragū" (one who has reached the further shore) in six ways: through higher knowledge (abhiññā), full understanding (pariññā), abandoning (pahāna), development (bhāvanā), realization (sacchikiriyā), and attainment (samāpatti); thus reaching the further shore, which is the end of all phenomena. "Akhilo" means one free from the fallow of lust (rāga), etc. "Paṭibhānavā" means one endowed with the two types of analytical clarity. "Brahmacariyassa kevalī" means one who is consummate in the entire holy life. The remaining words here are clear.

## ၃။ လောကသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ

In the third Sutta, the Loka Sutta, "loka" means the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca). "Abhisambuddho" means known, personally realized. "Lokasmā" means from the truth of suffering. "Pahīno" means abandoned by the knowledge of the path of Arahantship at the terrace of the Great Enlightenment. "Tathāgatassa bhāvitā" means developed by the Tathāgata.

Having thus declared his state of Buddhahood through the Four Truths by this much, he now speaks the words beginning with "Yaṃ bhikkhave" to declare his state of being a Tathāgata. In that Pali text, "diṭṭhaṃ" means the base of visible forms (rūpāyatana). "Sutaṃ" means the base of sounds (saddāyatana). "Mutaṃ" means the base of smells (gandhāyatana), the base of tastes (rasāyatana), and the base of tangibles (phoṭṭhabbāyatana), because they are apprehended by reaching [the sense organ]. "Viññātaṃ" means the base of mental objects (dhammārammaṇa) such as pleasure and pain. "Pattaṃ" means an object reached whether by seeking or without seeking. "Pariyesitaṃ" means an object sought whether reached or not reached. "Anuvicaritaṃ manasā" means an object repeatedly wandered over by the mind.
269: "The Tathāgata has fully realized [this]"—with these words, this meaning is shown. In the immeasurable world-systems, whatever visual object, such as a blue or yellow appearance, of this world with its devas comes into the range of the eye-door: "This being, at this moment, having seen this particular visual object, has become happy, or sad, or indifferent"—all this is thus fully realized by the Tathāgata. Likewise, in the immeasurable world-systems, whatever sound, such as the sound of a large drum or a mudiṅga drum, of this world with its devas comes into the range of the ear-door; whatever odor, such as the odor of roots or bark, comes into the range of the nose-door; whatever flavor, such as the flavor of roots or stems, comes into the range of the tongue-door; whatever tangible object, consisting of the earth element, fire element, or air element, such as roughness or softness, comes into the range of the body-door: "This being, at this moment, having touched this particular tangible object, has become happy, or sad, or indifferent"—all this is thus fully realized by the Tathāgata. Likewise, in the immeasurable world-systems, whatever mental object, consisting of pleasure, pain, and so on, of this world with its devas comes into the range of the mind-door: "This being, at this moment, having known this particular mental object, has become happy, or sad, or indifferent"—all this is thus fully realized by the Tathāgata. Monks, there is the object seen, heard, sensed (by nose, tongue, and body), and cognized (by mind-consciousness) by all beings. Among those objects, there is nothing not seen, not heard, not sensed, or not cognized by the Tathāgata. For this mass of people, there are objects not reached even after seeking, objects not reached without seeking, objects reached after seeking, and objects reached without seeking. For the Tathāgata, however, there is absolutely no object that is not reached, that is, not realized through knowledge. Therefore, he is called "Tathāgata." Because he has known exactly as it is known by the world, he is called "Tathāgata." In the Pāḷi text, the word "abhisambuddha" (fully realized) has the same meaning as the word "gata" (gone/known). In this way, the meaning of the conclusion "Tathāgata" should be understood in all sections. The suitability of that meaning has already been stated in the detailed explanation of the word "Tathāgata" in the commentary on the Ekapuggala-vagga. However, in this context, the word "aññadatthu" is a particle meaning "certainly." He is called "dasa" because he sees. He is called "vasavattī" because he wields mastery. "Having fully known the entire world" means having known the world of beings within the three realms. "Everything in the world as it really is" means having known everything that should be known in that world of beings within the three realms, without distortion. "Visamyutto" (detached) means...
270:
He is detached by abandoning the four yokes (yogas). 'Anūpayo' means being free from the attachments of craving (taṇhā) and views (diṭṭhi). 'Sabbābhibhū' means remaining after having conquered all sense objects, such as forms (rūpa) and others. 'Dhīro' means being endowed with steady courage. 'Sabbaganthappamocano' means remaining liberated from all four knots (ganthas). 'Phuṭṭhassa' means 'of the one who has touched' (the Buddha). Here, the genitive case (sāmivibhatta) is used in the sense of the instrument (karaṇattha). 'Paramā santī' refers to Nibbāna. Because that Nibbāna is touched by the knowledge of realization, it is called 'Nibbāna, where there is no fear.' Alternatively, 'paramā santī' means supreme peace. What is that peace? It is Nibbāna itself. Since there is no danger from anywhere in Nibbāna, it is called 'akutobhaya' (fearless). 'Vimutto upadhisaṅkhaye' means being liberated by the fruition of liberation (phalavimutti) which has Nibbāna—the destruction of acquisitions (upadhi)—as its object. 'Sīho anuttaro' means the Buddha is called the peerless lion because of His endurance of dangers and His crushing of defilements (kilesas). 'Brahma' means the noble one. 'Itī' means thus, having known the virtues of the Tathāgata. 'Saṅgammā' means having assembled. 'Taṃ namassantī' means those who have gone for refuge pay homage to that Tathāgata. Now, to show the words they speak while paying homage, the words beginning with 'Danto' are spoken. The meaning of those words is very clear.

## 4. Kāḷakārāmasutta-vaṇṇanā
The fourth sutta was delivered due to a specific occasion. What was that occasion? It was due to a discussion concerning the virtues of the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala). It is said that Cūḷasubhaddā, the daughter of Anāthapiṇḍika, thinking, "I shall go to the house of the merchant Kāḷaka's son in the city of Sāketa," approached the Teacher and took a promise, saying, "Venerable Sir, I am going to a family of wrong views. If there is an opportunity to invite You there, it would be a delay if a person had to be sent. Therefore, may the Blessed One keep me in mind." The great merchant, saying, "My daughter-in-law has arrived," performed a wedding ceremony, prepared a great amount of food and snacks, and invited five hundred naked ascetics (acelakas). While they were seated, the merchant sent for Cūḷasubhaddā, saying, "Let my daughter come and pay homage to the Arahants." The noble female disciple (ariyasāvikā), who had attained the fruit of Stream-entry, as soon as the word 'Arahants' was mentioned, thought, "How fortunate I am!" and went joyfully. However, upon seeing those naked ascetics of ungraceful appearance, she said, "Father, those called monks are not of such a nature. Those who have no shame (hiri) within themselves and no dread (ottappa) externally are not monks. How loathsome!" Having said this, she spat and returned to her own quarters.
271:
Then the Acelakas (naked ascetics) threatened the merchant, saying, "Great Merchant, from where did you get such an ill-omened, wretched woman? Is there no other maiden in the entire Jambudīpa?" The merchant replied, "Teachers, whether it was done knowingly or unknowingly, let it be. I will see to this matter myself." After dismissing the Acelakas, he went to Cūḷasubhaddā and asked, "Dear daughter, why did you do such a thing? Why did you cause the Arahants to be ashamed?"

"Father, those who are called monks are not of such a nature," she replied. Then the merchant asked her:

"What kind of monks are yours, whom you praise so greatly?
What is their virtue, what is their conduct? Tell me when asked."

She replied:

"With tranquil faculties and tranquil minds, with tranquil power, they are established in the path of virtue.
With downcast eyes and measured speech, such are my monks.

They dwell having entered the forest, like an elephant that has broken its bonds.
Solitary and without a companion, such are my monks."

Having said this, she stood before the merchant and spoke of the virtues of the Triple Gem. Upon hearing her words, the merchant said, "If it is so, let us invite your monks and perform a blessing ceremony." She asked, "Father, when will you do it?" The merchant thought, "I will send for them after a few days have passed," but he told her, "Dear daughter, we will do it tomorrow."

In the evening, she ascended to the upper palace, took a large flower basket, and while recollecting the virtues of the Buddha, she scattered eight handfuls of flowers towards the Buddha. With hands joined in reverence, she stood and made this aspiration: "Blessed One, please accept my alms tomorrow together with five hundred monks."

Those flowers traveled and remained as a canopy over the head of the Buddha. The Buddha, through reflection, saw the reason. At the conclusion of the Dhamma teaching, the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika paid homage to the Buddha and said, "Venerable Sir, please accept alms at my house tomorrow together with five hundred monks." The Buddha replied, "Merchant, we have already accepted the invitation of Cūḷasubhaddā." "Venerable Sir, I did not see anyone coming," he said. "It is true, Merchant, but a faithful laywoman, even if staying a hundred or a thousand yojanas away, is as visible as the Himalayan mountains," the Buddha said, and uttered this verse:

"The virtuous shine from afar like the Himalayan mountains. The wicked, like arrows shot in the night, are not seen even when near."

Anāthapiṇḍika said, "Venerable Sir, please favor me tomorrow," and then departed. The Buddha called Venerable Ānanda and said, "Ānanda, I shall go to the city of Sāketa. Give the voting tickets (salāka) to five hundred monks. In giving them, give only to those monks who possess the six supernormal powers (chalabhiññā)." The Elder did as the Buddha commanded. At the end of the night, Cūḷasubhaddā thought, "The Buddhas have many duties and many things to do. Will he remember me or not? What shall I do?" At that moment, the Great King Vessavaṇa said to Cūḷasubhaddā, "Dear daughter, do not be troubled, do not be dejected. The Blessed One has accepted your meal for tomorrow together with the Saṅgha of monks."
272:
"The virtuous shine from afar like the Himalayan mountains.
The wicked are not seen in this world, like arrows shot in the night."

The Blessed One uttered this verse. The merchant Anāthapiṇḍika paid homage and said, "Venerable Sir, please show favor to my daughter," and then departed. The Buddha addressed the Elder Ānanda: "Ānanda, I shall go to Sāketa. Give the voting tickets to five hundred monks. When giving them, give only to those monks who possess the six supernormal powers." The Elder did as instructed. At the end of the night, Cūḷasubhaddā thought, "The Buddhas have many duties and many things to do. Will he remember me, or will he not? What should I do?" At that moment, the Great King Vessavaṇa said to Cūḷasubhaddā, "Dear lady, do not be troubled, do not be dejected. The Blessed One has accepted your meal for tomorrow together with the Saṅgha of monks."

Greatly delighted, Cūḷasubhaddā prepared the offerings. Sakka, the King of Gods, also called the celestial architect Vissakamma and ordered, "Dear son, the Buddha will go to the city of Sāketa to Cūḷasubhaddā. Create five hundred peaked mansions (kūṭāgāra)." He did as commanded. Surrounded by five hundred monks with the six supernormal powers, the Buddha traveled to the city of Sāketa by means of the peaked mansions, as if painting the emerald-colored sky.

Cūḷasubhaddā, having offered alms to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, paid homage to the Buddha and said, "Venerable Sir, my in-laws are of wrong view. Please preach a suitable Dhamma to them." The Buddha preached the Dhamma. The merchant Kāḷaka became a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) and offered his park to the Buddha. The Acelaka ascetics, saying "This was given to us first," did not wish to leave. "Go! Evict them by the manner of those who must be evicted," it was said, and after having all the Acelakas evicted, a monastery was built for the Buddha in that very park. Having made a noble gift, he poured the water of dedication. Because it was built and offered by the merchant Kāḷaka, it became known as the Kāḷakārāma. The Blessed One resided there at that time. Therefore, it is said, "He dwells in Sāketa at the Kāḷakārāma."

"He addressed the monks" means he addressed the five hundred monks. It is heard that those monks were sons of good families residing in the city of Sāketa who, having heard the Buddha's Dhamma teaching, had ordained in the presence of the Buddha. While sitting in the assembly hall, they spoke of the Buddha's virtues: "Oh, how great are the virtues of the Buddhas! The Buddha has freed such a person of wrong view as the merchant Kāḷaka from his views, established him in the Fruit of Stream-entry, and made the entire city of Sāketa like a celestial realm."
273:
## 
"The Blessed One has made the entire city of Sāketa like a celestial realm," they spoke of the Buddha's virtues. The Blessed One, reflecting on the minds of those monks who were speaking of his virtues, thought: "When I depart, a great discourse will arise. At the conclusion of the discourse, these five hundred monks will be established in Arahantship, and the great earth will shake as far as the water's edge." He then went to the hall of Dhamma, sat upon the noble Buddha-seat that had been prepared, and, with those monks as the primary audience, began this discourse: "Monks, in the world with its devas..." and so forth. Thus, it should be understood that this Sutta was delivered on account of the talk concerning his virtues.

In that discourse, at the conclusion of the phrase "I know that," the great earth shook as far as the water's edge. "Abbhannāsiṃ" means "I have known with higher knowledge." "Viditaṃ" means "it is known by making it manifest." By this, he shows: "Others merely know; I, however, have known by making it manifest." By these three terms, the Ground of Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-bhūmi) is described. "Taṃ tathāgato na upaṭṭhāsi" means that the Tathāgata does not cling to or approach the objects arising at the six sense-doors through craving or views. Indeed, the Blessed One sees a form with the eye, yet the Blessed One has no intense lust (rāga); that Blessed One has a mind that is well-liberated. He hears a sound with the ear. He smells an odor with the nose. He tastes a flavor with the tongue. He touches a tangible object with the body. He cognizes a mental object with the mind, yet the Blessed One has no intense lust; that Blessed One has a mind that is well-liberated. Therefore, it is said: "Taṃ tathāgato na upaṭṭhāsi." By this phrase, the Ground of the One whose Taints are Destroyed (Khīṇāsava-bhūmi) is described.

"Taṃ mamassa musā" means "that word of mine would be a lie." "Taṃ passa tādisameva" means "that word too would be just a lie." "Taṃ mamassa kalī" means "that word would be my fault." By this much, the Ground of Truth (Sacca-bhūmi) is described.

"Daṭṭhā daṭṭhabbaṃ" means "having seen what is to be seen." "Diṭṭhaṃ na maññati" means he does not conceive that seen visible object through craving, conceit, or views, thinking, "I see exactly what the multitude sees." "Adiṭṭhaṃ na maññati" means he does not conceive through craving and so on, thinking, "I see this which the multitude does not see." "Daṭṭhabbaṃ na maññati" means he does not conceive through those conceits, thinking, "I see what is to be seen." This is because what is to be seen can also be unseen. Since such words can be found in all three periods of time, this meaning is stated. "Daṭṭhāraṃ na maññati" means...
274:
...he does not conceive any single being as a "seer" through those conceits of craving, conceit, and views. In the remaining instances as well, the meaning should be understood in this same way. By this much, the Ground of Emptiness (Suññatā-bhūmi) is described.

"Iti kho bhikkhave" means "Thus indeed, monks." "Tādī" refers to "Tāditā," which is the state of being consistently the same. The Tathāgata is of such a nature in the face of gain and the like, and he is of that same nature in the face of loss and the like. Therefore, it is said: "He is 'Such' in gain, and 'Such' in loss. He is 'Such' in fame, and 'Such' in obscurity. He is 'Such' in blame, and 'Such' in praise. He is 'Such' in pleasure, and 'Such' in pain." Because of this state of being unshaken by the eight worldly conditions, he is called "Tādī." It should be understood that there is no other "Such One" who is superior or more sublime than that "Suchness" of the Tathāgata. By this much of the text, the Ground of Suchness (Tādi-bhūmi) is described. As the Blessed One brought the discourse to a close with these five grounds, the great earth shook as a witness at each of the five points. At the conclusion of the discourse, beginning with those five hundred clansmen who had recently ordained, eighty-four thousand beings among the devas and humans who had reached that place drank the nectar of the Deathless (Nibbāna).

The Blessed One, having concluded the Sutta and wishing to crown it with verses, spoke the words beginning with "Yaṃ kiñci." In those verses, "Ajjhositaṃ sacca-mutaṃ paresaṃ" means clinging to something as truth, having swallowed and finalized it, based on the faith of others or through the power of others' convictions. "Sayasaṃvutesu" means among those with wrong views who have taken up and cherished their own self-restrained beliefs. Those with wrong views are said to be "self-restrained." Among those with wrong views, known as the self-restrained, the Tathāgata, the Such One, would not hold any of their words—whether true or false—as supreme, nor would he believe or place confidence in them, thinking, "This alone is truth, all else is empty." "Etancā sallanti" means "this dart of views." "Paṭikacca disvā" means "having seen beforehand at the foot of the Bodhi tree." "Visattā" means "attached, bound, or obstructed." "Jānāmi passāmi tatheva etaṃ" means "I know and see in that very way how this generation is clinging, having swallowed and finalized their attachment." It means that such clinging to views as held by this generation does not exist for the Tathāgatas.
275:
## 5. Brahmacariya Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the fifth sutta, the term 'jana-kuhanatthaṃ' means for the purpose of impressing the multitude of people through the three modes of deception. 'Na jana-lapanatthaṃ' means it is not for the purpose of cajoling or flattering the multitude. 'Na lābhasakkārasilokānisaṃsatthaṃ' means it is not for the benefit of receiving robes and other requisites, nor for the sake of praise. 'Na itivādappamokkhānisaṃsatthaṃ' means it is not for the benefit of engaging in various debates, nor for the purpose of escaping the accusations of others. 'Na iti maṃ jano jānatū' means it is not for the purpose of having people know, "This monk is indeed such and such."

'Saṃvaratthaṃ' means for the purpose of restraint through the five kinds of restraint. 'Pahānatthaṃ' means for the purpose of abandoning through the three kinds of abandoning. 'Virāgatthaṃ' means for the purpose of the fading away of lust and other defilements. 'Nirodhatthaṃ' means for the purpose of the cessation of those very same defilements. 'Anītihaṃ' means being free from hearsay; it has the meaning of not following the faith of others. 'Nibbānogadhagāminaṃ' means having the nature of entering into Nibbāna. Indeed, the holy life of the Path (magga-brahmacariya) arises and exists within Nibbāna, having Nibbāna as its object. 'Paṭipajjanti' means they practice both kinds of practice. In this sutta, both the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) are discussed, whereas in the verses, only the cessation of the round is discussed.

## 6. Kuha Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the sixth sutta, 'kuhā' refers to those who are deceivers. 'Thaddhā' refers to those who are stubborn due to anger and pride. 'Lapā' refers to those who speak to cajole or flatter donors. 'Siṅgī' refers to those possessed of manifest defilements resembling horns, as described in the text: "What therein is 'siṅga' (horn/ostentation)? That which is ostentation, cleverness, craftiness, being well-guarded like a gatepost," and so on. 'Unnalā' refers to those who stand lifting up empty pride. 'Asamāhitā' refers to those who do not attain even mere one-pointedness of mind.

'Na me te, bhikkhave, bhikkhū māmakā' means, "Monks, those monks do not belong to me; they are not mine." This is said because they had ordained in reference to the Teacher [but do not follow his teaching]. In the phrase 'te kho me, bhikkhave, bhikkhū māmakā', the word 'me' is also used because they ordained in reference to himself, and because they practice rightly, he says 'māmakā' (they are mine).

'Vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ āpajjanti': they reach 'vuddhi' (growth) through the increase of virtues such as morality; 'virūḷhi' (increase) through their unwavering stability; and 'vepulla' (expansion) through their spreading in all directions. These monks are in the process of increasing until the Path of Arahantship; when they reach the Fruit of Arahantship, they are called 'virūḷhā' (those who have increased). Thus, in this sutta as well as in the verses, both the round of rebirth and the cessation of the round are discussed.
276:
## 7. Santuṭṭhi Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, 'appāni' means things that are trifling or few. 'Sulabhāni' means things that are easily obtained, which can be found anywhere. 'Anavajjāni' means things that are faultless. 'Piṇḍiyālopabhojanaṃ' means food obtained as a mere morsel by wandering through the strength of one's calves. 'Pūtimuttaṃ' means any kind of cow's urine. Just as even a body with a golden complexion is called a 'putrid body' (pūtikāya), so too, even fresh urine is called 'putrid urine' (pūtimutta).

'Vighāto' means the state of being free from distress; it means there is no suffering of the mind. In the phrase 'disā nappaṭihanyati', if a thought arises in a monk, "If I go to such and such a place, I will obtain robes and other requisites," then for him, the quarter is said to be obstructed (paṭihanyati). If such a thought does not arise, the quarter is said to be unobstructed (nappaṭihanyati). 'Dhammā' refers to the practices (paṭipatti-dhamma). 'Sāmaññassānulomikā' means those things that are suitable for the state of a recluse (samaṇa-dhamma). 'Adhiggahitā' means all these things are mastered by a monk with a contented mind, overcoming opposing states, and they remain within him, not outside.

## 8. Ariyavaṃsa Sutta Vaṇṇanā

The eighth sutta is delivered according to the inclination of the Blessed One and the inclinations of other individuals. It is heard that the Blessed One, while seated on the noble Buddha-seat prepared in the assembly hall of the Jetavana Monastery, addressed forty thousand monks who were seated surrounding him according to his own inclination and theirs, saying, "Monks, there are these four lineages of the Noble Ones," and thus began this Mahā-ariyavaṃsa Sutta. In that context, 'ariyavaṃsā' means the lineages of the Noble Ones. Just as there are lineages of kings (khattiya), brahmins, merchants, laborers, recluses, families, and dynasties, so too this eighth 'ariyavaṃsa' is the tradition of the Noble Ones, the lineage of the Noble Ones. This lineage of the Noble Ones is declared to be the foremost among these lineages, just as black sandalwood (kāḷānusārī) and other fragrances are the best among root-fragrances and the like.

Who are those Noble Ones (Ariyas) whose lineages these are? Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Tathāgata are called Noble Ones; because these are the lineages of those Noble Ones, they are called 'ariyavaṃsā'. In the past, four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand cycles ago, there were those known as Taṇhaṅkara, Medhaṅkara, Saraṇaṅkara, and Dīpaṅkara...
277:
Four Buddhas have arisen; they are Noble Ones (Ariyas). Because they are the lineage of those Noble Ones, they are called the Noble Lineages (Ariyavaṃsa). After the Parinibbāna of those Buddhas, after an incalculable period (asaṅkheyya) had passed, the Buddha named Koṇḍañña arose... In this Auspicious Aeon (Bhaddakappa), four Buddhas have arisen: Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, Kassapa, and our Buddha Gotama. Because they are the lineage of those Noble Ones, they are called the Noble Lineages. Alternatively, because they are the lineage of all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Noble Disciples (Buddhasāvaka Ariyas) of the past, future, and present, they are called the Noble Lineages.

These Noble Lineages should be known as the foremost (agga), as having existed for a long time (rattaññū), and as the lineage (vaṃsa). They are ancient and not recently arisen. They are unmixed, unconfused, and not discarded. The Buddhas of the past did not mix them, nor did they discard them, thinking, 'What shall we do with these?' Even now, they are not discarded. The Buddhas of the future will also not discard them. They are not reviled by wise recluses and brahmins in the world; they are not blamed or censured by wise recluses and brahmins.

'He is content' means he is content by way of contentment with the four requisites. 'With whatever kind of robe' means he is not content with just any robe among those that are coarse, fine, rough, excellent, durable, or worn out, but rather he is content with whatever kind of robe he receives. There are three types of contentment regarding robes: contentment with what is obtained (yathālābhasantuṭṭha), contentment according to one's strength (yathābalasantuṭṭha), and contentment with what is suitable (yathāsāruppasantuṭṭha). The same applies to almsfood and so on. Their detailed explanation should be understood according to the method stated in this sutta: 'Monks, for one who is content, wholesome states that have not yet arisen do arise.' Thus, referring to these three types of contentment, it is said: 'He is content with whatever kind of robe; he is content with any robe among those he receives.'

In this context, the robe should be known, the field of the robe should be known, the refuse-rag (paṃsukūla) should be known, contentment with the robe should be known, and the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) connected with the robe should be known. Therein, 'the robe should be known' means the six types of robes such as linen (khoma) and the six types of subordinate robes such as silk (dukūla) should be known. These twelve are allowable (kappiya) robes. However, robes made of kusa-grass, bark, planks, hair, animal wool, owl feathers, tree bark, creepers, etc., are unallowable (akappiya) robes.
278:
Cīvarakkhetta (the field of origin for robes) means there are six fields of origin, such as 'from the Saṅgha, from a group, from relatives, from friends, by one's own wealth, or from refuse-rags.' It should also be known that there are eight fields according to the eight matrices (mātikā).

Paṃsukūla (refuse-rag) means there are twenty-three types of refuse-rags to be known: robes dropped in a cemetery, at a market door, on a main road, on a rubbish heap; robes used for cleaning childbirth impurities (sotthiya); robes discarded after washing the head (sinānaṃ); robes discarded at a bathing place; robes brought back after being taken to a cemetery to shroud a corpse (gatapaccāgata); robes burnt by fire; robes gnawed by cows, termites, or mice; robes with torn edges or ends; robes discarded after being hoisted as a banner (dhajāhaṭa); robes offered at an anthill (thūpa); robes of monks; robes cast up on the shore by ocean waves (sāmuddika); robes discarded at a consecration ceremony (ābhisekiya); robes hidden under stones by travelers due to fear of thieves (panthika); robes brought by the wind; robes created by psychic power (iddhimaya); and robes given by devas (devadattiya). Among these twenty-three, sotthiya is a robe that removes childbirth impurities. Gatapaccāgata is a robe brought back after shrouding a corpse and taking it to the cemetery. Dhajāhaṭa is a robe brought from where a banner was hoisted. Thūpa is a robe offered at an anthill. Sāmuddika is a robe cast onto the land by ocean waves. Panthika is a robe hidden and worn by travelers after being beaten with stones due to fear of thieves. Iddhimaya is the robe of 'Ehi Bhikkhu' monks. The rest are clear.

Cīvarasantosa (contentment with robes) consists of twenty types: contentment in thinking, in going, in seeking, in obtaining, in accepting the right measure, in avoiding greed, contentment with what is obtained, according to strength, with what is suitable, with water, in washing, in making, in measurement, in thread, in sewing, in dyeing, in marking (kappabindu), in using, in avoiding hoarding, and in giving away.

Among these types of contentment with robes, a monk who has robes given by donors, after living permanently for the three months of the rains, should think for about a month. He makes the robe in the robe-month after the invitation (pavāraṇā). A monk who wears refuse-rags makes it in only half a month. This thinking for a month or half a month is called contentment in thinking (vitakkasantosa). A monk who is content with vitakkasantosa should be like the refuse-rag-wearing elder who lived in the Pācīnakhaṇḍarāji region.

It is heard that the elder, thinking, 'I will worship the shrine at Cetiyapabbata Vihāra,' came and worshipped the shrine. Then he thought, 'My robe is worn out; I will obtain one in a place where many monks live.' He went to the Mahāvihāra, saw the Elder of the Saṅgha, asked for a place to stay, and after staying there, he brought a robe the next day and paid respects to the Elder. The Elder...
279:
## 

“Venerable, what is it?” the Elder asked. “Venerable sir, I will go to the village gate,” he replied. “Venerable, I will go too,” he said. Saying “Very well, venerable sir,” that monk went and stood at the gatehouse of the Mahābodhi wall, thinking, “I will obtain a pleasing robe in the dwelling place of those with merit.” Then, reflecting “My thought is impure,” he turned back from that very spot. The next day, he turned back from near Ambaṅgaṇa, and the day after that, from the north gate of the Mahācetiya. On the fourth day, he went to the Elder. The Elder, thinking “This monk's thought might not be pure,” took his robe and entered the village with him, asking questions.

That night, a man, pressed by the need to defecate, did so in his cloth and discarded it on a rubbish heap. When the Paṃsukūlika Elder saw that cloth surrounded by black flies, he raised his hands in salutation (añjali). The Mahāthera asked, “Venerable, why do you pay homage to a rubbish heap?” “Venerable sir, I am not paying homage to a rubbish heap; I am paying homage to my father, the Dasabala Buddha. The Buddha, who performed a very difficult task, picked up from a cemetery the rag-robe (paṃsukūla) that had been discarded after being used to wrap the corpse of the slave girl named Puṇṇā, shaking off the worms that were about the size of a thumb-measure,” he replied. The Mahāthera thought, “The thought of the Paṃsukūlika monk is indeed pure.” The Paṃsukūlika Elder, standing right there, developed insight (vipassanā) and attained the three lower fruits. He took that cloth, made it into a robe, wore it, and went to Pācīnakhaṇḍarāji, where he attained the supreme fruit, Arahantship.

For one going for the sake of a robe, going with meditation as the priority without thinking “Where shall I get it?” is called contentment in going (gamanasantoṣa). When seeking a robe, seeking it by taking along a modest and virtuous monk, rather than seeking it with just anyone, is called contentment in seeking (pariyesanasantoṣa). While seeking, if one sees a robe being brought from afar and does not think “This will be pleasing” or “This will be unpleasing,” but is content with whatever is received, whether coarse or fine, it is called contentment in obtaining (paṭilābhasantoṣa). Even when receiving such a robe, being content with only as much as is sufficient for oneself, thinking “This much will be for a double-layered robe, this much for a single-layered robe,” is called contentment in the measure of receiving (mattappaṭiggahaṇasantoṣa). When seeking a robe, wandering from house to house in order without thinking “I will get something pleasing at the door of such-and-such a person,” is called contentment in avoiding greed (loluppavivajjanasantoṣa).

For one who can subsist on any robe, whether coarse or excellent, subsisting on whatever is obtained is called contentment with whatever is obtained (yathālābhasantoṣa). Subsisting on a robe that one can manage according to one's own strength is called contentment according to one's strength (yathābalasantoṣa). Pleasing...
280:
## 

Giving a pleasing robe to another and subsisting on any robe for oneself is called contentment with what is appropriate (yathāsāruppasantoṣa).

Washing with any water suitable for washing without investigating or reflecting “Where is the water pleasing? Where is it unpleasing?” is called contentment with water (udakasantoṣa). However, one should avoid water that is defiled by fine clay, red earth, rotten wood, or leaf-mold. When washing, washing by kneading with the hands without beating it with a club (muggara) or similar tools is called contentment in washing (dhovanasantoṣa). If it does not become clean that way, it is proper to wash it with water boiled with leaves. A person making a robe after washing it in this way, without spoiling his contentment by thinking “This robe is coarse, this robe is fine,” but making it in a manner that is just sufficient, is called contentment in making (karaṇasantoṣa). Making it just enough to cover the three circles (ti-maṇḍala) is called contentment in measurement (parimāṇasantoṣa). For the purpose of making a robe, taking any thread placed at one's feet, whether brought from a main road or a shrine, without investigating “I will search for pleasing thread,” is called contentment with thread (suttasantoṣa).

At the time of binding the borders (kusi), one should not pierce seven times within the space of one finger-breadth. For a monk doing this, if another monk does not become a companion (helper), there is no breach of duty (vattabheda) for him. However, one should pierce seven times within the space of three finger-breadths. For a monk doing this, there must be a companion who is a fellow traveler. If a monk does not become a companion, there is a breach of duty for him. This is called contentment in sewing (sibbanasantoṣa). A monk dyeing a robe should not go about seeking black cloth or similar items; he should dye it with whatever dye is obtained from Somavakkala bark or similar sources. A monk who does not obtain such should take the dye-liquid discarded by people in the forest after taking the bark, or the dregs discarded by monks after boiling, and dye with that. This is called contentment in dyeing (rajanasantoṣa). Taking any of the colors—blue, dark mud, or golden—and making a mark (kappabindu) that is visible to someone sitting on an elephant's back is called contentment in making allowable (kappasantoṣa).

Using it only for the purpose of covering one's shame is called contentment in usage (paribhogasantoṣa). A monk who has obtained cloth for a robe but has not yet obtained thread, a needle, or someone to make it, may keep that cloth; if he has obtained them, he should not keep it. Even if it is a finished robe, if he wishes to give it to a pupil or similar person who is not nearby, he may keep it until they arrive. As soon as they arrive, it should be given. A monk who is unable to give it should perform the formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna). If there is another robe, it is also proper to determine a bedspread. Only a robe that is not formally determined is called hoarding (sannidhi); a robe that is formally determined is not called hoarding—so said the Elder Mahāsīva. This is the delimitation of hoarding (sannidhiparivaccheda).
281:
Mahāsīva Thera stated that only a robe that is not formally determined (adhiṭṭhita) constitutes hoarding (sannidhi); a robe that is formally determined does not constitute hoarding. This is called contentment in avoiding hoarding (sannidhiparivajjanasantoṣa). A monk who relinquishes a robe should not give it by looking at the face [of the recipient], but should relinquish it while established in the principles of cordiality (sāraṇīyadhamma). This is called contentment in relinquishing (vissajjanasantoṣa).

The ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) related to robes are the refuse-rag-robe practice (paṃsukūlikaṅga) and the three-robe practice (tecīvarikaṅga). The detailed explanation of these ascetic practices should be understood from the Visuddhimagga. Thus, a monk who fulfills the Great Lineage of Noble Ones (Ariyavaṃsa) regarding contentment with robes protects these two ascetic practices. By protecting these ascetic practices, he becomes one who is content by virtue of the Great Lineage of Noble Ones regarding contentment with robes.

'Vaṇṇavādī' (one who speaks in praise) means: One monk is content himself but does not speak in praise of contentment. Another is not content himself but speaks in praise of contentment. Another is neither content himself nor speaks in praise of contentment. Another is both content himself and speaks in praise of contentment. To show the monk who is both content and speaks in praise of it, it is said: 'He also speaks in praise of contentment with any kind of robe.'

'Anesana' refers to various types of improper search, such as acting as a messenger or running errands. 'Appatirūpa' means unsuitable. 'Aladdhā ca' means not having obtained. Just as some monks, wondering 'How can I obtain a robe?', stay together with meritorious monks and act with hypocrisy, being agitated and anxious, a content monk does not feel such anxiety even when he does not obtain a robe. 'Laddhā ca' means having obtained it rightfully and fairly. 'Agadhita' means being free from the greed of attachment. 'Amucchita' means not falling into a daze through excessive craving. 'Anajjhopanno' means not being overwhelmed or enveloped by craving. 'Ādīnavadassāvī' means seeing the danger in the offenses arising from improper search and in the consumption with greed. 'Nissaraṇapañño' means knowing only the escape from consumption, as stated: 'Only for the purpose of warding off cold.'

'Itarītaracīvarasantuṭṭhi' means contentment with any kind of robe. 'Does not exalt himself' means he does not exalt himself by saying, 'I am a refuse-rag-robe wearer; I have undertaken the refuse-rag-robe practice since my ordination; who is equal to me?' 'Does not disparage others' means he does not disparage others by saying, 'These other monks are not refuse-rag-robe wearers; they do not have even a bit of the refuse-rag-robe practice.' One who is skillful and proficient in that contentment with robes and in speaking in praise of it...
282:
...must be skillful and proficient. 'Analasa' means being free from laziness through constant practice. 'Sampajāna paṭissata' means being endowed with both clear comprehension (sampajañña-paññā) and mindfulness (sati). 'Ariyavaṃse ṭhita' means being established in the Lineage of Noble Ones.

'Itarītara piṇ膽apāta' means (contentment) with any kind of almsfood. In this contentment regarding almsfood, one should know the almsfood, the source of almsfood (piṇḍapātakkhetta), the contentment in almsfood, and the ascetic practices related to almsfood. Therein, almsfood consists of sixteen types: cooked rice, barley meal, flour, fish, meat, milk, curd, ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, molasses, gruel, hard food, soft food, and drinkable food.

The source of almsfood (piṇḍapātakkhetta) consists of fifteen types: food for the Saṅgha, food for specific monks, invited food, food by lottery (salāka-bhatta), fortnightly food, Uposatha day food, food on the day after the Uposatha, food for guests, food for travelers, food for the sick, food for the attendants of the sick, regular food (dhura-bhatta), food for a specific hut, food by rotation (vāra-bhatta), and food for a monastery.

Contentment regarding almsfood consists of fifteen types: contentment in thought, contentment in going, contentment in seeking, contentment in obtaining, contentment in receiving, contentment in receiving the right amount, contentment in avoiding greed, contentment with whatever is obtained, contentment according to one's strength, contentment according to suitability, contentment in being helpful, contentment in measurement, contentment in consumption, contentment in avoiding hoarding, and contentment in relinquishing.

Among these fifteen types of contentment, a monk who delights in almsfood thinks about it after washing his face. However, a monk who practices the alms-gatherer's practice (piṇḍapātika) while traveling with a group, when attending to the elder in the evening, should only think as far as asking, 'Venerable sir, where shall we go for alms tomorrow?' and 'To such and such a village, bhante.' Beyond that, he should not think [about the food]. A monk who travels alone should only think while standing at the place of reflection. A monk who thinks beyond that falls away from the Lineage of Noble Ones and becomes an outsider. This is called contentment in thought (vitakkasantoṣa).

A monk entering for alms should go with meditation as his primary focus, without thinking 'Where will I get it?' This is called contentment in going (gamanasantoṣa). A monk seeking alms should not seek by taking along just any monk, but only by taking along a modest and well-behaved monk. This is called contentment in seeking (pariyesanasantoṣa). Seeing almsfood being brought from afar and thinking 'This food...'
283:
One should not give rise to the thought: "This person's alms food is pleasing; this person's alms food is not pleasing." This is called contentment with what is obtained (paṭilābha-santuṭṭhi). Without thinking, "I will take this pleasing food; I will not take this unpleasing food," one should take only what is sufficient for sustenance. This is called contentment in receiving (paṭiggahaṇa-santuṭṭhi).

In this regard, if the gift is abundant but the donor wishes to give only a little, one should take only a little. If the gift is abundant and the donor wishes to give much, one should take only the amount sufficient for oneself. If the gift is not abundant and the donor wishes to give only a little, one should take only a little. If the gift is not abundant but the donor wishes to give much, one should take only the amount sufficient for oneself. One who does not know the proper measure in receiving destroys the faith of the people, wastes the gift given out of faith, does not follow the Dispensation (the instruction), and cannot even win the heart of the mother who gave him birth. Therefore, one should receive only after knowing the proper measure; this is called contentment in receiving the right amount (matta-paṭiggahaṇa-santuṭṭhi). One should not go specifically only to wealthy families but should go from house to house in order. This is called contentment by avoiding greed (loluppa-vivajjana-santuṭṭhi). Contentment with whatever is obtained (yathālābha-santuṭṭhi) and so forth are to be understood in the same way as explained regarding robes.

Consuming alms food with the thought, "I will maintain the ascetic practice," thus knowing its benefit, is called contentment regarding the benefit (upakāra-santuṭṭhi). One should not accept alms food brought after filling the bowl. If there is an unordained person (layperson or novice), one should have them take it; if not, one should have it brought and take only the amount to be formally offered. This is called contentment regarding quantity (parimāṇa-santuṭṭhi). Consuming with the thought, "The removal of hunger is the escape from [craving for] this food," is called contentment in usage (paribhoga-santuṭṭhi). The instruction that one should not consume food after storing it is called contentment by avoiding storage (sannidhi-parivajjana-santuṭṭhi). Without looking at the donor's face, one should give it away while established in the qualities of communal living (sāraṇīya-dhamma). This is called contentment in sharing (vissajjana-santuṭṭhi).

Furthermore, there are five ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) connected with alms food: the alms-food-eater's practice (piṇḍapātikanga), the house-to-house-walking practice (sapadānacārikanga), the one-sessioner's practice (ekāsanikanga), the bowl-food-eater's practice (pattapiṇḍikanga), and the later-food-refuser's practice (khalupacchābhattikanga). The detailed explanation of these five ascetic practices is stated in the Visuddhimagga. Thus, a monk who fulfills the Great Noble Lineage of contentment with alms food protects these five ascetic practices. A monk who protects these five ascetic practices is said to be content with the Great Noble Lineage of contentment with alms food. The words "praising the virtues" and so forth should be understood in the same way as previously explained.

In the passage "with lodging" (senāsanena), one should know the lodging, the field of lodging, contentment with lodging, and the ascetic practices connected with lodging...
284:
...one should know the ascetic practice. In that context, "lodging" (senāsana) refers to these fifteen types: a bed, a chair, a mattress, a pillow, a monastery roofed on both sides, a monastery roofed on one side, a long mansion, a flat-roofed mansion, a mountain cave, a grotto, a hut, a pavilion, a bamboo grove, the foot of a tree, or wherever monks frequent—these fifteen lodgings should be known.

The "field of lodging" (senāsana-khetta) refers to these six fields: from the Saṅgha, from a group, from relatives, from friends, through one's own wealth, or as a refuse-rag item.

"Contentment with lodging" (senāsana-santuṭṭhi) refers to the fifteen types of contentment, such as contentment regarding thoughts (vitakka-santuṭṭhi), in the context of lodging. These fifteen types of contentment should be understood in the same way as explained regarding alms food. The five ascetic practices connected with lodging are: the forest-dweller's practice (āraññikanga), the tree-root-dweller's practice (rukkhamūlikanga), the open-air-dweller's practice (abbhokāsikanga), the charnel-ground-dweller's practice (sosānikanga), and the any-bed-user's practice (yathāsanthatikanga). The detailed explanation of these five ascetic practices is stated in the Visuddhimagga. Thus, a monk who fulfills the Great Noble Lineage of contentment with lodging protects these five ascetic practices. A monk who protects these five ascetic practices is said to be content with the Great Noble Lineage of contentment with lodging.

Medicinal requisites are included within alms food. Regarding those medicinal requisites, one should be content with whatever is obtained, content according to one's strength, and content with what is suitable for oneself. The sitter's practice (nesajjikanga) belongs to the Noble Lineage of delight in meditation. This has also been said:

"Five [ascetic practices] are stated regarding lodging, five are dependent on food, one is connected with energy, and two are dependent on robes."

Thus, the Blessed One, as if spreading out the earth, as if filling the belly of the great ocean, and as if expanding the sky, first taught the Noble Lineage of contentment with robes. Then, as if making the moon rise and as if making the sun shine, He taught the second Noble Lineage of contentment with alms food. Then, as if lifting Mount Sineru, He taught the third Noble Lineage of contentment with lodging. Now, to teach the fourth Noble Lineage of delight in meditation, adorned with a thousand methods, He began the discourse: "Furthermore, monks, a monk is one who delights in meditation."

In that passage, delight is called ārāma; abhirati (intense delight) is the meaning. Because that person has delight in meditation, he is called "one who delights in meditation" (bhāvanārāma). Because he is fond of meditation, he is called "one who finds pleasure in meditation" (bhāvanārata). Because he has delight in the five kinds of abandoning (pahāna), he is called "one who delights in abandoning" (pahānārāma). In another way...
285:
He is called 'Bhāvanārāma' because he delights while developing [meditation]. He is called 'Pahānārāma' because he delights while abandoning [defilements]. This is how the meaning should be understood here. Indeed, this means that this monk delights in and finds pleasure in developing the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). Likewise, he delights in and finds pleasure in developing the four right efforts (sammappadhāna), the four bases of power (iddhipāda), the five faculties (indriya), the five powers (bala), the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), the seven contemplations (anupassanā), the eighteen great insights (mahāvipဿanā), the thirty-seven factors contributing to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma), and the thirty-eight classifications of objects (ārammaṇavibhatti). He also delights in and finds pleasure in abandoning defilements such as sensual desire (kāmacchanda).

Among these four noble lineages (ariyavaṃsa), the entire Vinaya Piṭaka is taught through the first three by way of the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) and contentment with the four requisites. Through the Bhāvanārāma Ariyavaṃsa, the remaining two Piṭakas are taught. A monk teaching this Bhāvanārāma Ariyavaṃsa should teach it by way of the Nekkhammapāḷi in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, by way of the Dasuttara Sutta in the Dīgha Nikāya, by way of the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta in the Majjhima Nikāya, and by way of the Niddesa in the Abhidhamma.

Among those four methods, the teaching by way of the Nekkhammapāḷi in the Paṭisambhidāmagga is as follows: "He delights while developing renunciation (nekkhamma) and delights while abandoning sensual desire (kāmacchanda). He delights while developing non-ill will (abyāpāda) and abandoning ill will (byāpāda)... developing the perception of light (āloka-saññā) and abandoning sloth and torpor (thina-middha)... developing non-distraction (avikkhepa/samādhi) and abandoning restlessness (uddhacca)... developing the definition of phenomena (dhamma-vavatthāna) and abandoning doubt (vicikicchā)... developing knowledge (ñāṇa) and abandoning ignorance (avijjā)... developing joy (pāmojja) and abandoning discontent (arati)... developing the first jhāna and abandoning the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa)... developing the second jhāna and abandoning initial and sustained thought (vitakka-vicāra)... developing the third jhāna and abandoning rapture (pīti)... developing the fourth jhāna and abandoning pleasure and pain (sukha-dukkha)... he delights while developing the attainment of the base of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana) and delights while abandoning the perception of form (rūpa-saññā), the perception of resistance (paṭigha-saññā), and the perception of diversity (nānatta-saññā). He delights while developing the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana)... (and so on) ...he delights while developing the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana) and delights while abandoning the perception of the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana-saññā).

He delights while developing the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) and delights while abandoning the perception of permanence (nicca-saññā). Developing the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā) and abandoning the perception of pleasure (sukha-saññā)... developing the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā) and abandoning the perception of self (atta-saññā)... developing the contemplation of revulsion (nibbidānupassanā) and abandoning delight (nandi)... developing the contemplation of fading away (virāganupassanā) and abandoning lust (rāga)... developing the contemplation of cessation (nirodhānupassanā) and abandoning origination (samudaya)... developing the contemplation of relinquishment (paṭinissaggānupassanā) and abandoning grasping (ādāna)... developing the contemplation of destruction (khayānupassanā) and abandoning the perception of compactness (ghana-saññā)... developing the contemplation of vanishing (vayānupassanā) and abandoning accumulation (āyūhana)... developing the contemplation of change (vipariṇāmānupassanā) and abandoning the perception of stability (dhuva-saññā)..."
286:
...developing the signless contemplation (animittānupassanā) and abandoning the sign (nimitta)... developing the desireless contemplation (appaṇihitānupassanā) and abandoning desire (paṇidhi)... developing the contemplation of emptiness (suññatānupassanā) and abandoning adherence [to self] (abhinivesa)... developing the insight into phenomena of higher wisdom (adhipaññā-dhamma-vipassanā) and abandoning the adherence to the core in the coreless (sārādānābhinivesa)... developing the knowledge and vision according to reality (yathābhūta-ñāṇadassana) and abandoning the adherence to delusion (sammohābhinivesa)... developing the contemplation of danger (ādīnavānupassanā) and abandoning the adherence to attachment (ālayābhinivesa)... developing the reflective contemplation (paṭisaṅkhānupassanā) and abandoning non-reflection (appaṭisaṅkhā)... developing the contemplation of turning away (vivaṭṭānupassanā) and abandoning the adherence to bondage (saṃyogābhinivesa)... developing the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga) and abandoning the defilements that have the same standing as wrong view... developing the path of once-returning (sakadāgāmimagga) and abandoning gross defilements... developing the path of non-returning (anāgāmimagga) and abandoning subtle defilements... he delights while developing the path of arahantship (arahattamagga) and delights while abandoning all defilements" (thus it is said in the Paṭisambhidāmagga).

In this way, it is taught in the Nekkhammapāḷi of the Paṭisambhidāmagga.

I shall further speak by way of the teaching in the Dasuttara Sutta of the Dīgha Nikāya:

"He delights while developing one thing, he delights while abandoning one thing... (and so on) ...he delights while developing ten things, he delights while abandoning ten things. What is the one thing that he delights in while developing? He delights while developing mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati) accompanied by gratification; he delights while developing this one thing. What is the one thing that he delights in while abandoning? He delights while abandoning the conceit 'I am' (asmimāna); he delights while abandoning this one thing. What are the two things... (and so on) ...What are the ten things that he delights in while developing? He delights while developing the ten kasina bases (kasiṇāyatana); he delights while developing these ten things. What are the ten things that he delights in while abandoning? He delights while abandoning the ten wrongnesses (micchatta); he delights while abandoning these ten things. In this way, monks, a monk is one who delights in development (bhāvanārāma)" (thus it is said in the Dīgha Nikāya).

In this way, it is taught by way of the Dasuttara Sutta in the Dīgha Nikāya.

I shall further speak by way of the teaching in the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya:

"Monks, this [path of right view, etc.] is the direct path (ekāyana magga)... (and so on) ...only for the sake of knowledge and for the sake of mindfulness. He dwells independent, and he does not cling to anything in the world. In this way also, monks, a monk is one who delights in development, one who is devoted to development. He is one who delights in abandoning, one who is devoted to abandoning. Furthermore, monks, a monk, when walking, knows 'I am walking'... (and so on) ...Furthermore, monks, just as a monk might see a body discarded in a cemetery... (and so on) ...bones that have become rotten and turned to dust. He [reflects] on this very body [that it is of such a nature]..."
287:
"This body too is of such a nature, will become such, and cannot escape such a nature"—thus he applies this to his own body. In this way, he dwells contemplating the body in his own body, or the physical body starting from hair and so forth... "Monks, in this way a monk is one who delights in meditation" (M. Ni. 1.106 etc.).

Thus it is spoken according to the method of the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta in the Majjhima Nikāya.

"By way of the Abhidhamma Niddesa method" means: he delights in contemplating all conditioned things (saṅkhata) as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil... as things that are objects of the defilements which oppress and cause distress. "Monks, in this way a monk is one who delights in meditation" (Mahāni. 13, Cūḷani. Upasīvamāṇavapucchāniddesa 39, Nandamāṇavapucchāniddesa 51). Thus it is spoken by way of the Niddesa method.

"He does not exalt himself" means he does not exalt himself thus: "Today, for sixty or seventy years, I have been performing the work of insight (vipassanā) as impermanent, suffering, and non-self; who is there like me?" "He does not disparage others" means he does not disparage others thus: "These monks wander about having abandoned their meditation subjects, without even as much as the work of insight into impermanence and suffering." The rest is as previously stated.

"Monks, these are the four noble lineages" means: Monks, these four noble lineages are the ancient lineages of the noble ones, the traditions of the noble ones, the successions of the noble ones, the path of the noble ones, the highway of the noble ones. Having concluded the Ariyavaṃsa Sutta, he now spoke the words beginning with "And with these [qualities], monks," wishing to show the dwelling place of a monk who fulfills the Great Noble Lineage (Mahā-ariyavaṃsa). In that text, "He alone can endure discontent" means that only the monk established in the noble lineage can endure and overcome discontent, boredom, or dissatisfaction. "Discontent cannot overcome him" means that the discontent that may arise while developing higher wholesome states in secluded lodgings is unable to overcome or overwhelm that monk. "One who can endure discontent and delight" means he can endure both discontent and delight in the five cords of sensual pleasure; he is able to overcome them.

Now, bringing it to a climax with verses, he spoke the words beginning with "Discontent cannot overcome." In that text, "Dhīra" refers to an energetic person. "Discontent cannot overcome the wise (dhīra)" is the explanation for the preceding statement. Because that discontent cannot overcome or overwhelm the person of firm energy, therefore...
288:
Discontent cannot overcome the wise (dhīra). For the wise one is an endurer of discontent; because he endures discontent, he is called "dhīra" (the wise/energetic); therefore, it means he endures discontent. "Sabbakammavihāyīnaṃ" refers to the person who stands having abandoned all kamma pertaining to the three planes and having limited the round of rebirth. What lust or hatred could hinder the person who stands having dispelled the defilements? Like a nikkhu (gold plate) of pure Jambonada gold, who is worthy of blaming that person who is free from blameworthy faults? Even the Great Brahma has praised such a person. At the conclusion of the teaching, forty thousand monks were established in Arahantship.

## 9. Dhammapadasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, "Dhammapadāni" means portions of the Dhamma. In the words beginning with "Anabhijjhā" (non-greed), it should be understood that Anabhijjhā is by the abandonment of greed (abhijjhā), Abyāpāda (non-ill will) is by the abandonment of ill will (byāpāda), Sammā-sati (right mindfulness) is by the abandonment of wrong mindfulness (micchā-sati), and Sammā-samādhi (right concentration) is by the abandonment of wrong concentration (micchā-samādhi).

"Anabhijjhālu" means being without craving. "Abyāpannena cetasā" means with a mind that does not abandon its natural state at all times. "Sato ekaggacittassa" means being endowed with mindfulness, one should have a mind one-pointed on the object. "Ajjhattaṃ susamāhito" means a person whose mind is well-placed within himself. In this sutta and in the verse, the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) are taught.

## 10. Paribbājakasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, "Abhiññātā" means known or well-known. Names such as "Annabhāra" are the names of those wanderers (paribbājakas). "Paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito" means having emerged from the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). In this context, "paṭisallāna" is intended as that attainment of fruition. "Paccakkhāya" means having abandoned. "Abhijjālu" means having craving. "Kāmesu tibbasārāga" means having intense passion for the objects of sensual pleasure. "I would say thus to him in that matter." "Paṭikkositabbaṃ maññeyya" means he would consider them as things to be rebuked or rejected. "Sahadhammikā" means together with reasons.
