## 7. Ahirājasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, the phrase "these four royal snake families" is spoken with reference only to venomous snakes that bite. Whatever snakes there are that bite, all of them are included within these four royal snake families. "Attaguttiyā" means for the purpose of self-guarding. "Attarakkhāyā" means for the purpose of self-protection. "Attaparittāyā" means for the purpose of self-warding. It means He allows the paritta (protection).

Now, wishing to show how that paritta should be performed, He spoke the words beginning with "Virūpakkhehi me." In that passage, "Virūpakkhehi" means with the Virūpakkha family of snakes. The same method applies to the remaining terms. "Apādakehi" means with footless creatures. The same method applies to the remaining terms. Having previously taught the specific loving-kindness (odissaka-mettā) with this much of the passage, He now begins to teach non-specific loving-kindness (anodissaka-mettā) with the words "Sabbe sattā." In that passage, the words 'sattā', 'pāṇā', and 'bhūtā' are all synonyms for 'person' (puggala). "Bhadrāni passantu" means may they see auspicious objects. "Mā kañci pāpamāgamā" means may no low evil come to any being. In the phrase "Appamāṇo Buddho," the virtues of the Buddha should be understood by the word "Buddho." Those virtues are indeed immeasurable. The same method applies to the remaining two terms (Dhamma and Saṅgha). "Pamāṇavantāni" means they are endowed with measurable qualities. "Uṇṇanābhi" is a spider with hair on its navel. "Sarabū" is a house lizard. "Katā me rakkhā, katā me parittā" means I have performed guarding and protection for this many people. "Paṭikkamantu bhūtāni" means may all beings for whom I have performed protection depart; may they not harm me.

## 8. Devadattasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the eighth sutta, "Acirapakkante Devadatte" means not long after Devadatta had departed after splitting the Saṅgha. "Parābhavāya" means for decline and ruin. "Assatarī" is a female mule born from a donkey in the womb of a mare. "Attavadhāya gabbhaṃ gaṇhāti" means she conceives for her own destruction; when the time for birth arrives, she is unable to give birth and stands kicking the ground with her feet. Then, having tied her four legs to four posts, they cut open her belly and take out the foal. She dies right there. For that reason, this was spoken.
317: ## 9. Commentary on the Padhāna Sutta In the commentary on the ninth sutta, the Padhāna Sutta: Effort for the purpose of restraining the defilements and for the purpose of closing the door through which defilements enter is called Saṃvara-padhāna (effort of restraint). Effort for the purpose of abandoning the defilements is called Pahāna-padhāna (effort of abandoning). Effort for the purpose of cultivating and increasing wholesome states is called Bhāvanā-padhāna (effort of development). Effort for the purpose of preserving those very wholesome states is called Anurakkhaṇā-padhāna (effort of preservation). ## 10. Commentary on the Adhammika Sutta In the commentary on the tenth sutta, the Adhammika Sutta: "They are unrighteous" means that by not taking the one-tenth tax and the fines appropriate to the offense established by ancient kings, but instead taking excessive taxes and excessive fines, the kings become unrighteous. "Royal officials (rājāyutta)" are the officials who manage various affairs in the king's provinces. "Brahmins and householders" are the brahmins and householders living within the city. "Town and country folk" are those living in the market towns and the countryside. "Unevenly (visamaṃ)" means that they blow irregularly and at the wrong time. "Uneven (visamā)" means not even, being either too harsh or too soft. "Off-course (apañjasā)" means having departed from the path, they blow by going the wrong way. In the passage "the deities become angry," when the winds blow unevenly and off-course, trees break and celestial mansions are destroyed. Therefore, the deities become angry and do not allow the rain-god to rain properly. For that reason, it is said, "The rain-god does not cause the rain to fall properly." "Crops ripen unevenly" means that in one place they are still in the womb stage, in another place they are at the milky stage, and in another place they are already ripe; thus, the crops ripen unevenly. "The constellations and stars revolve evenly" means that just as the full moon of Kattika coincides only with the Kattika constellation, and the full moon of Migasira coincides only with the Migasira constellation, in this way, in each respective month, the respective full moon coincides only with the respective constellation, and thus they revolve properly. "The winds blow evenly" means that they blow not unevenly but only at the proper time; for six months the north wind blows, and for six months the south wind blows, thus they blow at the time appropriate for those respective provinces. "Evenly (samā)" means proceeding evenly, being neither too harsh nor too soft. "On course (pañjasā)" means having entered the path, they blow only along the path and not off the path.
318:
"Jimhaṃ gacchati" means going crookedly, taking a wrong path (going the wrong way). In the phrase "nette jimhaṃ gate sati," "nettā" refers to the leader (the lead bull). If that lead bull goes crookedly and takes a wrong path, the other cows also take only the wrong path. There is also a variant reading "nete." "Dukkhaṃ seti" means sleeping miserably, or reaching a state of suffering.

## Second Chapter: Pattakamma Vagga

## (8) 3. Apaṇṇaka Vagga

## 1. Commentary on Padhāna Sutta

In the first sutta of the third chapter, "apaṇṇakappaṭipadā" refers to the unerring practice. "Yoni cassa āraddhā hoti" means that the monk's cause of instruction and hearing (suta) is complete. "Āsavānaṃ khayāya" is for the sake of the fruit of Arahantship. The commentary on the second sutta is clear.

## 3. Commentary on Sappurisa Sutta

In the third sutta, "avaṇṇa" means lack of virtue (fault). "Pātu karoti" means speaking to make it manifest. "Pañhābhinīto" means brought forward for the purpose of a question. "Ahāpetvā alambitvā" means completing without falling away.

In this sutta, an unworthy person (asappurisa) hides their own faults due to evil desire, whereas a worthy person (sappurisa) hides their own virtues due to shame (hiri). Now, because an unworthy person lacks a sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri-ottappa), their unworthiness is known through living together; however, because a worthy person is endowed with shame and fear of wrongdoing, they are not known as unworthy even through living together. Therefore, to make manifest the nature of an unworthy person, the Buddha gave the simile of a newly arrived daughter-in-law, saying, "Monks, just as a new daughter-in-law..." and so on. Therein, "vadhukā" refers to a daughter-in-law. "Tibbaṃ" means thickly (intensely). The remaining meanings here are clear.

## 4-5. Commentary on the Two Agga Suttas

74-75. In the fourth sutta, "sīlagga" refers to the supreme virtue that has reached the peak. This method applies everywhere. In the fifth sutta, "rūpagga" refers to the form (rūpa) by contemplating which one attains the fruit of Arahantship; this is called rūpagga. This same method applies to the remaining terms. In the term "bhavagga," however, it refers to the existence (attabhāva) in which one stands to attain the fruit of Arahantship; that existence is called bhavagga.

## 6. Commentary on Kusināra Sutta

In the sixth sutta, "upavattane" refers to the central location where the row of Sāla trees, which extends eastward, turns back toward the north. "Antarena yamakasālānaṃ" means between two Sāla trees. "Kaṅkhā" means being two-pronged (doubt). "Vimati" means the inability to decide. "Whether it is the Buddha or not, the Dhamma or not, the Saṅgha or not, the Path or not, the practice or not"—if anyone should have such a doubt, "I say this to you, monks, ask questions"—this is the summary of the meaning here.

"Do not refrain from asking even out of respect for the Teacher" means: "We were ordained in the presence of the Teacher; the four requisites are also possessions received from the Teacher. We, who have not entertained doubt for such a long time, should not entertain doubt today at the final hour"—if they should remain without asking out of respect for the Teacher in this way... "Monks, let a friend also inform a friend" means: among you, whichever monk is a seen and trusted friend of another monk, let him inform that monk. "I will speak to one monk; by hearing his words, may you all become free of doubt"—this is what is shown.

"I have confidence in this way" means "I believe in this way." "Only knowledge" means that here, the Tathāgata has only the knowledge that directly realizes the state of being free from doubt, not mere faith. "In these monks, Ānanda" means among these five hundred monks sitting within the curtain. "The one who is the last" refers to Elder Ānanda, who is the last (lowest) in terms of spiritual qualities.

## 7. Commentary on Acinteyya Sutta

In the seventh sutta, "acinteyyāni" are things that are improper to think about. "Na cintetabbāni" means things that should not be thought about precisely because they are unthinkable. "One who thinks about these reasons" means one who ponders these causes. "Ummādassa" means madness. "Vighātassa" means distress (suffering).

"Buddhavisayo" refers to the range of the Buddhas, the manifestation and power of the Buddha's qualities such as omniscience. "Jhānavisayo" refers to the range of the meditative absorptions and direct knowledge. "Kammavipāko" refers to the result of kammas, such as kamma to be experienced in this very life (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya). "Lokacintā" refers to speculation about the world such as: "By whom were the moon and sun made? By whom was the great earth made? By whom was the great ocean made? By whom were beings produced? By whom were the mountains made? By whom were mango, palm, coconut trees, etc., made?"—such is the nature of speculation about the world.
320:
## 8. Dakkhiṇasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the eighth commentary, the Dakkhiṇasutta-vaṇṇanā— "Dakkhiṇāvisuddhiyo" refers to the causes for the purification of the offering known as dakkhiṇā. "Dāyakato visujjhati" means it is purified by way of having great fruit; the meaning is that it becomes of great fruit. "Kalyāṇadhammo" refers to one who has a pure nature. "Pāpadhammo" refers to one who has a low or evil nature. Regarding the phrase "Dāyakato visujjhati" (purification by the giver), the great King Vessantara should be mentioned here. That great king, by giving his son and daughter to the Brahmin Jūjaka, caused the great earth to shake. Regarding "Pဋိဂ္ဂါဟကတော ဝိသုဇ္ဈတိ" (purification by the receiver), the fisherman living at the mouth of the Kalyāṇī River should be mentioned. It is said that after giving alms to Elder Dīghasuma three times, while lying on his deathbed, he said, "The alms given to the Venerable Elder Dīghasuma are lifting me up."

Regarding "Neva dāyakato" (lack of purification by either the giver or the receiver), the hunter living in the Vaḍḍhamāna region should be mentioned. It is said that while giving an offering dedicated to a deceased relative, he gave it to an immoral person three times. On the third time, the spirit (amanussa) cried out, "The immoral person is robbing me!" Only when he gave to a virtuous monk and shared the merit did the offering reach that spirit. Regarding "Dāyakato ceva visujjhati paṭiggāhakato ca" (purification by both the giver and the receiver), the Asadisa-dāna (Incomparable Alms-giving) should be mentioned here.

## 9. Vaṇijjasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth commentary, the Vaṇijjasutta-vaṇṇanā— "Tādisā vā" refers to those who are similar to those whose wishes are not fulfilled. "Chedagāminī hotī" means it leads to the loss of capital. The meaning is that all the desired capital and wealth are destroyed. "Na yathādhippāyā hotī" means not turning out according to one's own desire. "Parādhippāyā hotī" means turning out according to another's desire, or having a result that exceeds one's own desire. In the phrase "Samaṇaṃ vā brāhmaṇaṃ vā," the status of being a recluse (samaṇa) or a Brahmin should be understood by the calming and removal of evil. "Vadatu, bhante, paccayena" means "Venerable sir, please speak (ask) for what you need among the four requisites such as robes, etc."; thus one invites or requests. "Yena pavāreti" means inviting by specifying the amount of requisites. "Taṃ na deti" means not giving that invited requisite at all. "Na yathādhippāyaṃ deti" means being unable to give as the receiver wishes and giving only a small amount instead. "Yathādhippāyaṃ deti" means giving exactly as much as the receiver wishes. "Parādhippāyaṃ deti" means having invited for only a small amount but giving a vastly greater amount of requisites.
321:
## 10. Kamboja-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, "Neva sabhāyaṃ nisīdati" means not sitting at all in the assembly hall of judgment for the purpose of making legal decisions. "Na kammantaṃ payojeti" means not engaging in or managing major businesses such as farming or trade. "Na kambojaṃ gacchati" means not going to the Kamboja country for the purpose of accumulating wealth. This is merely a teaching method; the meaning is not going to any foreign country whatsoever. In the words beginning with "Kodha-no," a person (woman) overwhelmed by anger due to being quick-tempered does not know what is beneficial or harmful. Due to being envious, she cannot tolerate the prosperity of others. Due to being stingy, she cannot perform necessary tasks by giving wealth. Due to being devoid of wisdom, she is unable to organize affairs. Therefore, she does not perform these actions such as sitting in the assembly.

## Apaṇṇaka-vagga, the Third.

## (9) 4. Macala-vagga

## 1-5. Pāṇātipātādi-sutta-pañcaka-vaṇṇanā
81-85. The first suttas of the fourth vagga have meanings that are clear. In the fifth sutta, in the passage beginning with "Nīce kule paccājāto," one is called "Tama" (Darkness) because of being associated with the darkness of being obscure and low-born. One is called "Tamaparāyaṇo" (Bound for Darkness) because, due to bodily misconduct and so forth, one again approaches the darkness of hell. Thus, by both terms, only the darkness of the five aggregates is meant. In the passage beginning with "Aḍḍhe kule paccājāto," one is called "Joti" (Light) because of being associated with light, being prominent; it means being like a light. One is called "Jotiparayano" (Bound for Light) because, due to bodily good conduct and so forth, one again approaches the light of rebirth in heaven. In this manner, the other two types should also be understood.

"Vena-kule" means born in the family of bamboo-workers. "Nesāda-kule" means born in the family of hunters and the like. "Rathakāra-kule" means born in the family of leather-workers. "Pukkusa-kule" means born in the family of flower-scavengers. "Kasira-vuttike" means one who has a difficult livelihood. "Dubbaṇṇo" means one who is ugly, having the color of a burnt stump like a dust-goblin. "Duddasiko" means one who has an unpleasant appearance even to the mother who gave birth. "Okoṭimako" means a dwarf. "Kāṇo" means one who is blind in one eye or both eyes. "Kuṇī" means one who has one crooked hand or both hands crooked. "Khañjo" means one who is lame in one foot or both feet. "Pakkhahato" means one who is paralyzed on one side of the body.
322:
A pīṭhasappī is one who moves about using a board with wheels. Padīpeyyassa refers to lighting equipment such as oil and lamps. In the phrase "Thus, bhikkhus," a certain person dies within the mother's womb without seeing the light of the external world, and being reborn in the lower realms, wanders for an entire eon. That person is also one who is headed for darkness (tamotamaparāyaṇa). That person would be a deceitful (kuhaka) individual. Indeed, it is meant that such a result occurs for a deceitful person.

In this sutta, by the words "in a low family" (nīce kule) and so on, the failure of descent (rebirth) and the failure of present causes are shown. By the words "poor" (dalidde) and so on, the failure of ongoing causes is shown; by "with a difficult livelihood" (kasiravuttike) and so on, the failure of the means of livelihood; by "ugly" (dubbaṇṇo) and so on, the failure of the physical form (attabhāva). By "much illness" (bahvābādho) and so on, the association with the causes of suffering is shown; and by "not a receiver" (na lābhī) and so on, the failure of the causes of happiness and the failure of enjoyment are shown. By "bodily misconduct" (kāyena duccaritaṃ) and so on, the association with the causes for being headed for darkness is shown; and by "after the breakup of the body" (kāyassa bhedā) and so on, the arrival at the state of darkness in the afterlife is shown. The bright side (sukkapakkha) should be understood by the method opposite to what has been stated.

## 6. Oṇatoṇatasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the sixth sutta, oṇatoṇata means one who is low in the present and will also be low in the future. Oṇatuṇṇata means one who is low in the present but will be high in the future. Uṇṇatoṇata means one who is high in the present but will be low in the future. Uṇṇatuṇṇata means one who is high in the present and will also be high in the future. The details of these terms should be understood in the same way as in the previous sutta.

## 7. Puttasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the seventh sutta, samaṇamacalo means an unwavering recluse (samaṇa-acala); the letter 'm' is a sandhi consonant. This term refers to the seven types of learners (sekha). Such a learner is called "unwavering" (acala) because of being established in the faith (saddhā) that is the root in the Dispensation. Samaṇapuṇḍarīko is a recluse like a white lotus (puṇḍarīka). A puṇḍarīka is a white lotus with fewer than a hundred petals. This term refers to a dry-insight Arahant (sukkhavipassaka-khīṇāsava). Such an Arahant is called a "white-lotus recluse" because his qualities are not full, as he lacks the jhānas and direct knowledges (abhiññā). Samaṇapadumo is a recluse like a red lotus (paduma). A paduma is a red lotus with a full hundred petals. This term refers to an Arahant liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta). Because of possessing jhānas and direct knowledges, his qualities are full, and thus he is called a "red-lotus recluse" (samaṇapaduma).
323:
Because of the absence of jhānas and direct knowledges, and because of having incomplete qualities, he is called a white-lotus recluse (samaṇapuṇḍarīka). Samaṇapadumo means a recluse like a red lotus (paduma). A paduma is a lotus with a full hundred petals. By this, the Arahant liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta) is shown. Indeed, that Arahant, because of possessing jhānas and direct knowledges and having complete qualities, is called a red-lotus recluse. Samaṇesu samaṇasukhumālo means a delicate recluse among all those recluses. He is one with a soft mind and body, free from physical and mental suffering, and is purely happy. By this, [the Buddha] shows himself and those recluses similar to him.

Having thus laid down the table of contents (mātikā), he now says "And how, bhikkhus" (katamañca bhikkhave) and so on, wishing to analyze them in order. In that passage, sekho refers to the seven types of learners. Pāṭipado means one who is practicing. "Dwelling while aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage" (anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ patthayamāno viharati) means dwelling while longing for the fruit of Arahantship, which is the unsurpassed security from bondage. Muddhāvasittassa means one whose head has been anointed, one who has undergone consecration. Ābhiseko means one who is worthy of being consecrated. Anabhisitto means one who has not yet been consecrated. Macalappatto means one who, by being the son of a khattiya king who rules the land and by being the eldest among the sons, has reached a state of being unwavering (firm) for the sake of attaining consecration, even though he has not yet been consecrated. The letter 'm' is merely a particle. "Touching with the body" (kāyena phusitvā) means touching and realizing with the mental body (nāmakāya).

"Mostly uses robes only when requested" (yācitova bahulaṃ cīvaraṃ paribhuñjati) means mostly using robes that are brought and offered by donors who request, "Venerable sir, please use this robe." Like the Elder Bākula, he uses unrequested robes only slightly. Regarding almsfood (piṇḍapāta), like the Elder Sīvalī on the journey through the Khadiravana forest; regarding lodging (senāsana), like the Elder Ānanda in the Aṭṭhakanāgara Sutta; regarding medicinal requisites (gilānappaccaya), like the Elder Pilindavaccha—he mostly uses only what is offered by donors upon request. The term tyassa should be resolved as te assa. Those fellow monks perform the necessary duties for that monk with a pleasing (heart-attaching) manner. "They bring an offering" (upahāraṃ upaharanti) means they bring and present physical and mental honor.

Sannipātikāni refers to diseases arising from the collection of the three [humors: bile, phlegm, and wind]. Utupariṇāmajāni refers to diseases arising from seasonal changes, such as extreme cold or extreme heat. Visamaparihārajāni refers to diseases arising from uneven care, such as excessive sitting or standing. Opakkamikāni refers to diseases arising from external efforts, such as assault or binding. Kammavipākajāni refers to diseases arising solely from the result of past kamma, even without these other causes. In the phrase "of the four jhānas" (catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ), only the functional jhānas (kiriyajhāna) of Arahants and Buddhas are intended. The remaining words have clear and obvious meanings.

The explanation of the seventh sutta is finished.

## 8. Saṃyojanasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the eighth sutta, because of being established in the Dispensation, only the Sotāpanna is called an "unwavering recluse" (samaṇamacalo). Because his qualities are not yet numerous, like a lotus with few petals, the Sakadāgāmī is called a "white-lotus recluse" (samaṇapuṇḍarīka). Because his qualities are more numerous than that, like a hundred-petaled lotus, the Anāgāmī is called a "red-lotus recluse" (samaṇapaduma). Because of having completely cut off the harsh defilements and reached a state of delicacy, the Arahant is called a "delicate recluse" (samaṇasukhumāla).

The explanation of the eighth sutta is finished.

## 9. Sammādiṭṭhisutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, by the power of the eightfold path starting with "one of right view" (sammādiṭṭhika)...
324:
A Sakadāgāmī is called a "Samaṇapuṇḍarīka" (Ascetic White Lotus), like a lotus with not too many petals. Because an Anāgāmī possesses more special qualities than a Sakadāgāmī, they are called a "Samaṇapaduma" (Ascetic Red Lotus), like a lotus with a hundred petals. An Arahant (Khīṇāsava) is called a "Samaṇasukhumāla" (Delicate Ascetic) because they have completely eradicated the defilements that cause hardness and have attained a state of gentleness.

## 9. Samma-diṭṭhi Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, the Samma-diṭṭhi Sutta, by the words beginning with "Samma-diṭṭhiko," the seven types of Sekha (learners) are taken by way of the Eightfold Path, as in the first sutta. In the second turn (vāra), the dry-insight Arahant (sukkhavipassaka) is spoken of either by way of the Tenfold Path or by way of the Eightfold Path together with the knowledge of the fruit of Arahantship and the liberation of the fruit of Arahantship. In the third turn, the one liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta) is spoken of. In the fourth turn, the Tathāgata and an Arahant similar to the Tathāgata are spoken of. Thus, this sutta is spoken only by way of the persons mentioned in the first sutta. However, there is a difference only in the sequence of the teaching (desanā).

## 10. Khandha Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, the Khandha Sutta, in the first turn, the Sekha person who lives negligently, remaining without initiating effort for the sake of the fruit of Arahantship, is spoken of. In the second turn, the Sekha person who lives diligently, having initiated insight (vipassanā) although not yet having produced jhāna, is spoken of. In the third turn, the Sekha person who lives diligently, having initiated insight and attained the eight liberations (vimokkha), is spoken of. In the fourth turn, the most delicate Arahant is spoken of.

## (10) 5. Asura Vagga

## 1. Asura Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the fifth vagga, "Asura" refers to one who is repulsive like an asura. "Deva" refers to one who is very beautiful and inspiring in appearance due to the power of their qualities, like a deva.
325:
## 2. Paṭhama Samādhi Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, "ajjhattaṃ cetosamathassa" (internal tranquility of mind) refers to the concentration associated with the absorption mind (appanācitta) occurring within oneself. "adhipaññādhammavipassanā" (insight into phenomena through higher wisdom) refers to the insight knowledge that grasps the formations (saṅkhāra). Indeed, that insight knowledge is called "higher wisdom" (adhipaññā), and because it contemplates the phenomena called the five aggregates (pañcakkhandha) in various modes such as impermanence, it is called "adhipaññādhammavipassanā."

## 3. Dutiya Samādhi Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, "yogo karaṇīyo" means that the application of effort should be made. "chando" is the desire to act (kattukamyatā-chanda). "vāyāmo" is effort (payoga). "ussāho" is energy (vīriya) that is more intense than that vāyāma. "ussoḷhī" is great energy like an ox pulling a cart stuck in the mud. "appaṭivānī" is the state of not turning back.

## 4. Tatiya Samādhi Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, in the words beginning with "evaṃ kho āvuso saṅkhāra daṭṭhabbā," it means: "Friends, formations should be regarded as impermanent (anicca), should be contemplated as impermanent, should be seen as impermanent." Likewise, the meaning should be taken as they should be regarded as suffering (dukkha) and non-self (anatta). In the words beginning with "evaṃ kho āvuso cittaṃ saṇṭhapetabbaṃ," it means: "Friends, the mind should be well-settled by the power of the first jhāna, should be well-stilled by the power of the first jhāna, should be made one-pointed by the power of the first jhāna, should be well-concentrated by the power of the first jhāna." Likewise, the meaning should be noted by the power of the second jhāna and so on. In all these three suttas, only mundane and supramundane tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) are spoken of.

## 5. Chavālāta Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, "chavālātaṃ" refers to a firebrand from a cemetery. "majjhe gūthagataṃ" means being smeared with excrement in the middle. "neva gāme kaṭṭhatthaṃ pharati" means it does not serve as wood in the village because it cannot be used for roof-peaks, rafters, pillars, or stairs, etc.; nor does it serve as wood in the forest because it is not suitable for making the legs of a field-watchman's hut or the legs of a couch. If held by the two ends, it burns the hand; if held in the middle, it smears one with excrement. "tathūpamaṃ" refers to a person similar to that firebrand used for cremating a corpse. "abhikkantataro" means a person who is especially better. "paṇītataro" means a person who is especially noble. "gavā khīraṃ" means milk from a cow. In the words "khīramhā dadhi" and so on, each subsequent stage is nobler than the preceding one; however, the cream of ghee (sappimaṇḍa) is [the best] among all of them...
326:
The clarified butter is indeed superior. In the words 'agga' and so forth, it should be understood as being superior by way of qualities, as well as being excellent, foremost, sublime, and noble. By the simile of the firebrand from a funeral pyre, it is not only the immoral person who is spoken of; it should be understood that the person of little learning who is distracted in his work and is like an ox is also spoken of. In the sixth sutta, the entire meaning is quite clear.

## 7. Khippanisantisutta-vaṇṇanā
In the seventh sutta, 'khippanisantī' means one who is capable of understanding quickly. 'Sutānañca dhammānaṃ' refers to the meaning of the scriptural teachings that have been learned and mastered. 'Atthūpaparikkhī' means one who investigates the meaning. 'Attham-aññāya dhammam-aññāya' means having known the commentary and the Pali text. 'Dhammānudhamma-paṭipanno hoti' means one has entered upon the practice of insight (vipassanā) belonging to the preliminary stage, accompanied by virtue, which is the appropriate practice for the nine supramundane states. 'No ca kalyāṇavāco' means not being one of beautiful speech. 'Na kalyāṇavākkaraṇo' means not having a beautiful voice or a pleasant tone. The negative particle 'na' (no) should be joined with terms such as 'poriyā' and so forth. The meaning is that one is not endowed with speech that is full of merit, unconfused by phlegm or bile, faultless, without defective syllables or letters, and capable of conveying the meaning. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all terms.

## 8. Attahitasutta-vaṇṇanā
98-99. The eighth sutta is taught by way of the person's disposition and by way of the splendor of the Buddha's knowledge in teaching. The ninth sutta is taught by way of the five enmities (pañcavera).

## 10. Potaliyasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, 'kālena' means at the proper and appropriate time. 'Khamati' means it is pleasing. 'Yadidaṃ tattha tattha kālaññutā' means knowing the time in various circumstances. It shows that it is the nature of the wise to blame those who deserve blame and praise those who deserve praise, having known the respective time.

## 3. Tatiya-paṇṇāsakaṃ
## (11) 1. Valāhaka-vagga
## 1-2. Valāhakasutta-dvaya-vaṇṇanā

101-2. In the first sutta of the Third Fifty, 'valāhakā' means clouds. 'One who speaks but does not act' refers to one who merely says, 'I will do this and that,' but does not actually do it. 'One who acts but does not speak' refers to one who, without speaking, thinks, 'It is proper for me to do this and that,' and then does it. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all terms. The second sutta has a clear meaning.

## 3. Kumbhasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, 'kumbhā' means pots. 'An empty pot that is closed' is a pot with nothing inside whose mouth is covered. 'A full pot that is open' is a pot full of water whose mouth is uncovered. The same method applies to the remaining two terms.

## 4. Udakarahadasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fourth sutta, regarding terms such as 'a pool that is shallow but appears deep'—water that is dark in color, mixed with the juice of rotten leaves, is called 'appearing deep.' Water that is extremely clear, with the color of gems, is called 'appearing shallow.'

## 5-6. Ambasutta-vaṇṇanā

105-6. In the fifth sutta, 'a mango that is raw but has the appearance of being ripe' means that although it is raw inside, it appears to those looking at it as if it were ripe. In this way, all terms should be understood. The sixth sutta has a clear meaning.

## 7. Mūsikasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, if a mouse digs a hole but does not live there, that mouse is called 'one who digs but is not a dweller.' There is also a variant reading 'khantā'. By this method, all terms should be understood.
328:
## 8. Balībaddasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the eighth sutta, if a bull oppresses its own herd but not another's herd, this bull is understood as 'fierce toward its own but not fierce toward others.' In this way, all terms should be understood. 'Ubbejetā hoti' means one who, by striking and piercing, causes others to reach a state of terror.

## 9. Rukkhasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, 'pheggu pheggu-parivāro' means a sapless tree surrounded only by sapless trees. 'Sāra-parivāro' means a heartwood tree, such as the khadira (catechu), surrounded only by heartwood trees. This method applies everywhere.

## 10. Āsīvisasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, 'āgataviso na ghoraviso' refers to a snake whose venom comes but is not fierce, and does not oppress for a long time. The same method applies to the remaining terms.

## Valāhaka-vagga, the First.

## (12) 2. Kesi-vagga

## 1. Kesisutta-vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the second vagga, 'Kesi' is the name of that horse trainer. He is called 'assadamma-sārathi' (a trainer of horses to be tamed) because he trains horses that are to be tamed. In the words 'trains with gentleness' and so forth, performing appropriate service for the horse, feeding it good food, giving it sweet drinks to drink, and addressing it with soft words to tame it is called 'taming with gentleness.' Taming by binding the knees, binding the mouth, and so forth, as well as by prodding with a goad, striking with a whip, and using harsh words is called 'taming with harshness.' Performing both types of training at the appropriate time is called 'taming with both gentleness and harshness.'
329:
## 2. Javasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, *ajjavena* means by way of uprightness. *Javena* means by the momentum called physical speed. *Khantiyā* means by the patience called forbearance. *Soraccena* means by the habit of virtue called purity. Regarding the qualities of a person, *javena* means by the speed of wisdom. The remaining words in this sutta have clear meanings.

## 3. Patodasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, *patodacchāyaṃ* refers to the shadow of the goad raised for the purpose of piercing. *Saṃvijjati* means being stirred by the power of noting, "I must take up speed." *Saṃvegaṃ āpajjati* means attaining spiritual urgency. *Lomavedhaviddho* means just being pierced by the goad at the hair pores. *Cammavedhaviddho* means being pierced by the goad that cuts the skin. *Atthivedhaviddho* means being pierced by the goad that breaks the bone. *Kāyena* means with the mental body (*nāmakāya*). *Paramasaccaṃ* means Nibbāna. *Sacchikaroti* means realizes or sees. *Paññāya* means with the path-wisdom (*maggapaññā*) together with insight (*vipassanā*).

## 4. Nāgasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, *atthikatvā* means being desirous or attentive. In this Pali text, *tiṇavoninndasaddānaṃ*, *tiṇavo* refers to a drum. *Ninnādasaddo* is the loud sound of all types of musical instruments mixed together. Among the terms starting with *ḍaṃsā*, *ḍaṃsā* refers to gadflies with tawny eyes. *Makasā* refers to mosquitoes. *Khippaññeva gantā hoti* means one who goes quickly after fulfilling virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

## 5. Ṭhānasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, *ṭhānāni* means causes. *Anatthāya saṃvattati* means it leads to harm and lack of growth. Here, the first cause should be understood as evil kamma accompanied by suffering and distress, such as digging pits, catching fish, and breaking into houses. The second cause should be understood as the work of laypeople with similar livelihoods, such as throwing away withered flowers, pounding plaster, roofing houses, and sweeping impure places. The third cause should be understood as actions such as drinking intoxicants, applying perfumes, and wearing garlands, as well as actions like killing (*pāṇātipāta*) performed for the sake of enjoyment. Regarding the fourth cause, when going to listen to the Dhamma, wearing clean clothes and taking flowers and perfumes...
330:
...going to pay homage to the Cetiya, paying homage to the Bodhi tree, listening to the sweet Dhamma talk, and undertaking the five precepts; in such matters, wholesome kamma (*kusala kamma*) associated with joy (*somanassa*) should be understood. *Purisathāma* means in the strength of a man's wisdom. The same method applies to the remaining two terms.

## 6. Commentary on Appamādasutta
In the sixth sutta, *yato kho* means when. *Samparāyikassa* is merely a manner of teaching; in truth, an Arahant (*khīṇāsava*) fears neither death in the future life nor death in the present life. Here, the Arahant is intended. However, some teachers say that because of the phrase "Right View has been developed," all Noble Ones (*ariyas*) starting from the Stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) are intended.

## 7. Commentary on Ārakkhasutta
In the seventh sutta, *attarūpena* means one who is suitable for oneself and desires one's welfare. *Rajanīyesu* means in things that are causes for lust (*rāga*); *dhammesu* means in natures, which refers to pleasant objects (*iṭṭhārammaṇa*). This method should be understood everywhere. *Na rajjati* means one is not attached by way of views. The same method applies to the remaining terms. *Na ca pana samaṇavacanachetupi gacchati* means not giving up one's own view and following the views of other recluses (*paravādī*) because of their words. In this sutta also, the Arahant is intended.

## 8-10. Commentary on the Three Suttas starting with Saṃvejanīya
118-120. In the eighth sutta, *dassanīyāni* means worthy of being seen or visited. *Saṃvejanīyāni* means things that cause spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). In the ninth sutta, *jātibhayaṃ* means fear arising on account of birth. The same method applies to the remaining terms. In the tenth sutta, *aggibhayaṃ* means fear arising on account of fire. The same method applies to the remaining terms.

## (13) 3. Bhayavagga
## 1. Attānuvāda Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the third chapter, 'Attānuvāda-bhaya' refers to the fear that arises in one who reproaches oneself. 'Parānuvāda-bhaya' refers to the fear that arises due to being reproached by others. 'Daṇḍa-bhaya' refers to the fear that arises on account of the thirty-two types of punishment (kammakiāraṇā). 'Duggati-bhaya' refers to the fear that arises on account of the four planes of misery.

Regarding the words, "Monks, this is called the fear of self-reproach," and so forth: first, in one who contemplates the fear of self-reproach, moral shame (hiri) arises within his own continuity. That moral shame generates restraint in the three doors for him. Restraint in the three doors constitutes the morality of fourfold purification (catupārisuddhisīla). Established in that morality, he develops insight (vipassanā) and becomes established in the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala), which is the highest.

However, in one who contemplates the fear of being reproached by others (parānuvāda-bhaya), moral dread (ottappa) arises externally. That moral dread generates restraint in the three doors for him. Restraint in the three doors constitutes the morality of fourfold purification. Established in that morality, he develops insight and becomes established in the fruit of Arahantship, which is the highest.

In one who contemplates the fear of an unhappy destination (duggati-bhaya) as well, moral shame (hiri) arises within his own continuity. That moral shame generates restraint in the three doors for him. Restraint in the three doors constitutes the morality of fourfold purification. Established in that morality, he develops insight and becomes established in the fruit of Arahantship, which is the highest.

## 2. Ūmibhaya Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, 'udakorohantassa' means for one who descends into the water. 'Pāṭikaṅkhitabbāni' means things that are to be expected (or desired). 'Susukābhaya' refers to the fear of fierce fish. 'Mukhāvaraṇaṃ maññe karonti' means they act as if they are closing the mouth. 'Odari-kattassa' means for one who is gluttonous by nature because of having a large belly. In the words 'arakkhiteneva kāyena' and so forth, it means with an unguarded body because of the absence of the three types of restraint in the bodily door. It means with unguarded speech because of the absence of the four types of restraint in the verbal door.

## 3. Paṭhamanānākaraṇa Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, 'tadassādeti' means he enjoys that jhāna with the enjoyment of pleasure. 'Nikāmeti' means he desires or longs for it. 'Vittiṃ āpajjati' means he attains delight.
332:
'Tadadhimutto' means being intent upon that first jhāna, or being inclined towards that first jhāna. 'Tabbahulavihārī' means one who dwells frequently in that jhāna. 'Sahabyataṃ upapajjati' means he reaches companionship; the meaning is that he is reborn there in that Brahma realm. In the phrase 'kappo āyuppamāṇaṃ' (the lifespan is an aeon), the first jhāna can be inferior, medium, or superior. Among these three, for those born through the inferior first jhāna, the lifespan is one-third of an incalculable aeon (asaṅkheyya-kappa). For those born through the medium first jhāna, the lifespan is half an incalculable aeon. For those born through the superior first jhāna, the lifespan is one full aeon. Although the lifespan in that first jhāna varies, the Blessed One spoke the words 'kappo āyuppamāṇaṃ' with reference to the maximum limit.

'Nirayampi gacchati' means that because the unwholesome kamma leading to hell has not yet been abandoned, one goes to hell in successive lives; it does not mean going to hell immediately after passing away. 'Tasmiṃyeva bhave parinibbāyati' means that one remains in that fine-material realm (rūpa-bhava) and attains Parinibbāna there, without descending back to lower realms. 'Yadidaṃ gatiya ဥပပတ္တိယာ သတိ' means that although there are still destiny (gati) and rebirth (upapatti), the noble disciple (ariya-sāvaka) who is a trainee (sekha) does not descend back to lower realms by way of rebirth, but attains Parinibbāna either in that fine-material realm or in one of the higher Brahma realms such as the second or third jhāna planes. For the ordinary person (puthujjana), however, there is the going to hell and so forth; the meaning is that this is the distinction.

In the phrase 'dwe kappā' (two aeons), the second jhāna also has three levels according to the method already mentioned. Therein, for those reborn by developing the superior second jhāna, the lifespan is eight great aeons (mahā-kappa). For the medium, it is four aeons; for the inferior second jhāna, it is two aeons. These words 'dwe kappā' are spoken with reference to that inferior limit. In the phrase 'cattāro kappā' (four aeons), the meaning should be understood by also including the previously mentioned words 'kappo, dwe kappā'. The word 'kappa' is also a name for multiplication (guṇa). Therefore, the meaning of one aeon, two aeons, and four aeons should be understood here.

This is the intended meaning: if the first mentioned aeon is counted twice and multiplied once, it becomes two aeons; if multiplied twice, it becomes four aeons. Furthermore, when those four aeons are multiplied by these four factors: if multiplied once, they become eight; if twice, sixteen; if thrice, thirty-two; if four times, sixty-four. Thus, it should be understood that sixty-four aeons are taken here by virtue of the superior jhāna. The words 'pañcakappasatāni' (five hundred aeons) are spoken by virtue of the superior rebirth-jhāna. Alternatively, in the Vehapphala realms, because there is no division into three Brahma worlds as in the first jhāna planes and others, the lifespan is exactly this much, five hundred aeons. Therefore, it is spoken in this way.

## 4. Dutiyanānākaraṇasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, *rūpagataṃ* refers to the form (*rūpa*) itself. The same method applies to the remaining terms. Regarding the terms beginning with *aniccato*: it is called 'as impermanent' (*aniccato*) because of the meaning of non-existence after having come to be; 'as a disease' (*rogato*) because of the meaning of affliction; 'as a boil' (*gaṇḍato*) because of the meaning of internal suppuration; 'as a dart' (*sallato*) because of the meaning of constant piercing; 'as a calamity' (*aghato*) because of the meaning of being accompanied by suffering; 'as an affliction' (*ābādhato*) because of the meaning of being oppressive; 'as alien' (*parato*) because of the meaning of not following one's will; 'as disintegrating' (*palokato*) because of the meaning of crumbling; 'as empty' (*suññato*) because of the meaning of being devoid of a being; and 'as non-self' (*anattato*) because of the meaning of being uncontrollable. 

Here, it should be understood that the characteristic of impermanence (*anicca-lakkhaṇa*) is shown by the two terms *aniccato* and *palokato*; the characteristic of non-self (*anatta-lakkhaṇa*) by the two terms *suññato* and *anattato*; and the characteristic of suffering (*dukkha-lakkhaṇa*) by the remaining terms. *Samanupassati* means seeing with insight knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*). Thus, one who sees by applying the three characteristics to the five aggregates realizes the three paths and three fruits. "Is reborn in the company of the Suddhāvāsa devas" means that while remaining in that sense-sphere realm, one develops the fourth jhāna and is reborn there.

## 5-6. Mettāsutta-dvaya-vaṇṇanā
125-126. In the fifth sutta, loving-kindness (*mettā*) is shown by way of the first jhāna, and compassion (*karuṇā*) etc. are shown by way of the second jhāna and so on. The sixth sutta should be understood in the same manner as stated in the fourth sutta.

## 7. Paṭhamatathāgata-acchariya-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the seventh sutta, *pātubhāvā* means because of the manifestation. In the phrase *kucchiṃ okkamati*, the meaning is "has entered the mother's womb." This is because such a radiance occurs only when the Bodhisatta has already entered the womb, not while he is in the process of entering. *Appamāṇo* means having a great dimension, i.e., vast. *Uḷāro* is a synonym for that same *appamāṇo*. Regarding "the divine majesty of the devas" (*devānaṃ devānubhāvaṃ*), the majesty of the devas is as follows: the radiance of their garments spreads for twelve yojanas; likewise the radiance of their bodies and their mansions. The meaning is "surpassing that majesty of the devas." *Lokantarikā* refers to the Lokantarika hells, each of which exists in the space between every three world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*). It is like the empty space in the middle of three cartwheels or three bowls placed touching each other. That Lokantarika hell is eight thousand yojanas in extent.
335:
The five cords of sensual pleasure are called 'ālaya' (attachment) because they are the objects of clinging through craving and views. Alternatively, the entire round of suffering (vaṭṭa) is called ālaya. Because beings delight in those five cords of sensual pleasure, they are called 'ālayārāma'. Because those beings possess the five cords of sensual pleasure as their place of delight, they are called ālayārāma. Because they take pleasure in attachment, they are called 'ālayarata'. Because they rejoice in attachment, they are called 'ālayasammudita'. 'Anālaye dhamme' refers to the Noble Dhamma based on Nibbāna, the cessation of the round, which is the opposite of attachment. 'Suṭṭhūsati' means desiring to hear. 'Sotaṃ odahati' means lending an ear (listening). 'Aññā cittaṃ upaṭṭhapeti' means directing the mind for the sake of realization. 'Māna' (conceit) means imagining; or, in the sense of what is imagined, it refers to the entire round of suffering itself. 'Mānavinaya dhamme' refers to the Dhamma that destroys conceit. The state opposite to peace is called 'anupasama'; or, in the sense of being unpeaceful, the round of suffering itself is called anupasama. 'Opasamika' refers to the Dhamma based on Nibbāna, the cessation of the round, which brings about peace. Being associated with ignorance, one is called 'avijjāgata'. Because they are shrouded by the shell of ignorance, those who have become like an egg are called 'aṇḍabhūta'. Being shrouded from all sides, they are called 'pariyonaddha'. In the term 'avijjāvinaya', the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala) is called the 'removal of ignorance'; it means the Dhamma based on that fruit of Arahantship is being taught. Thus, in this sutta, the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) is spoken of in four places, and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) is spoken of in four places.

## 9. Ānanda-acchariya-sutta-vaṇṇanā

In the commentary on the ninth sutta, regarding the phrase 'bhikkhuparisā ānandaṃ dassanāya', it refers to the monks who approach the Venerable Ānanda because they wish to see the Blessed One, or to those who come after hearing of the Elder's virtues, thinking, 'The Venerable Ānanda is pleasant in every way, handsome, attractive, very learned, and an ornament to the Saṅgha.' Thus it is said, 'The assembly of monks approaches to see the Venerable Ānanda.' This method applies everywhere. 'Attamanā' (joyful) means being delighted in one's own mind, thinking, 'What we have heard matches what we see.' 'Dhammaṃ' refers to the Dhamma of friendly greeting (paṭisanthāra) such as: 'Friends, are you well? Are you comfortable? Do you practice wise attention? Do you fulfill your duties toward your teachers and preceptors?' In that context of greeting, for the bhikkhunīs, there is this distinction: 'Sisters, do you undertake and practice the eight heavy rules (garudhamma)?' For the laymen (upāsakas), he does not make a greeting like: 'Lay follower, your coming is good; do you have any pain in your head or limbs? Are your sons and brothers healthy?' Instead, he greets them thus: 'Lay followers, how do you observe the three refuges and the five precepts? Do you observe the eight Uposatha days a month? Do you fulfill the duty of supporting your parents? Do you look after the monks and brahmins who practice according to the Dhamma?' For the laywomen (upāsikās), the method is the same.

## 10. Cakkavatti-acchariya-sutta-vaṇṇanā

In the commentary on the tenth sutta, 'khattiyaparisā' refers to both consecrated and unconsecrated warrior-nobles. It is said that those kings, having heard of the Universal Monarch's virtues, thinking, 'The king called the Universal Monarch is handsome and pleasant...'
336:
"...traveling through the air, he governs the kingdom; he is a righteous king, a king of Dhamma," they become joyful when their hearing matches their seeing (when they see him as they had heard). 'Bhāsati' means he makes a friendly greeting (paṭisanthāra) such as: 'Dear ones, how is it? Do you fulfill the royal duties? Do you preserve the ancient traditions?' Among the Brahmins, however, he makes a greeting thus: 'Teachers, how is it? Do you teach the mantras? Do the students learn the mantras? Do you receive offerings, garments, or virtue?' Among the householders, he makes a greeting thus: 'Dear ones, how is it? Is there no oppression from the royal family by way of punishment or imprisonment? Does the sky rain properly? Are the crops successful?' Among the monks, he makes a greeting thus: 'Venerable sirs, how is it? Are the requisites of a monk easy to obtain? Are you diligent in the monk's Dhamma?'

## (14) 4. Puggala-vagga

## 1. Saṃyojana-sutta-vaṇṇanā

In the first sutta of the fourth chapter, 'upapattipaṭilābhiyāni' refers to those fetters by which one obtains rebirth in the immediate future. 'Bhavapaṭilābhiyāni' refers to the fetters that are the conditions for obtaining existence in the realm of rebirth (upapatti-bhava). The phrase 'sakadāgāmissa' (of the Once-returner) is taken here as the highest stage among the noble ones (ariyas) who still have unabandoned fetters. This is because for the 'antarāparinibbāyī' (one who attains Nibbāna in the interval), there is no rebirth in the interval; however, whatever meditative absorption (jhāna) he attains there, because it is wholesome, it is counted only as a 'condition for the existence in the realm of rebirth.' Therefore, it is said of him: 'The fetters pertaining to obtaining rebirth are abandoned, but the fetters pertaining to obtaining existence are not yet abandoned.' Among the lower fetters (orambhāgiya), based on the unabandoned fetters of the Once-returner, it is said without distinction that 'the lower fetters are not yet abandoned.' The rest of the text here is clear.

## 2. Paṭibhāna-sutta-vaṇṇanā

In the second sutta, 'yuttappaṭibhāno no muttappaṭibhāno' means that when answering a question, he speaks only what is appropriate, but he does not speak quickly; he speaks only slowly. In this way, all terms should be understood.

## 3. Commentary on the Ugghaṭitaññū Sutta
In the third sutta, the distinction between the four types of persons should be understood by this sutta.

What is the person who is an 'ugghaṭitaññū'? For whichever person there is the realization of the Dhamma (the Four Noble Truths) at the very moment it is briefly stated; this person is called an 'ugghaṭitaññū' person. What is the person who is a 'vipañcitaññū'? For whichever person there is the realization of the Dhamma when the meanings are analyzed in detail; this person is called a 'vipañcitaññū' person. What is the person who is a 'neyya'? For whichever person there is the realization of the Dhamma gradually through learning the Pāḷi, questioning the commentaries, wise reflection, and associating with, following, and attending to good friends; this person is called a 'neyya' person. What is the person who is a 'padaparama'? For whichever person, though hearing much of the Dhamma, speaking much, memorizing much, and teaching much, there is no realization of the Dhamma in that life; this person is called a 'padaparama' person.

## 4. Commentary on the Uṭṭhānaphala Sutta
In the fourth sutta, one spends the day only with the effort of exertion (uṭṭhāna-vīriya) and makes a living by obtaining only some material things which are merely the result of that effort; however, based on that exertion, one does not obtain any fruit of merit (puññaphala). This person is called an 'uṭṭhānaphalūpajīvī' (one who lives by the fruit of effort), not a 'kammaphalūpajīvī' (one who lives by the fruit of kamma). Starting from the devas of the Cātumahārājikā realm, all devas live by depending only on the fruit of merit without the effort of exertion; therefore, they are called only 'kammaphalūpajīvī', not 'uṭṭhānaphalūpajīvī'. Kings, royal ministers, and the like are both 'uṭṭhānaphalūpajīvī' and 'kammaphalūpajīvī'. Beings in hell are neither 'uṭṭhānaphalūpajīvī' nor 'kammaphalūpajīvī'. In this sutta, only the fruit of merit is intended as the fruit of kamma (kammaphala), and that fruit of merit does not exist for those beings in hell.

## 5. Commentary on the Sāvajja Sutta
In the fifth sutta, the first person is a blind worldling (andhabāla-puthujjana). The second person is a mundane worldling (lokiya-puthujjana) who performs wholesome deeds occasionally. The third person is a stream-enterer (sotāpanna).
338:
Once-returners (sakadāgāmī) and non-returners (anāgāmī) are also included within that stream-enterer. The fourth person is an Arahant (khīṇāsava). That Arahant is indeed entirely blameless (anavajja).

## 6-7. Commentary on the Sīla Sutta, etc.
136-137. In the sixth sutta, the first person is the mundane mass of people. The second person refers to the dry-insight (sukkhavipassaka) stream-enterer and once-returner. The third person is the non-returner. This is because that non-returner obtains jhāna, which is the sign of rebirth, even at that imminent moment; therefore, even a dry-insight non-returner is one who fulfills concentration (samādhi). The fourth person is indeed an Arahant. Because he has abandoned all defilements that are contrary to virtue and so on, he is called one who is fulfilled in everything.

In the seventh sutta, the classification of persons should be understood in the same manner as stated in the sixth.

## 8. Commentary on the Nikaṭṭha Sutta
In the eighth sutta, 'nikaṭṭhakāya' means one whose body has departed (from the village). 'Anikaṭṭhacitta' means one whose mind has entered (the village). It means that although one has left the village with the body and is living in the forest, one has entered the village with the mind. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all terms.

## 9. Commentary on the Dhammakathika Sutta
In the ninth sutta, 'asahita' means not connected with the meaning (benefit). 'Not skilled' means not expert. 'Whether connected to the meaning or not'—in this way, the meaning should be understood in all terms.

## 10. Commentary on the Vādī Sutta
In the tenth sutta, 'reaching exhaustion in terms of meaning' means when asked about the commentary (aṭṭhakathā), one reaches exhaustion or depletion without being able to answer; one is unable to speak. 'Not in terms of phrasing' means that the phrasing and words continue to flow for him and are not exhausted. This same method applies to all terms.

In the first sutta of the fifth chapter, by way of radiance, the moon itself is 'candābhā' (moon-radiance). In the remaining terms, the method is the same.

## (16) 1. Indriyavagga
## 1. Indriyasuttādivaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the Fourth Fifty, it is called the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) because it exercises lordship in the sense of purifying conascent states through the burden of faith. In the remaining terms, the method is the same. In the second sutta, it is called the power of faith (saddhābala) because of its unshakable nature against the unwholesome state of faithlessness. In the remaining terms, the method is the same. In the third sutta, 'anavajjabala' means the power of being faultless. 'Saṅgahabala' means the power of integrating those who are worthy of being integrated. The fourth and fifth suttas have clear meanings.

## 6. Kappasuttavaṇṇanā
In the sixth sutta, regarding the word 'saṃvaṭṭati' (it dissolves), there are three types of dissolution: dissolution by water (āposaṃvaṭṭa), dissolution by fire (tejosaṃvaṭṭa), and dissolution by wind (vāyosaṃvaṭṭa). There are also three boundaries of dissolution (saṃvaṭṭasīmā): the Ābhassara realm, the Subhakiṇha realm, and the Vehapphala realm. When the world dissolves by fire, it burns everything below the Ābhassara realm. When the world dissolves by water, it melts everything below the Subhakiṇha realm. When the world dissolves by wind, it is destroyed by wind everything below the Vehapphala realm. In detail, one Buddha-field (buddhakhetta) is always destroyed. This is a summary here; the detailed explanation should be understood according to the method stated in the Visuddhimagga.

## 7. Rogasuttavaṇṇanā
In the seventh sutta, 'vighātavā' (distressed) means being endowed with the suffering called distress caused by great desire. 'Asantuṭṭho' (dissatisfied) means being unable to be satisfied with the four requisites through the three types of contentment. 'Anavaññappaṭilābhāya' (to gain non-contempt) means for the sake of obtaining non-disdain from others. 'Lābhasakkārasilokappaṭilābhāya' (to gain gain, honor, and fame) means for the sake of obtaining gain and honor consisting of well-prepared requisites, and fame consisting of the speaking of one's praise. 'Saṅkhāya kulāni upasaṅkamati' (approaches families with calculation) means approaching families for the sake of being known, thinking, 'In this way, they will know me.' In the remaining terms, the method is the same.

## 8. Parihānisuttavaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the eighth sutta, the Parihāni Sutta: 'Gambhīresu' means in matters of deep meaning. 'Ṭhānāṭhānesu' means in what is a cause and what is not a cause. 'Na kamati' means it does not enter or proceed. In the term 'paññācakkhu' (eye of wisdom), wisdom arising from learning and inquiry is appropriate, and wisdom arising from investigation and penetration is also appropriate.

## 9. Bhikkhunīsuttavaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the ninth sutta, the Bhikkhunī Sutta: Regarding 'ehi tvaṃ' (come here), that nun, being bound by lustful thoughts toward the Elder Ānanda, said this to have the Elder invited. 'Sasīsaṃ pārupitvā' means covering the body including the head. 'Mañcake nipajji' means having a couch quickly prepared and lying down on that couch. 'Etadavoca' means that after noting the nun's behavior, the Elder said this to preach a discourse on foulness (asubha) in a subtle manner for the purpose of removing greed.

'Āhārasambhūto' means born of nutriment, grown depending on nutriment. 'Āhāraṃ nissāya āhāraṃ pajahati' (depending on nutriment, one abandons nutriment) means that by depending on the present physical nutriment (kabaḷīkārāhāra) and consuming it appropriately, one abandons the nutriment called past kamma. However, even regarding the present physical nutriment, the craving that clings to it must be abandoned.

'Taṇhaṃ pajahati' (one abandons craving) means that by depending on the present craving that has arisen now, one abandons the past craving rooted in the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa). If one asks whether this present craving is wholesome or unwholesome, it is unwholesome. If one asks whether it should be cultivated or not, it should be cultivated. If one asks whether it pulls one toward rebirth or not, it does not. However, even in this present craving that should be cultivated, attachment must be abandoned.

"That venerable one will live having reached [the fruit of Arahantship] through the destruction of the taints; why should I not live so?" In this statement, 'kimanga pana' is a reflection on the cause. This is what is meant: That venerable one will live having realized the fruit of Arahantship; for what reason should I live without realizing it? That venerable one is a son of the Fully Enlightened One, and I too am a child of the Fully Enlightened One; this fruit of Arahantship will also arise for me.

'Mānaṃ nissāya' means depending on this conceit that has arisen and should be cultivated. 'Mānaṃ pajahati' means abandoning the past conceit rooted in the round of rebirths. That conceit depending on which one abandons the former conceit is, like craving, unwholesome and yet to be cultivated, and it does not pull one toward rebirth. However, even in that conceit, attachment must be abandoned.

"Setughāto vutto bhagavatā" means the Blessed One spoke of the destruction of the cause. When Venerable Ānanda Thera redirected the teaching using these four factors, the intense lustful desire that had arisen in that bhikkhunī towards the Thera vanished. That bhikkhunī also confessed her fault to the Thera to ask for forgiveness. The Thera also accepted her apology. To show that acceptance, the words beginning with "Atha kho sā bhikkhunī" were spoken.

## 10. Sugatavinaya Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the tenth sutta, "duggahitaṃ" means wrongly grasped, out of order. "Pariyāpuṇanti" means they master or they speak. In this Pali phrase "padabyañjanehi," the word (pada) itself is called "byañjana" because it manifests the meaning. "Dunnikkhittassa" means badly placed, set out of order. "Atthopi dunnayo hoti" means it is not possible to extract and explain the commentary. "Chinnamūlako" means the root is cut because the monks who are the root cause are cut off. "Appaṭisaraṇo" means having no refuge or foundation. "Bāhulikā" refers to those who practice primarily for the abundance of the four requisites. "Sāthalikā" refers to those who practice the three trainings laxly. In the Pali phrase "okkamane pubbaṅgamā," the five hindrances are called "okkamana" because they cause one to descend [into lower realms]; it means being foremost in those hindrances. "Paviveke" refers to the three kinds of seclusion. "Nikkhittadhurā" means being without effort. In this manner, the meaning of all terms should be understood.

## (17) 2. Paṭipadā Vagga

## 1. Saṅkhitta Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the first sutta of the second vagga, the practice of one who practices painfully, having rejected happiness, is called "dukkhā paṭipadā" (painful practice). The slow intuition of one whose progress is not rapid and is heavy is called "dandhābhiññā" (sluggish intuition). In this manner, the meaning of all terms should be understood.

## 2. Vitthāra Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the second sutta, "abhikkhaṇaṃ" means repeatedly. "Ānantariyaṃ" refers to the concentration of the path (magga-samādhi) which gives results immediately. "Āsavānaṃ khayāya" means for the sake of the fruit of Arahantship. "Pañcindriyāni" refers to the five faculties, with insight-wisdom as the fifth. In this text, "paññindriyaṃ" specifically refers to insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā). The remaining words in this sutta are clear according to the Pali text.

The explanation for clarifying these practices (paṭipadā) is as follows: In this Dispensation, a monk who has not previously applied his mind [to meditation] struggles in the preliminary stage in defining materiality, struggles in defining mentality, struggles in defining causes, struggles regarding the three periods of time, and struggles regarding what is the path and what is not the path. Thus, struggling in these five areas, he reaches insight (vipassanā). Even after reaching insight, he struggles in these nine insight knowledges: the knowledge of contemplation of rise and fall, the knowledge of contemplation of dissolution, the knowledge of appearance as fear, the knowledge of contemplation of danger, the knowledge of contemplation of disenchantment, the knowledge of desire for deliverance, the knowledge of equanimity towards formations, the knowledge of conformity, and the change-of-lineage knowledge; only after struggling does he reach the supramundane path. Because that supramundane path was realized with such pain and difficulty, it is called "dukkhā paṭipadā dandhābhiññā" (painful practice, sluggish intuition). However, for one who struggles in the five knowledges in the preliminary stage but realizes the path without struggling in the nine insight knowledges in the later stage, that path is called "dukkhā paṭipadā khippābhiññā" (painful practice, quick intuition) because it was realized with pain but without difficulty. In this way, the other two should also be understood.

These practices should be clarified by the similes of a man searching for lost oxen: Four oxen belonging to a certain man ran away and entered a forest. While searching for those oxen in a forest full of thorns and thickets, the owner traveled with difficulty and hardship through the thicket-path and saw the oxen, which were hiding in a thicket, also with difficulty and hardship. Another man, though traveling with difficulty, quickly saw the oxen standing in an open space. Another man traveled easily by an open road but saw the oxen hiding in a thicket with difficulty and hardship. Another man traveled easily and comfortably by an open road and quickly saw the oxen standing in an open space. In this simile, the four Noble Paths should be understood like the four oxen. The practitioner (yogāvacara) should be understood like the man searching for the oxen. The painful practice of one who struggles in the five knowledges in the preliminary stage should be understood like traveling with difficulty and hardship through the thicket-path. Seeing the oxen hiding in the thicket with difficulty should be understood like [struggling] in the nine knowledges in the later stage...
344:
It is the seeing of the Noble Paths by one who is weary. In this way, the remaining similes should also be applied.

## 3. Commentary on the Asubha Sutta

In the third sutta, the phrase 'asubhānupassī kāye viharati' (dwells contemplating foulness in the body) means that one dwells repeatedly contemplating foulness in one's own physical body (karajakāya) by way of comparison, thinking, 'Just as this [external corpse] is, so is this [body of mine],' comparing it to the ten kinds of foulness seen externally. The meaning is that one sees one's own body with wisdom as foul and repulsive. 'Āhāre paṭikūlasaññī' (perceiving the repulsiveness of food) means having the perception of repulsiveness in edible food (kabaḷīkārāhāra) by way of the nine kinds of repulsiveness. 'Sabbaloke anabhiratisaññī' (perceiving non-delight in the whole world) means being endowed with the perception of dissatisfaction (ukkaṇṭhita-saññā) that does not delight in the entire world consisting of the three realms. 'Sabbasaṅkhāresu aniccānupassī' (contemplating impermanence in all formations) means repeatedly contemplating all formations of the three planes as impermanent. 'Maraṇasaññā' (perception of death) is the perception that arises concerning death. 'Ajjhattanṃ supaṭṭhitā hoti' (is well-established within) means it is firmly established within one's own internal continuity. By this sequence of words, powerful insight (vipassanā) is described. 'Sekhabalāni' (powers of a trainee) refers to the powers of the noble persons who are still undergoing training. The remaining terms in this sutta are clear according to the Pali text. However, the terms beginning with 'asubhānupassī' are stated to show the painful practice (dukkha-paṭipadā), while the first jhāna and so on are stated to show the pleasant practice (sukha-paṭipadā). Indeed, foulness and such are repulsive objects; the mind, which naturally tends to love [pleasant things], does not cling to those objects of foulness. Therefore, a person who develops those [contemplations of] foulness and so on is said to have undertaken the painful practice. The first jhāna and so on are sublime happiness; therefore, a person who practices those jhānas is said to have undertaken the pleasant practice.

In this context, the general simile is as follows: A warrior skilled in battle builds a wooden chamber (phalakakoṭṭhaka), equips himself with five weapons, and enters the battlefield. When that warrior wishes to rest in between, he enters that wooden chamber to rest and partakes of drinks and food. After that, he enters the battlefield again and performs the work of fighting. In that simile, the battle of defilements (kilesa) should be understood as the battlefield. The five powers (balas), which are the means of escape from suffering, should be understood as the wooden chamber. The practitioner (yogāvacara) should be understood as the warrior entering the battlefield. The five faculties (indriyas), with insight as the fifth, should be understood as the equipment of five weapons. The time of performing the work of insight should be understood as the time of entering the battlefield. The time when the warrior wishing to rest enters the wooden chamber to rest and partake of drinks and food...
345:
...should be understood as the time when the practitioner performing the work of insight gladdens the mind by relying on the five powers at the moment when the momentum of the arising of consciousness is joyless (just as the time of entering the battlefield and the time of resting and partaking of drinks and food). The time when the person, having gladdened the mind with the five powers, performs the work of insight again, dispels [defilements], and attains the fruit of Arahatship should be understood as the time when the warrior, having rested, eaten, and drunk, enters the battlefield again. In this sutta, the powers and the faculties are taught as a mixture [of mundane and supramundane].

## 4. Commentary on the First Khama Sutta

In the fourth sutta, 'akkhama' (intolerant) refers to the practice of a person who cannot endure the insults of others and so on. 'Khama' (tolerant) refers to the practice of a person who can endure the insults of others and so on. 'Dama' (restraint) refers to the practice called the restraint of the faculties such as the eye. 'Sama' (calming) refers to the practice that calms unwholesome thoughts. 'Rosantaṃ paṭirosatīti' means striking back at one who strikes. 'Bhaṇḍantaṃ paṭibhaṇḍatīti' means striking back at one who strikes. The fifth and sixth suttas have clear meanings.

## 7. Commentary on the Mahāmoggallāna Sutta

In the seventh sutta, the lower three paths of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna were pleasant practice with slow intuition (sukha-paṭipadā dandhābhiññā). The path of Arahatship was painful practice with quick intuition (dukkha-paṭipadā khippābhiññā). Therefore, he said: "This practice is painful and has quick intuition; by means of this practice, my mind is liberated from the taints (āsavas) without clinging."

## 8. Commentary on the Sāriputta Sutta

In the eighth sutta, the lower three paths of the Elder Dhammasenāpati (Sāriputta) were pleasant practice with slow intuition. The path of Arahatship was pleasant practice with quick intuition (sukha-paṭipadā khippābhiññā). Therefore, he said: "This practice is pleasant and has quick intuition." It should be understood that in both of these suttas, the practices are taught as a mixture [of mundane and supramundane].

## 9. Commentary on the Sasaṅkhāra Sutta

In the ninth sutta, the first and second persons are dry-insight practitioners (sukkhavipassaka). They make the sign of formations (saṅkhāra-nimitta) appear with instigation and with effort. Among them, the first person, due to the strength of the faculties involved in insight, attains Nibbāna through the extinction of defilements in this very life. The second person, due to the weakness of the faculties involved in insight, is unable to attain Nibbāna through the extinction of defilements in this life; having obtained that same original meditation subject again in the next existence, he makes the sign of formations appear with instigation and with effort, and attains Nibbāna through the extinction of defilements. The third and fourth persons are those who have tranquility as their vehicle (samathayānika). Among them, the third person, due to the strength of the faculties involved in insight, exhausts the defilements in this very life without instigation and without effort. The fourth person, due to the weakness of the faculties involved in insight, is unable to exhaust the defilements in this life; having obtained that same original meditation subject again in the next existence, he exhausts the defilements without instigation and without effort. This is how it should be understood.
346:
Because the faculties are weak, being unable in this life, one regains that same original meditation subject (mūla-kammaṭṭhāna) in the immediately following existence. With effort and application, one establishes the sign of formations (saṅkhāra-nimitta) and attains parinibbāna through the extinction of defilements. The third and fourth individuals are those who have calm as their vehicle (samatha-yānika). Among them, one person (the third) exhausts the defilements in this very life without effort or application because their faculties are strong. One person (the fourth) is unable to exhaust the defilements in this life because their faculties are weak; having regained that same original meditation subject in the immediately following existence, they exhaust the defilements without effort or application. This is how it should be understood.

## 10. Commentary on the Yuganaddha Sutta

In the tenth sutta, 'calm preceded by insight' (samatha-pubbaṅgama) means making calm the precursor or forerunner (in practice). 'The path is born' (maggo sañjāyati) means the first supramundane path arises. 'He [develops] that path' (so taṃ maggaṃ): although there is no such thing as repetition (āsevana) etc. for a path that lasts only a single mind-moment, it is said that when one produces the second path and so on, one resorts to, develops, and cultivates that very first path. 'Insight preceded by calm' (vipassanā-pubbaṅgama) means developing insight after making calm the precursor. This means that a person who has naturally attained insight stays within that insight and produces concentration (samādhi).

'Develops in tandem' (yuganaddhaṃ bhāveti) means developing by yoking [calm and insight] together. In that process, it is not possible to enter an attainment with that very mind and contemplate formations with that same mind. However, this person contemplates formations for as long as they enter attainments, and enters attainments for as long as they contemplate formations. How? One enters the first jhāna, and after emerging from it, contemplates formations. Having contemplated formations, one enters the second jhāna. After emerging from that, one again contemplates formations. Having contemplated formations, [one enters] the third jhāna... (p) ...enters the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and after emerging from it, contemplates formations. In this way, this person is said to develop calm and insight in tandem.

'Distracted by restlessness regarding the Dhamma' (dhammuddhacca-viggahita) means being distracted by restlessness known as the ten imperfections of insight (vipassanūpakkilesa) regarding the states of calm and insight; it means 'wrongly grasped.' By the words 'That, friend, is the occasion' (so āvuso samayo), the time of obtaining the seven suitable conditions (sappāya) is spoken of. 'That mind' (yaṃ taṃ cittaṃ) refers to the mind that occurs having entered the process of insight (vipassanā-vīthi) at that time.
347:
'It settles internally' (ajjhattameva santiṭṭhati) means re-entering the process of insight and settling well in that very internal object known as the object of insight. 'It becomes steady' (sannisīdati) means it settles well by way of the object. 'It becomes unified' (ekodhi hoti) means it becomes one-pointed. 'It becomes concentrated' (samādhiyati) means it is well-placed (established in concentration). The remaining terms in this sutta have clear meanings.

## The Chapter on Practice is the second.

## (18) 3. The Chapter on Volition

## 1. Commentary on the Cetanā Sutta

In the first sutta of the third chapter, 'in the body' (kāye) means when there is bodily intimation (kāya-viññatti) at the body-door. In the phrases such as 'due to bodily volition' (kāya-sañcetanā-hetu), bodily volition refers to the planning or volition occurring at the body-door. That volition is of twenty kinds: eightfold by way of wholesome sense-sphere consciousness and twelvefold by way of unwholesome consciousness. Verbal volition is the same. Mental volition is also the same. However, in this mental volition, nine lofty (mahaggata) volitions are also obtained. 'Due to bodily volition' means because of the condition of bodily volition. 'Pleasure and pain arise internally' (uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ) means pleasure arises in one's own continuity due to the condition of the eight wholesome kamma, and pain arises due to the condition of the twelve unwholesome kamma. The same method applies to the other doors. 'Or conditioned by ignorance' (avijjā-paccayā vā) means only because of the cause of ignorance. For if ignorance, while concealing, acts as a condition, then volition which is the cause of pleasure and pain arises in the three doors. Thus, this is stated by way of ignorance being the root cause.

'By oneself' (sāmaṃ vā) and so forth: one who prepares and performs [an action] by oneself without being commanded by others is said to prepare a bodily formation by oneself. As for the bodily formation which one causes to be done by instigating and commanding others, others are said to prepare that bodily formation for him. One who prepares the twentyfold bodily formation at the body-door while knowing 'this is wholesome' as wholesome, 'this is unwholesome' as unwholesome, 'this is the result of wholesome kamma' as the result of wholesome kamma, and 'this is the result of unwholesome kamma' as the result of unwholesome kamma—this person is said to prepare it knowingly (sampajāna). One who prepares it without knowing thus is said to prepare it unknowingly (asampajāna). The same method applies to the other doors.
348:
Regarding the distinction between acting with full awareness and acting without full awareness, action without full awareness (asampajāna-kamma) should be understood as follows: Young children, thinking 'We shall do as our parents do,' pay homage to a pagoda (cetiya), make offerings of flowers, and pay homage to the Saṅgha of monks. Even though they do not know it is wholesome (kusala), that action is indeed wholesome.
