Similarly, when animals such as birds and beasts listen to the Dhamma, pay homage to the Saṅgha, or pay homage to a pagoda, whether they know it or not, it is indeed wholesome for them. However, when young children strike their parents with hands or feet, raise their palms in a threatening manner toward monks, throw sticks or spears, or use abusive language; and when cows chase the Saṅgha of monks, or dogs chase and bite them, or lions, tigers, and the like chase and deprive them of life—whether they know it or not, it should be understood that such actions are unwholesome kamma (akusala-kamma).

Now, to summarize the accumulating intentions (āyūhana-cetanā) occurring in all three doors: In the body-door (kāya-dvāra), there are 20 intentions rooted in self-action, 20 intentions rooted in commanding others, 20 intentions rooted in acting with full awareness, and 20 intentions rooted in acting without full awareness, totaling 80 intentions. The same applies to the speech-door (vacī-dvāra). In the mind-door (mano-dvāra), there are 29 intentions for each of the four variations, totaling 116. Thus, there are 276 intentions in total across the three doors. All these intentions are classified only as the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). The aspect of experiencing associated with those intentions is the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha); the aspect of perceiving is the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha); the mind is the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha); the body (kāya) is derived matter (upādā-rūpa); and the four great elements which are the causes of that derived matter are the primary elements (bhūta-rūpa). These five aggregates are called the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca). Monks, in these states of intention, ignorance (avijjā) is present by way of conascence (sahajāta) and by way of decisive support (upanissaya). In this way, the round of existence (vaṭṭa) and ignorance, which is the root of the round, are shown.

Having developed insight (vipassanā) through this much teaching and reached the fruit of Arahantship, the Buddha now, wishing to praise the Arahant whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava), said: 'avijjāyatveva asesa-virāga-nirodhā' (through the complete fading away and cessation of that very ignorance). In that text, 'asesa-virāga-nirodhā' means through fading away without remainder and through cessation without remainder. Regarding 'so kāyo na hoti' (that body does not exist), although the bodily actions of an Arahant—such as sweeping the pagoda terrace, sweeping the Bodhi tree terrace, moving forward, moving backward, and performing major and minor duties—are evident, the 20 intentions occurring in the body-door of that Arahant have reached the state of being non-resultant (avipāka-dhamma).
349:
(The twenty intentions occurring in the body-door of that Arahant) reach the state of being non-resultant. For this reason, it is said: 'For that Arahant, because of the complete fading away and cessation [of ignorance], that body no longer exists, by reason of which pleasure and pain would arise within himself.' Indeed, in this context, only the intention occurring in the body-door is intended by the word 'body' (kāya). The same method applies to the remaining two doors (speech and mind). Names such as 'field' (khetta) and so on are also just names for wholesome and unwholesome kamma. This is because that kamma is called a 'field' (khetta) in the sense of being the place where the result (vipāka) grows; a 'base' (vatthu) in the sense of being a foundation; a 'source' (āyatana) in the sense of being a cause; and a 'basis' (adhikaraṇa) in the sense of being the ground for action.

Thus, the Teacher, having shown the kamma accumulated through the three doors by this much teaching, now said 'cattārome bhikkhave' (monks, there are these four...) and so on, to show the place where that kamma matures. In that text, 'attabhāva-paṭilābha' refers to those who have acquired an individual existence. 'Attasañcetanā kamati' means the intention accumulated by oneself carries or proceeds.

In the words 'due to their own intention, those beings pass away from that body' and so on, the devas corrupted by play (khiḍḍāpadosikā) pass away due to their own intention. Indeed, while those devas are endowed with divine delight and playing in the Nandana Grove, Cittalatā Grove, Phārusaka Grove, and so on, they forget to eat and drink. Due to the interruption of nutriment, they wither and pass away like flowers cast into the heat of the sun. The devas corrupted by mind (manopadosikā) pass away due to the intention of others; these are the devas in the realm of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājikā). Among them, it is said that one young deva, thinking 'I shall play at the star festival,' enters the street in a chariot with his retinue. Then, another young deva coming out sees him going ahead and becomes angry, thinking, 'Friend, what is this lonely deva? Seeing him as if he has never been seen before, he goes as if puffed up with joy and as if thundering.' The deva going ahead also turns back and, seeing the other's angry expression—since those who are angry are easily recognized—knows his state of anger and gets angry in return, saying, 'What can you do to me by being angry? I have acquired this prosperity by the power of my own giving, virtue, and so on, not by your power.' If only one is angry and the other is not, it serves as protection. But when both are angry, the anger of one becomes a condition for the anger of the other, and the anger of the latter becomes a condition for the other; thus, both pass away while their consorts are weeping and wailing. Humans pass away due to both their own intention and the intention of others. This means they pass away with their own intention and another's intention as the cause. For humans, when angry, strike themselves with their own hands or sticks, bind themselves with ropes and so on, cut off their own heads with a sword, take poison, leap from cliffs, enter water, or enter fire. They also strike and kill others with hands or weapons. In this way, both their own intention and the intention of others arise in those humans.
350:
The meaning is: 'Which gods should be regarded as such?' Or it also means: 'Which gods should be regarded by that state of existence (attabhāva)?' Why does the Elder Mahāsāriputta ask this question? Is he unable to answer it himself? He is able; however, the Elder did not explain this term by his own nature because it is a question within the Buddha's domain (buddhavisaya). 'Tena daṭṭhabbā' means they should be regarded by that state of existence. Although this question can be found in the lower sense sphere (kāmāvacara) and the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), the Blessed One spoke thus because it is defined by the highest point of existence (bhavagga) and is taught as a complete teaching (nippadesa).

'Āgantāro itthattaṃ' means those who return only to this human state, which is the state of the five aggregates of the sense sphere; they are neither those reborn there nor those reborn above. 'Anāgantāro itthattaṃ' means those who do not return to these five aggregates; they are not reborn in the lower realms, but are reborn either there or in the higher realms, or they attain Parinibbāna right there. Here, rebirth in the higher realms should be understood by the power of those born in the lower existences. However, in the highest point of existence (bhavagga), there is no such rebirth in a higher realm. The remaining words are clear in all places.

## 2. Vibhatti Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the second sutta, 'Atthapaṭisambhidā' is the knowledge of the distinctions among the five meanings. 'Odhi-so' means by way of cause. 'Byañjana-so' means by way of syllables. 'Aneka-pariyāyena' means by many methods (causes). 'Ācikkhāmi' means 'I shall tell.' 'Desemi' means 'I shall teach by making it clear.' 'Paññāpemi' means 'I shall make it known.' 'Paṭṭhapemi' means 'I shall teach by establishing and setting it in motion.' 'Vivarāmi' means 'I shall teach by opening it up.' 'Vibhajāmi' means 'I shall teach by analyzing.' 'Uttānīkaromi' means 'I shall teach by making the profound clear.' 'So maṃ pañhena' means 'Let him approach me with a question.' 'Ahaṃ veyyākaraṇena' means 'I shall satisfy his mind by answering the question.' 'Yo no dhammānaṃ sukuso' means 'That Teacher who is very skilled in the Dhamma we have attained is present before us.' If I had not yet realized the analytical knowledge of meanings, the Teacher would have sat before me and restrained me, saying, 'Sāriputta, realize it first.' Thinking thus, while sitting in the presence of the Teacher, he roars a lion's roar. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all places. Among these four analytical knowledges, three are mundane (lokiya), while the analytical knowledge of meanings (Atthapaṭisambhidā) is both mundane and supramundane (lokuttara).
352:
"Knowing and seeing as it really is, one becomes an end-maker" means that one stands having made an end to the suffering of the round by knowing and seeing with the wisdom of the Path according to reality. Thus, the question is concluded by culminating with the fruit of Arahantship. The sixth sutta should be understood in the same manner as stated in the commentary on the Ekakanipāta below.

## 7. Commentary on the Rāhula Sutta
In the seventh sutta, "internal" (ajjhattikā) refers to the earth element (pathavīdhātu) characterized by the quality of hardness in the twenty parts, such as hair and so forth. "External" (bāhirā) refers to the earth element characterized by the quality of hardness in external things not connected with the faculties, such as rocks and mountains. In this same way, the remaining elements should also be understood. "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self"—these three are stated as a rejection of the graspings of craving, conceit, and views. "Should be seen with correct wisdom" means it should be seen with the wisdom of the Path, which is the cause. "Having seen" means after seeing with the wisdom of the Path together with insight. "Has cut off craving" means he has cut off craving, which is to be abandoned by the Path, along with its root. "Has transcended the fetters" means he has transcended and abandoned the ten types of fetters. "Due to the correct full understanding of conceit" means due to the realization of the abandonment of the nine types of conceit through the proper cause. "Has made an end of suffering" means he has delimited the suffering of the round and made it come to an end; the meaning is that he stands having done so.

In this way, the Teacher taught insight in the Rāhulovāda Sutta of the Saṃyutta Nikāya; he also taught insight in the Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta. In the Ambalaṭṭhikarāhulovāda Sutta, he taught the abstinence from false speech even while [Rāhula] was young. In the Mahārāhulovāda Sutta, he taught insight. In this Aṅguttara Nikāya, however, the insight called "emptiness of the four extremes" (catukoṭika-suññatā) is taught.

## 8. Commentary on the Jambālī Sutta
In the eighth sutta, "peaceful liberation of mind" (santā cetovimutti) refers to any one of the eight attainments. "Cessation of the existing body" (sakkāyanirodha) means Nibbāna, which is the cessation of the existing body known as the round of suffering in the three planes. "Does not enter" means not entering by way of the object. In the remaining terms, the method is the same. "Should not be longed for" means it is not to be desired. "Smeared with resin" (lepagatena) means smeared with sticky resin.
353:
In this matter, the simile of a man wishing to go to the further shore of a river should be brought forward. In detail: It is said that a man, wishing to go to the further shore of a river with a violent current and infested with fierce fish, thought, "This near shore is suspicious and dangerous; that further shore is safe and free from danger. What can I do to go to the further shore?" Then, seeing eight kakudha trees standing in a row, he thought, "It is possible to go by this row of trees." However, he reflected, "The kakudha trees have smooth branches; hands might not hold firm on the branches." So, he smeared his hands and feet with the resin of one of the trees like the banyan or the pilakkha and grasped a branch with his right hand. His hand stuck right there. Then his left hand, right foot, and left foot—all four limbs—stuck right there. Hanging head down, he was submerged in the river current, which had become full due to rain in the upper reaches, and became food for crocodiles and other creatures.

In that simile, the flood of saṃsāra should be seen like the river current. The practitioner (yogāvacara) is like the man wishing to go to the further shore of the current. The existing body (sakkāya) is like the near shore. Nibbāna is like the further shore. The eight attainments (samāpatti) are like the eight kakudha trees standing in a row. Entering the attainments without clearing away the defilements that are obstacles to jhāna and insight is like grasping the branch with hands smeared with resin. The time of being attached by the craving of delight (nikanti-taṇhā) in the first jhāna is like hanging from the branch by the four limbs. The time when defilements arise in the six doors is like the rain in the upper reaches. The time of experiencing suffering in the four woeful planes, being submerged in the flood of saṃsāra, should be understood like the time of being submerged in the full river current and becoming food for crocodiles and so forth.

"With a clean hand" (suddhena hatthena) means with a well-washed, pure hand. In this matter also, a similar simile should be made. In detail: In the same way, the man wishing to go to the further shore thought, "The kakudha trees have smooth branches; if one grasps them with dirty hands, the hands might slip." Having well washed his hands and feet, he grasped a branch and climbed the first tree. Descending from that, he went to the second... (and so on)... descending from that, he went to the eighth tree. Descending from the eighth tree, he reached the ground of safety on the further shore.

In that simile, the time when the practitioner thinks, "Having entered the eight attainments and having emerged from them, I will reach the fruit of Arahantship," should be understood like the time when that man thought, "I will go to the further shore by these kakudha trees." Entering the attainments after clearing away the defilements such as the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), which are opposed to jhāna and insight, is like grasping the branch with clean hands. The time of entering the first jhāna attainment is like the time of climbing the first tree among those eight trees. From the first tree...
354:
The time when one thinks, 'I will emerge from the attainment and reach Arahantship,' is the entering into attainment after clearing away the states that are obstacles to jhāna and vipassanā, like grasping a branch with a clean hand. In that simile, the time of entering the attainment of the first jhāna should be understood as the time of climbing the first khataka tree. The time of emerging from the first jhāna without being bound by the attachment of craving and entering the second jhāna is like descending from the first khataka tree and climbing the second... (omitted text)... The time of emerging from the attainment of the base of nothingness without being bound by the attachment of craving and entering the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is like descending from the seventh khataka tree and climbing the eighth. The time of emerging from the attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception without being bound by the attachment of craving, contemplating conditioned formations (saṅkhāra), and reaching Arahantship should be understood as the time of descending from the eighth khataka tree and reaching the safe ground on the far shore.

‘Avijjāppabhedaṃ manasi karoti’ means reflecting on Arahantship, which is called the destruction of the great mass of ignorance (avijjā) that has the nature of unknowing in eight instances. ‘Na pakkhandati’ means not rushing in by way of the object. ‘Jambālī’ is a large pit (a large pool) which is the standing place of much water flowing out from a village. ‘Anekavassagaṇikā’ refers to a pool that has existed for many years because it appeared at the very time the village or city was established. ‘Āyamukhāni’ are the four small inlet channels. ‘Apāyamukhāni’ are the outlet holes. ‘Na āḷippabhedo pāṭikaṅkho’ means that the destruction of the embankment (dyke) is not to be expected (not desired). This is because the water from that pool cannot rise up, break the embankment, carry away the rubbish, and reach the great ocean.

To clarify this meaning, the simile of the man seeking a garden should be brought forth. It is said that a noble son living in a city, while seeking a garden, saw a large Jambālī pool in a place neither too far nor too near the city. He noted, 'This place will be a delightful garden,' took a hoe, closed all four inlet channels, opened the outlet holes, and stayed there. As the rain did not fall properly, the remaining water trickled out through the outlet holes. Pieces of leather, worn-out clothes, and so forth rotted right there in that pool, and maggots appeared, making it impossible to approach from all around. Even those who did approach had to go by closing their nostrils.
355:
It is so. (In that pool, maggots) appeared. They stayed all around. It became unapproachable. Even those who approached had to go by closing their nostrils. That man, having come after a few days, stood back, looked, and departed, saying, 'It is impossible to approach.'

In that simile, the practitioner (yogāvacara) should be understood as the noble son living in the city. The physical body (rūpakāya) dependent on the four great elements should be understood as the time the man seeking a garden saw the pool. The time of not receiving the instruction of hearing the Dhamma is like the time the inlets were closed. The time of releasing the lack of restraint in the six doors is like the time the outlets were opened. The time of not obtaining a suitable meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) is like the time the rain did not fall properly. The time when the qualities such as virtue (sīla) and concentration (samādhi) decline within oneself is like the time the remaining water trickled out through the outlets. The time of being unable to break the embankment of ignorance (avijjā) with the path of Arahantship (arahattamagga), destroy the mass of defilements, and realize Nibbāna is like the time the water was unable to rise, break the embankment, carry away the rubbish, and reach the great ocean. The time of being filled with defilements such as lust (rāga) within oneself is like the rotting of the pieces of leather and worn-out clothes right there in that pool. The time of a person possessed of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa) delighting in the round should be understood as the time that man, having come and seen it, departed with a dissatisfied heart.

'Āḷippabhedo pāṭikaṅkho' means the destruction of the embankment is to be expected. It means that the water will be able to rise, break the embankment, carry away the rubbish, and reach the great ocean.

In this case also, that same simile should be brought forth. In that simile, the time of obtaining the hearing of the suitable Dhamma is like the time the inlets were opened. The time when restraint in the six doors is established is like the time the outlet channels were closed. The time of obtaining a suitable meditation subject is like the time the rain fell properly. The time of destroying ignorance with the path of Arahantship, destroying the mass of unwholesome states, and realizing the fruition of Arahantship is like the time the water rose, broke the embankment, carried away the rubbish, and reached the great ocean. The time of being filled with supramundane states (lokuttara dhamma) within oneself is like the time the pool was filled with water entering through the inlets. The time of entering and dwelling in the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) having Nibbāna as its object, after ascending the mansion of Dhamma, is like the time of sitting and eating good food after making a fence all around, planting trees, building a mansion in the middle of the garden, and presenting dancers. The remaining words have an obvious meaning in this context. The teaching, however, is given by mixing the mundane and supramundane. Thus ends the commentary on the eighth sutta.

In the ninth sutta, in the phrases ‘hānabhāgiyā saññā’ and so forth: if perceptions and reflections associated with the cords of sensual pleasure overwhelm one who has attained the first jhāna... the meaning should be understood only by the method already stated in the Abhidhamma as ‘hānabhāginī paññā’. For a person who has attained the first jhāna, perceptions and reflections associated with the cords of sensual pleasure overwhelm him.
356:
The time when one has ascended the palace of the Dhamma and remains having attained the fruition attainment (phala-samāpatti) which has Nibbāna as its object should be understood. In this context, the remaining words have an obvious meaning. The teaching, however, is spoken as a mixture of the mundane (lokiya) and the supramundane (lokuttara).

## 9. Nibbānasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, regarding "hāna-bhāgiyā saññā" and so forth, the meaning should be understood in the same manner as stated in the Abhidhamma: "For one who has attained the first jhāna, if perceptions and reflections associated with sense-desires (kāma) occur, that is wisdom leading to decline (hāna-bhāginī paññā)." "Yathābhūtaṃ nappajānanti" means they do not know according to reality through path knowledge (magga-ñāṇa).

## 10. Mahāpadesasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, "Bhoganagare viharati" means that while wandering on a journey near the time of his Parinibbāna, he reached the city of Bhoga and stayed there. "Ānanda-cetiye" refers to a monastery established at the site of the dwelling of the yakkha named Ānanda. "Mahāpadesa" means a great opportunity or a great reason; it refers to great reasons stated by referring to great persons such as the Buddha. "Neva abhinanditabbā" means one should not accept it beforehand by rejoicing and saying "Sādhu." If this is done, even if it is later said, "This does not agree," one might not give up their view, saying, "Why was this Dhamma before, but now it is not Dhamma?" "Nappaṭikkositabbaṃ" means one should not disparage it beforehand by saying, "What is this fool saying?" If this is said, one might not say even what is proper to be said. Therefore, he said, "Without rejoicing, without rejecting" (anabhinanditvā appaṭikkositvā). "Padabyañjanāni" refers to the sentences known as words. "Sādhukaṃ uggahetvā" means having learned well, [noting] "In this place the Pali is stated, in this place the meaning is stated, in this place the sequence (anusandhi) is told, in this place the preceding and following are told." "Sutte otāretabbāni" means they should be entered into the Sutta. "Vinaye sandassetabbāni" means they should be compared with the Vinaya.

Here, by the word "Sutta," the Vinaya is meant. As it is said, "Where was it prohibited? It was prohibited in the Suttavibhaṅga at Sāvatthī." "Vinaya" refers to the Khandhaka. As it is said, "In the Vinayātisāra." In this way, the Vinaya Piṭaka is not yet fully encompassed. However, the Ubhatovibhaṅga, known as the Bhikkhu-vibhaṅga and Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga, is called Sutta.
357:
If it is said that the Khandhaka and Parivāra are called Vinaya, then the Vinaya Piṭaka is fully encompassed. Or, if it is said that the Suttanta Piṭaka is Sutta and the Vinaya Piṭaka is Vinaya, then only two Piṭakas are encompassed. Or, if it is said that the Suttanta and Abhidhamma Piṭakas are Sutta and the Vinaya Piṭaka is Vinaya, even then all three Piṭakas are not yet fully encompassed. Indeed, there are still Buddha-vaca (words of the Buddha) that are not named Sutta. These are: Jātaka, Paṭisambhidā, Niddesa, Suttanipāta, Dhammapada, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Vimānavatthu, Petavatthu, Theragāthā, Therီgāthā, and Apadāna.

The Elder Sudinna, however, rejected all those explanations, saying, "There is no Buddha-vaca that is not named Sutta," and said, "The three Piṭakas are called Sutta, while the Vinaya is the reason (kāraṇa)." Then, wishing to show that reason, he brought forth this sutta:

"Gotamī, if you should know certain qualities: 'These qualities lead to passion, not to dispassion; they lead to bondage, not to release; they lead to clinging, not to non-clinging; they lead to great desires, not to fewness of desires; they lead to discontent, not to contentment; they lead to laziness, not to the arousal of energy; they lead to socializing, not to seclusion; they lead to the accumulation [of rebirth], not to the reduction [of rebirth].' Gotamī, you may definitely hold: 'This is not the Dhamma, this is not the Vinaya, this is not the Teacher’s instruction.'

"But Gotamī, if you should know certain qualities: 'These qualities lead to dispassion, not to passion; they lead to release, not to bondage; they lead to non-clinging, not to clinging; they lead to fewness of desires, not to great desires; they lead to contentment, not to discontent; they lead to the arousal of energy, not to laziness; they lead to seclusion, not to socializing; they lead to the reduction [of rebirth], not to the accumulation [of rebirth].' Gotamī, you may definitely hold: 'This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction.'"

Therefore, in the word "Suttē," they should be entered into the three Piṭakas of the Buddha-vaca. In the word "Vinayē," they should be compared with the reasons for removing passion and so forth; this is the meaning here. "Sutte otaranti" means not coming in any place according to the sequence of the Sutta, the membrane...
358:
Uncovering the membrane, the meaning is that words and syllables appearing from any of the obscure texts such as the Guḷha-vessantara, Guḷha-ummagga, Guḷha-vinaya, or Guḷha-vedalla Piṭakas are evident. Indeed, such words and syllables, if they are not evident in the removal of lust and so forth, are to be discarded. For that reason, it was said: "Thus, O bhikkhus, you should discard this statement." By this illustrative method, the meaning should be understood in all sections. "Bhikkhus, you should bear in mind this fourth Great Authority (Mahāpadesa)" means "Bhikkhus, you should bear in mind this fourth occasion for the establishment of the Dhamma."

## The Chapter on Volition (Sañcetanika Vagga) is the third (chapter).

## (19) 4. The Brahmin Chapter (Brāhmaṇa Vagga)

## 1. Commentary on the Yodhājīva Sutta

In the first sutta of the fourth (Brāhmaṇa) chapter, "skilled in stance" (ṭhāna-kusalo) means one who is skilled in that position where, by standing there, he is able to shoot without missing. The rest should be understood exactly as the method previously mentioned below.

## 2. Commentary on the Pāṭibhoga Sutta

In the second sutta, "there is no guarantor" (natthi kōci pāṭibhōgō) means there is no one who is truly able to be a guarantor by saying, "I am the guarantor for you." "Subject to aging" (jarā-dhammaṃ) means the nature of aging. This method applies to all terms.

## 3. Commentary on the Suta Sutta

In the third sutta, "there is no fault therein" (natthi tatō dōsō) means that in that (stating what is seen as seen), there is no such thing as a fault.

## 4. Commentary on the Abhaya Sutta

In the fourth sutta, because it is the cause of living in distress and hardship, disease itself is called "disease-affliction" (rogātaṅka). "For one affected" (phuṭṭhassa) means for a person endowed with that disease-affliction. "Beating the breast, he laments" (urattāḷiṃ kandati) means he weeps while striking his chest. In the words beginning with "one who has not done good" (akata-kalyāṇo), meritorious action is called "good" (kalyāṇa). Because that meritorious action has not been performed, he is called "one who has not done good" (akata-kalyāṇa).
360:
Taking it as 'there is no attachment or impediment for me in anything,' that Arahant Brahmin does not see another's self as existing in the state of being an attachment for himself. He does not see another's self as something to be brought into this state of attachment by conceiving it as a brother in the place of a brother, a friend in the place of a friend, or an accessory in the place of an accessory in any instance. 

In this way, since he does not see a self anywhere, nor does he see that [self] as something to be brought into the state of being an attachment for another, nor does he see another's self, nor does he see another's self as something to be brought into the state of being an attachment for himself. 'The Brahmin speaking thus' means that even though he speaks of the emptiness of the four alternatives, the Arahant Brahmin speaks only the truth because he has rightly penetrated that practice, and not a falsehood. It should be understood that because misconceptions (maññanā) have been abandoned at all times, he does not conceive. 'Ākiñcaññameva paṭipadaṃ' means he stands having fulfilled the practice that is devoid of the state of attachment, free from impediments, and is simply non-clinging (niggahaṇa).

'O wanderers, these four truths of the Brahmins have been realized and made known by me through my own higher knowledge' means that, unlike the truths spoken by you 'Bhovādī' Brahmins, these four truths of the Brahmin who has warded off evil (the Buddha) have been known through the four paths and the sixteenfold function, realized, made known, preached, and illuminated by me. Thus, in this discourse, only the true speech of the Arahant is spoken of in these four instances.

## 6. Ummaggasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the sixth discourse, 'parikassati' means is dragged or pulled. 'Ummaggo' means investigation or the arising of wisdom. Or, wisdom itself is called 'ummagga' in the sense of emerging. That same [ummagga] is called 'paṭibhāna' (intuition) in the sense of perspicuity. 'He follows the will of the arisen mind' means that only those who follow the will of the mind should be understood as being included here. 'Atthamaññāya dhammamaññāya' means knowing both the meaning and the Pali text. 'Dhammānudhammapaṭipanno hoti' means he is one who practices the preliminary path (calm and insight) along with virtue, which is the practice suitable for the supramundane Dhamma. 'Nibbedhikapañño' means possessing wisdom that penetrates defilements. 'This is suffering' means that, setting aside craving, the group of the five aggregates belonging to the three realms is known as the truth of suffering. 'Paññāya' means through the wisdom of the path. 'This is the origin of suffering' means that craving, which is the root of the round of rebirth, is the origin of that truth of suffering...
361:
...is heard. In this way, the meaning of the remaining two [truths] should also be understood. It should be understood that by answering the fourth question, the fruit of Arahantship (Arahattaphala) was preached.

## 7. Vassakārasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the commentary on the seventh, the Vassakāra Sutta, 'Todeyyassa' means of the one residing in Tudi village. 'Parisati' means in the assembly that has gathered together. 'Parūpārambhaṃ vattenti' means they engage in blaming others; they speak [it]. It is said to show the words of blame they speak, such as 'This king is a fool,' and so on. 'Samaṇe Rāmaputte' means in the ascetic Udaka, the son of Rāma. 'Abhippasanno' means extremely confident. 'Paramanipaccakāraṃ' means the act of supreme humility, the state of being humble. 'Parihārakā' means attendants and servants. 'Yamako' and so on are their names. Among them, one is named Yamaka, one Moggalla, one Ugga, one Nāvindakī, one Gandhabba, and one Aggivessa. In the word 'Tyāssudaṃ', 'assudaṃ' is merely a particle; it means they were sitting in their own assembly. 'Leads by this way' means makes [one] know or understand by this reason. 'Karaṇīyādhikaraṇīyesu' means in duties to be done by the wise and in extra duties to be done. 'Vacanīyādhivacanīyesu' means in words to be spoken and in extra words to be spoken. In the term 'Alamatthadasatarehi', those capable of seeing the meaning are called 'alamatthadasā'; those who are superior to them are called 'alamatthadasatarā'; [it means] by those [who are superior]. 'Alamatthadasataro' is said with the intent to ask: is he more superior in the ability to see the meaning, more clever than the clever, or a wiser sage than the wise? Then they replied to the brahmin Vassakāra, 'Sir, it is so,' and so on.

Thus, the brahmin, due to his own state of being a good person (sappurisatā), praised King Eḷeyya, his retinue, and Udaka Rāmaputta. Indeed, a bad person (asappurisa) is like a blind person, while a good person (sappurisa) is like one with vision. Just as a blind person sees neither the non-blind nor the blind, so a bad person knows neither the good person nor the bad person. Just as one with vision sees both the blind and the non-blind, so a good person knows both the good person and the bad person. Todeyya, being a good person, also knew the bad persons. Based on this special benefit, the brahmin Vassakāra, with a joyful heart, said 'Wonderful, Master Gotama,' and so on, rejoiced in the Blessed One's teaching, and departed.
362:
## ၈။ ဥပကသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ

In the commentary on the eighth sutta, the Upaka Sutta:—

**Upaka** is the name of that person. **Maṇḍikāputta** means the son of a Brahmin woman named Maṇḍikā. **Approached** (upasaṅkami) means it is said that he was a supporter of Devadatta. He approached for the purpose of investigating: "When I go into the presence of the Blessed One, will he speak words of praise or words of blame to me?" It is also said that he approached because he wanted to harass the Blessed One after hearing the statement: "Devadatta is destined for hell, will remain there for an aeon, and is incurable."

**Criticizes others** (parūpārambha) means speaking words that blame others. **All those cannot produce** (sabbo so na upapādeti) means all those people cannot produce wholesome states (kusala dhamma), or they are unable to make their own words suitable and appropriate. **One who cannot produce is deserving of blame** means one who is unable to produce wholesome states and unable to make their own words suitable and appropriate is deserving of blame. **Upavajjo** means deserving of reproach, or it means one who is possessed of faults, i.e., one who is blameworthy.

Then the Blessed One, taking Upaka's own doctrine and turning it back upon his own neck, spoke the words beginning with "criticizing others." **Only one emerging from the water** (ummujjamanakaṃyeva) means only one who is lifting their head out of the water. In the phrase **immeasurable words** (aparimāṇā padā) and so on, in the designation of that which is unwholesome, the words, the letters, and the Dhamma teachings are indeed immeasurable.

**This is also unwholesome** (itipidaṃ akusalaṃ) means this nature is also unwholesome, and for this reason it is also unwholesome; thus, the words that come in the designation of the unwholesome are immeasurable. Furthermore, if the Tathāgata were to teach that Dhamma in another manner, even so, his teaching would be immeasurable. As it was said: "The Dhamma teaching of the Tathāgata is inexhaustible; the words and syllables of the Dhamma are inexhaustible." In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all sections.

**How this person indeed destroys virtues** (yāva dhaṃsī vatāyaṃ) means how this person is truly a destroyer of virtues. **Son of a salt-maker** (loṇakāradāraka) means a youth living in a village of salt-makers. **One who...** (yatra hi nāma) refers to the one named Upaka. **Thinks he should harass** (āsādetabbaṃ maññissati) means he thinks he should trouble [the Buddha]. **Go away** (apehi) means get out, do not stand in front of me. Having spoken thus, the Buddha had him taken by the neck and expelled.
363:
## ၉။ သစ္ဆိကရဏီယသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ

In the ninth sutta:—

**By the body** (kāyena) means by the mental body (nāmakāya). **To be realized** (sacchikaraṇīyā) means things that should be personally experienced. **By mindfulness** (satiyā) means by the mindfulness of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsānussati). **By the eye** (cakkhunā) means by the super-knowledge of the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). **By wisdom** (paññāya) means insight wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) should be realized by jhanic wisdom; path wisdom (magga-paññā) by insight wisdom; fruition wisdom (phala-paññā) by path wisdom; and reviewing wisdom (paccavekkhaṇa-paññā) by fruition wisdom. This is the meaning of 'should be realized' or 'should be attained.' However, the fruit of Arahantship, which is the destruction of the taints (āsavas), is said to be realized by reviewing wisdom through the power of reflection.

## ၁၀။ ဥပေါသထသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ

In the tenth sutta:—

**Silent, silent** (tuṇhībhūtaṃ tuṇhībhūtaṃ) means that in whichever direction the Buddha looked, there was only silence. **Addressed the monks** (bhikkhū āမန္တေသိ) means that after looking at the monks who were accomplished in practice with clear eyes, he called them because he wished to praise them, having joy in the Dhamma that had arisen. **Without chaff** (apalaapa) means those who are free from the chaff of defilements. The other term, *nippalaapa*, is a synonym for that same *apalaapa*. **Pure** (suddhā) means those without stain. **Established in the core** (sāre patiṭṭhitā) means established in the core of virtue (sīla) and so on. **Fit** (alaṃ) means it is suitable.

**Countless leagues** (yojanagaṇanāni): one league is just a league, and ten leagues are just leagues. Only beyond ten leagues is it called 'countless leagues.' In this context, however, it refers to a hundred leagues or a thousand leagues. In the term **even with a provision bag** (puṭosenaapi), provisions for a journey are called *puṭosa*; the meaning is that it is fit to approach even while carrying provisions. There is also a variant reading *puṭaṃsena*. Its meaning is: one who has a provision bag on their shoulder is called *puṭaṃsa*; it means even by that person carrying a provision bag on their shoulder.

Now, to show that there are monks endowed with such and such qualities in this assembly, he spoke the words beginning with **There are monks** (santi bhikkhave). In that passage, **attained to the divine** (devappattā) means those who have attained the divine abidings (dibba-vihāra) which produce rebirth as a deva, and those who have reached Arahantship through the divine abidings. **Attained to the Brahma** (brahmappattā) means those who have attained the Brahma-abidings (brahma-vihāra) which accomplish the state of a Brahma due to being faultless, and those who have reached Arahantship through the Brahma-abidings. **Attained to the imperturbable** (āneñjappattā) means those who have attained the imperturbable states (āneñja, i.e., formless jhanas) which accomplish the state of motionlessness, and those who have reached Arahantship through the imperturbable states. **Attained to the noble** (ariyappattā) means those who have transcended the state of a worldling (puthujjana) and reached the state of a Noble One (ariya). In the passages such as "Thus, monks, a monk is one who has attained to the divine," a monk who, established in the fourth jhana of the fine-material sphere, directs the mind and reaches Arahantship is called **one who has attained to the divine** (devappatta).
364:
One who, established in the four sublime abodes (brahmavihāra), turns the mind and attains the fruit of arahantship (arahattaphala) is called one who has attained the Brahma-state (brahma-ppatta). One who, established in the four formless absorptions (arūpajjhāna), turns the mind and attains the fruit of arahantship is called one who has attained the imperturbable state (āneñja-ppatta). Through the four truths such as "This is suffering," the four paths and three fruits are taught. Therefore, a monk who has reached this noble Dhamma (ariya-dhamma) is called one who has attained the noble state (ariya-ppatta).

## The fourth is the Brāhmaṇa Chapter (Brāhmaṇavagga).

## (20) 5. The Great Chapter (Mahāvagga)

## 1. Commentary on the Sotānugata Sutta

In the first sutta of the fifth Great Chapter, "sotānugatānaṃ" means those who have defined with the ear of wisdom (ñāṇa-sota) after applying the physical ear (pasāda-sota). "Cattāro āniśaṃsā pāṭikaṅkhā" means four advantages of merit should be expected (can be obtained). The Blessed One began this discourse due to a specific occasion. What was that occasion? It was due to the occasion of monks not approaching to listen to the Dhamma.

In detail, five hundred monks who were formerly Brahmins thought, "If the Blessed One teaches using gender, number, case, word, and syllable, etc., he will only teach what we already know; what can he teach that we do not know?" and thus did not go to listen to the Dhamma. The Teacher, hearing of this, had those monks summoned and began this teaching to show them, "Why do you do this? Listen to the Dhamma respectfully. For you who listen to the Dhamma respectfully and recite it, there are these many benefits."

In that teaching, "dhammāṃ pariyāpuṇāti" means one learns and makes use of the scriptural Dhamma (tanti-dhamma), which is the nine-fold Dispensation of the Teacher, such as Sutta and Geyya. "Sotānugatā honti" means they have reached the ear, they have entered the ear. "Manasānupekkhitā" means they are observed by the mind. "Diṭṭhiyā suppaṭividdhā" means they are well-penetrated by wisdom and realized both in terms of meaning and cause. The phrase "muṭṭhassatī kālaṃ kurumāno" (dying with muddled mindfulness) is not said because of the absence of mindfulness in recollecting the Buddha's words, but it is said with reference to the death of an ordinary person (puthujjana). This is because an ordinary person tends to die with muddled mindfulness. "Upapajjati" means being established in pure virtue, one is reborn in the celestial world. "Dhammapadā plavanti" means for a person with muddled mindfulness reborn in the intermediate state, all those scriptural Dhamma of the Buddha's words, which were previously based on recitation and familiarized by speech, become clear and manifest.
365:
They appear like a reflection on a clear mirror; they become evident and are clearly perceived by wisdom. "Monks, the arising of mindfulness is slow" (dandho, bhikkhave, satuppādo) means the arising of mindfulness in recollecting the Buddha's words (buddhavacanānussarati) is very slow and heavy. Then, that being quickly becomes one who attains distinction, one who reaches Nibbāna.

"One who has psychic power and has attained mastery over the mind" (iddhimā cetovasippatto) refers to an Arahant who is endowed with psychic power and has attained mastery (vasi-bhāva) over the mind. In the phrase "ayaṃ vā so dhammavinayo", the word "vā" has the sense of clarification. "Yattha" means in which Dhamma-Vinaya (Dispensation). "They lived the holy life" (brahmacariyaṃ acariṃsu) means they have lived the life of the holy practice. The phrase "I also made use of this Buddha's word before" is said by the power of recollecting the Buddha's words (buddhavacanānussaraṇa). "Devaputta" refers to a certain Dhamma-preaching deity like the deity Pañcālacaṇḍa, Hatthaka Mahābrahmā, and Sanaṅkumāra Brahmā. "A spontaneously born deity reminds a spontaneously born deity" means a deity born earlier reminds a deity born later. By the phrase "playfellows in the dust" (sahapaṃsukīḷikā), it shows their long-standing familiarity over a long time. "They might meet" (samāgaccheyyuṃ) means they might come face to face in a hall or at the foot of a tree. "He might speak thus" means one who is seated first in a hall or at the foot of a tree might speak thus to one who arrives later. The rest in this sutta should be understood according to the method in the Pali text.

## 2. Commentary on the Ṭhāna Sutta

In the second sutta, "ṭhānāni" means causes. "Ṭhānehi" means by causes. "Soceyyaṃ" means the state of purity. "Saṃvasamāno" means while living together. "Na santatakārī" means one who does not act continuously. "Na santatavutti sīlesu" means one does not live a life of virtue constantly at all times. "Saṃvohāramāno" means while conversing. "One converses with another" means being alone with one person and speaking. "Vokkamati" means he deviates. "From former speech to later speech" means the speech spoken before and the speech spoken after, or the speech spoken after and the speech spoken before, do not agree with each other.

In the terms such as "ñātibyasanena", the ruin of relatives is called ñātibyasana, meaning the destruction of relatives. The same method applies to the second term. In rogabyasana, however, the disease itself is called byasana (ruin) because it destroys health; thus it is called rogabyasana. "Anuparivattanti" means they follow closely. In "lābho ca" etc., gain follows one existence (attabhāva), and loss follows one existence; this method should be applied. "Sākacchāyamāno" means while engaging in discussion by way of asking and answering questions. "Yathā" means...
366:
...in such a manner (it should be known). *Ummaggo* means searching for the problem. *Abhinīhāro* means directing the mind by way of preparing the question. *Samudāhāro* means asking the question. *Santaṃ* means it does not mean saying it is peaceful when the opposing defilements are not yet stilled. *Paṇītaṃ* means a state that does not cause burning. *Atakkāvacaraṃ* means a state that cannot be grasped by logic or reasoning. *Nipuṇaṃ* means a subtle state. *Paṇḍitavedanīyaṃ* means a state to be known only by the wise. All remaining words should be understood according to the method already stated.

## ၃။ ဘဒ္ဒိယသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ
In the third sutta, *upasaṅkami* means approaching with the thought, "I will pay respects to the Blessed One," after having had breakfast and taking flowers, scents, and ointments. In the phrases beginning with "*mā anussavena*," the meaning should be understood as: "Do not accept my words merely because of hearsay." *Sārambho* is a state characterized by over-exertion beyond what should be done. Non-greed (*alobha*) and so on should be understood as the opposites of greed (*lobha*) and so on. *Kusaladhammūpasampadāya* means for the fulfillment or attainment of wholesome states. The words "Even these great Sal trees, Bhaddiya" were spoken while pointing to the Sal trees standing in front. The remaining words here are easy to understand because they follow the method already mentioned and because their meaning is clear. When the Blessed One concluded the teaching, Bhaddiya became a Stream-enterer (*Sotāpanna*).

## ၄။ သာမုဂိယာသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ
In the fourth sutta, *Sāmugiyā* refers to the residents of the market town of Sāmuga. He spoke addressing them with the word "*Byagghapajjā*." There are two names: Kolanagara, because it was built after clearing Kola trees, and Byagghapajja, because it was built on a tiger path. Since their ancestors lived there, they are called *Byagghapajjā* as residents of Byagghapajja. Addressing them, he spoke thus. *Pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgāni* means the factors or parts of energy (*vīriya*) to be exerted for the sake of purification. *Sīlapārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgaṃ* is the name for the energy that purifies virtue. It is called *sīlapārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgaṃ* because it is a factor of exertion for the fulfillment of the purification of virtue. The same method applies to the remaining terms. In various instances, "I will support with insight wisdom" means...
367:
...supporting with insight wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*). In the phrases beginning with "*yo tattha chando*," the meaning is the wholesome desire (*kusala-chanda*) to perform such support. Among these states like desire, mindfulness and clear comprehension (*sati-sampajañña*) are mentioned for the purpose of establishing mindfulness, discerning with knowledge, and supporting energy. "*Rajaniyesu dhammesu cittaṃ virājeti*" means that in the presence of desirable objects which are causes for lust, one acts in such a way that the mind becomes detached. "*Vimocaniyesu dhammesu cittaṃ vimoceṭi*" means that in the presence of those objects from which the mind should be liberated, one acts in such a way that it is liberated. In the word "*virājetvā*," it is called "detaching" at the moment of the Path (*magga*), and "detached" at the moment of Fruition (*phala*). The same method applies to the second term. "*Sammāvimuttiṃ phusati*" means one touches (attains) the liberation of the fruition of Arahantship through the touch of knowledge by way of the appropriate cause.

## ၅။ ဝပ္ပသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ
In the fifth sutta, "*Vappa*" was a Sakyan prince who was the nephew of the Blessed One. "*Nigaṇṭhasāvaka*" means he was an attendant of the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, like General Sīha in Vesālī or the householder Upāli in Nālandā. "*Kāyena saṃvuta*" means restrained by body because the bodily door is guarded and closed. The same method applies to the remaining two (speech and mind). "*Avijjāvirāgā*" means due to the destruction and fading of ignorance. "*Vijjuppādā*" means due to the arising of Path-knowledge (*magga-vijjā*). "*Taṃ ṭhānaṃ*" refers to that cause. "*Avipakkavipākaṃ*" refers to kamma that has results but has not yet had the opportunity to ripen. "*Tatonidānaṃ*" means because of that cause or condition. "*Dukkhavedaniyā āsavā assayuṃ*" means the defilements (*kilesā*) which are the causes of painful feelings would arise for that man. "*Abhisamparāyaṃ*" means in the second existence (the next life). "*Kāyasamārambhapaccayā*" means due to the cause of bodily action (*kāya-kamma*). "*Āsavā*" refers to the defilements. In the phrase "*vighātapariḷāဟာ*," "*vighāta*" means suffering (*dukkha*), and "*pariḷāha*" means the burning of body and mind. "*Phussa phussa byantīkaroti*" means one brings to an end the kamma to be abandoned by knowledge by repeatedly touching it with the touch of knowledge, and brings to an end the kamma to be abandoned by result by repeatedly touching it with the touch of result. "*Nijjarā*" is the practice that wears away the defilements. The same method applies to the remaining sections. Abiding here, this monk should be made an Arahant (*khīṇāsava*); the meditation (*kammaṭṭhāna*) up to the fruition of Arahantship is taught, showing the determination of the Four Noble Truths after extracting the four great elements.

Now, to show the constant abiding (*satatavihāra*) of that Arahant, he spoke the words beginning with "*evaṃ sammā vimuttacittassa*." In that passage, "*sammā vimuttacittassa*" means by the appropriate cause...
368:
For the person who is well-liberated through the right means (in the explanation): 'Satatavihāra' means constant abiding, continuous abiding. 'Neva sumano hoti' means not becoming joyful through the power of lust (rāga) for a pleasant object. 'Na dummano' means not becoming dejected through the power of aversion (paṭigha) for an unpleasant object. 'Upekkhako viharati sato sampajāno' means abiding as one who is equanimous and neutral towards those objects, with equanimity characterized by a neutral state, embraced by mindfulness and clear comprehension.

'Kāyapariyantikaṃ' means that which ends with the body, delimited by the body; it refers to the feeling occurring in the five doors as long as the body of the five doors persists. 'Jīvitapariyantikaṃ' means that which ends with life, delimited by the life-faculty; it refers to the feeling occurring in the mind-door as long as the life-faculty persists. Among these two feelings, the feeling occurring in the five doors arises later and ceases first; the feeling occurring in the mind-door arises first and ceases later. Indeed, that mind-door feeling is established only in the heart-base (hadayavatthu) at the moment of rebirth-linking. The feeling occurring in the five doors arises during the course of existence (pavatti) through the five doors; at the first stage of life, around the age of twenty, it is most extreme and powerful through the power of lust, hatred, and delusion. At the age of fifty, it is stable. From the age of sixty onwards, it declines, and at the age of eighty or ninety, it becomes weak and feeble. At that time, even when beings are told, "We sat and lay together for a long time," they say, "We do not know." They also say they do not see even prominent objects like forms, and do not know whether a smell is good or bad, whether a taste is delicious or not, or whether a touch is hard or soft. Thus, while their feeling in the five doors is broken, the feeling in the mind-door continues to occur. That mind-door feeling also gradually declines and, at the time of death, occurs depending only on the edge of the heart-base. As long as this mind-door feeling occurs, the being is said to be "alive." When it no longer occurs, then it is said, "He is dead, he has ceased."

This meaning should be illustrated by the simile of a reservoir. For example, a man might build a reservoir equipped with five water channels. First, when it rains, water enters through the five channels and fills the small pits inside the reservoir. When it rains repeatedly, the water fills the channels, overflows an area of about a league or half a league, and remains flowing from various places. Then, when the sluice-pipes are opened and work is done in the fields, the water goes out. When the crops are ripe, the water has gone out and decreased, reaching a state where one would say, "Let us catch fish." Then, after a few days...
369:
...water would remain only in the small pits. As long as that water is in the pits, the great reservoir is still considered to "have water." But when the water there is cut off, then it is said, "There is no water in the reservoir." This simile should be understood as follows:

Just as the time when the pits are filled as water enters through the five channels when it first rains, so should one understand the time when the mind-door feeling is established in the heart-base at the first moment of rebirth-linking. Just as the time when the five channels are filled when it rains repeatedly, so should one understand the occurrence of the feeling in the five doors during the course of existence. Just as the overflowing of an area of about a league or half a league, so should one understand the extremely powerful state of that feeling through lust, etc., at the first stage of life, the age of twenty. Just as the time when the water remains in the full reservoir as long as it does not flow out, so should one understand the time when that feeling is stable at the age of fifty. Just as the time when water goes out when the sluice-pipes are opened and work is being done, so should one understand the decline of that feeling from the age of sixty onwards. Just as the time when a small amount of water remains in the channels when the water has decreased, so should one understand the time when the five-door feeling is weak at the age of eighty or ninety. Just as the time when water remains only in the pits, so should one understand the time when the feeling occurs in the mind-door depending on the edge of the heart-base. Just as it is said, "There is water in the reservoir," as long as there is even a little water in the pits, so it is said, "The being is alive," as long as that mind-door feeling occurs. Just as it is said, "There is no water in the reservoir," when the water in the pits is cut off, so it is said, "The being is dead," when the mind-door feeling no longer occurs. With reference to this feeling, it is said: "Experiencing a feeling that ends with life."

"Kāyassa bhedā" means because of the breaking up of the body. "Uddhaṃ jīvitapariyādānā" means above/after the exhaustion of life. "Idheva" means right here in this present world, without going further by way of rebirth-linking. "Sītī bhavissanti" means they will become cool, free from the agitation and distress of the process of existence, having the nature of not occurring again.

"Thūṇaṃ paṭicca" means depending on a tree. "Kuddālapiṭakaṃ ādāya" means taking a hoe, a spade, and a basket. However, the teaching is given only by way of the hoe. "Mūle chindeyya" means one should cut at the root with a hoe. "Palikhaneyya" means one should dig all around with a spade.
370:
In this phrase 'Evameva kho', there is this comparison of simile and its application: The self (attabhāva) should be regarded as a tree. Wholesome and unwholesome kamma is like the shadow depending on the tree. The practitioner (yogāvacara) is like a man who wishes to make the shadow cease to exist. Wisdom (paññā) is like a hoe. Concentration (samādhi) is like a basket. Insight (vipassanā) is like a spade. The time of cutting ignorance (avijjā) with the path of Arhatship (arahattamagga) is like the time of digging around the roots with a spade. The time of seeing the self through the power of the aggregates (khandha) is like the time of cutting into pieces. The time of seeing the self through the power of the sense bases (āyatana) is like the time of splitting. The time of seeing the self through the power of the elements (dhātu) is like the time of making into chips and splinters. The time of making physical and mental effort (vīriya) is like the time of drying with hot wind. The time of burning defilements (kilesa) with knowledge (ñāṇa) is like the time of burning with fire. The time of the currently existing five aggregates is like the time of making charcoal. Again, the cessation of the five aggregates without rebirth is to be understood like the time of scattering in a great wind or the time of floating away in a river current. The state of not being designated (apaṇṇattika) due to the non-arising of resultant aggregates in a future life is to be understood like the state of not being designated due to scattering and floating away.

When the Teacher concluded the discourse, [that person] attained the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala) and spoke these words beginning with 'Just as, Bhante'. In those words, 'udayatthiko' means one who desires profit. 'Assapaṇiyaṃ poseyya' means he would rear five hundred young horses with the intention of selling them later. For a horse worth a thousand, he spent only about five hundred on maintenance such as perfumes and garlands. Then, those horses caught a disease in a single day and all reached the end of their lives; this is the meaning intended. 'Udayañceva nādhigaccheyya' means he would obtain neither the profit nor any of the original capital taken from the house. 'Payirupāsi' means he served with the four requisites. 'Svāhaṃ udayañceva nādhigacchiံ' shows: 'I obtained neither profit nor the money given from the house, and have become merely one who reared horses for sale.' The remaining words here are clear.

## 6. Sāḷhasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the sixth sutta, 'dwayena' means by two groups. 'Oghassa nittharaṇaṃ' is the crossing of the four floods. 'Tapojigucchāhetu' is because of the reason of loathing evil through the practice called difficult austerities (dukkarakārikā).
371:
'Pāpajigucchanahetu' means because of the reason of loathing evil. 'Aññataraṃ sāmaññaṅgaṃ' means a certain part of the monkhood (samaṇadhamma). In the terms beginning with 'apariśuddhakāyasamācārā', the first three terms show the impurity of virtue (sīla) of body, speech, and mind, and the last term shows the impurity of livelihood (ājīva). 'Ñāṇadassanāya' means for the sake of the vision called path knowledge (maggaññāṇa). 'Anuttarāya sambodhāya' means for the sake of the fruit of Arhatship (arahattaphala), meaning it cannot be touched (attained) by the contact of Arhatship knowledge. 'Sālalatthi' means a Sal tree. 'Navaṃ' means a young tree. 'Akukkuccakajātaṃ' means the absence of worry (kukkuca) that should not be produced, such as 'Will it be? Will it not be?'. 'Lekhaṇiyā likheyya' means one should scrape with a scraping tool. 'Dhoweyya' means one should rub or polish. 'Anto aviśuddhā' means an impure tree inside, with the heartwood removed.

In this context, the comparison of simile and its application is as follows: The self (attabhāva) should be noted like the Sal tree. The current of Saṃsāra should be noted like the river current. A man who holds sixty-two wrong views should be noted like a man who wishes to go to the other shore. The time of practicing severe austerities externally is like the time when the exterior of the Sal tree is well-prepared. The time when virtue is impure internally is like the time when the interior is impure. The sinking of the person with wrong views in the current of Saṃsāra is to be understood like the sinking and going down of the Sal tree.

'Phiyārittaṃ bandheyya' means one should join the oar and the rudder. Here too, the comparison of simile and its application is as follows: The self is like the Sal tree, the current of Saṃsāra is like the river current, and the practitioner (yogāvacara) is like the man who wishes to go to the other shore. The time when restraint (saṃvara) is present in the six sense doors is like the time when the exterior is well-prepared. The state of having pure virtue internally is like the state of being well-cleansed internally. Making physical and mental effort is like the binding of the oar and the rudder. Reaching Nibbāna by gradually fulfilling virtue, concentration, and wisdom is to be seen like reaching the other shore safely and happily.

'Kaṇḍacitrakāni' refers to various artistic works made with arrows, such as arrow-creepers, arrow-ropes, arrow-palaces, arrow-curtains, arrow-tanks, arrow-lotuses, and so forth. 'Atha kho so tīhi ṭhānehi' means that although that hero knows many such artistic works with arrows, he is not yet worthy of a king; he becomes worthy of a king only when he is endowed with three factors.
372:
"He has Right Concentration" means he is concentrated through the concentration of the Path and the concentration of the Fruit; this is the meaning here. "Right View" means being endowed with the Right View of the Path. Through the four Truths beginning with "This is suffering," the four Paths and three Fruits are taught. However, it should be understood that this person is said to pierce the Truth without fail only by the Path. "Right Liberation" means being endowed with the liberation of the Fruit of Arahantship. "He breaks the mass of ignorance" means he is said to break it by the Path of Arahantship. This is because this person has already broken the mass of ignorance by the Path of Arahantship below, and here it is appropriate to say "he breaks" based on what has already been broken.

## 7. Mallikādevī Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the seventh, the Mallikādevī Sutta, "Mallikādevī" is the queen of King Pasenadi Kosala. "Why some woman in this world" means some woman in this world due to a certain cause. "Ugliness" means having a repulsive color. "Ill-formed" means having a bad physical shape. "Very mean" means extremely inferior. "To behold" means for the purpose of seeing. "Poor" means poor in wealth. "Having little property" means devoid of one's own wealth. "Having few possessions" means devoid of goods for use and consumption. "Having little influence" means having few followers. "Rich" means being a lord. "Great wealth" means having much wealth for daily use. "Great possessions" means having many goods for use and consumption. "Great influence" means having many followers. "Beautiful" means having an excellent form. "Lovely" means fit to be seen. "Inspiring" means inspiring through being seen. "Beauty of complexion and good physical shape" means being endowed with both color and bodily form.

"Angry and clinging" means clinging like a burr through anger. "Distorted" means abandoning the natural state. "Stubborn" means reaching a state of dullness and stiffness through the power of anger. "Not a giver" means not being a donor. In the phrase "bed, dwelling, and lighting," "bed" means a couch, a throne, etc. "Dwelling" means a residence or house. "Lighting" refers to lighting equipment such as wicks and oil. "Envious-minded" means having a mind associated with envy (issā). In this way, the meaning should be understood in all places. "I was one with an angry mind" means I used to be one with an angry mind. "I was one with a mind free from envy" means I used to be one with a mind devoid of envy. The remaining words in this sutta have clear meanings.
373:
## 8. Attantapa Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the eighth, the Attantapa Sutta, among the terms such as "Attantapa," one who torments or causes suffering to oneself is called "Attantapa" (self-tormentor). The exertion that torments oneself is called "Attaparitāpanānuyoga." One who torments others is called "Parantapa." The exertion that torments others is called "Paraparitāpanānuyoga." "Diṭṭhe va dhamme" means in this very present existence. In the word "Nicchāto," the hunger called craving (taṇhā) does not exist for him, thus he is "Nicchāto" (hungerless). Because all defilements have been extinguished, he is "Nibbuto." Because of the absence of defilements that cause internal heat, one who has reached a state of coolness is called "Sītībhūto." Because he experiences the happiness of Jhana, the Path, the Fruit, and Nibbana, he is called "Sukhappaṭisaṃvedī." "Brahmabhūtena attanā" means with a self that has become sublime.

The meanings of terms like "Acelako" are just as previously stated. Among terms like "Orabbhika," sheep are called "urabbha," and one who kills those sheep is an "Orabbhika." The same method applies to "Sūkarika" (pig-butcher) and others. "Luddo" means one who is cruel and harsh. "Macchaghātako" means a fisherman who catches fish. "Bandhanāgāriko" means a jailer who guards the prison. "Kurūrakammantā" means those who perform cruel deeds.

"Muddhāvasitto" refers to a king who has received the consecration on his head through the kshatriya consecration. "Puratthimena nagarassa" means to the east of the city. "Santhāgāraṃ" means a sacrificial hall. "Kharājinaṃ nivāsetvā" means wearing a rough antelope skin along with the hooves. "Sappitelena" means with ghee and oil. If ghee is set aside, any remaining fat is called "tela" (oil). "Kaṇḍuvamāno" means because the fingernails have been cut, when it is time to scratch an itch, he relieves the itch without them. "Anantarahitāya" means on the ground without any covering. "Sarūpavacchāya" means a cow with a calf of the same color as the mother. If the cow is white, the calf is also white; if the cow is brindled or red, the calf is also like that. Thus, having a calf similar to the mother is "Sarūpavacchā." "So evamāha" means that king speaks thus. "Vacchatarā" means steers that have passed the stage of being young calves and have gained strength. The same applies to "Vacchatarī" (heifers). "Barihisatthāya" means for the purpose of making an enclosure and for strewing on the sacrificial ground.

To show the fourth person starting from the appearance of the Buddha, he said, "Here, bhikkhus, a Tathāgata appears in the world," and so on. Therein, terms like "Tathāgato" are just as previously explained. "Taṃ dhammaṃ" means that Dhamma endowed with the qualities mentioned. In the place where it says "A householder or a householder's son hears that Dhamma," why did the Blessed One mention the householder first? It is because of the removal of conceit and because of having great learning that the householder is mentioned first. To speak in detail, generally, those who go forth from the royal class tend to be conceited based on their caste. Those who go forth from the brahmin class also tend to be conceited based on the Vedas. Those who go forth from low castes are unable to endure in the Sasana because of their low birth. However, householders' sons are people of such [suitable] nature.
374:
Why is the householder mentioned first? It is because they have abandoned pride and because of their great number. Generally, those who go forth from the Khattiya (warrior) class tend to be proud, relying on their birth. Those who go forth from the Brahmin class tend to be proud, relying on their mantras (Vedas). Those who go forth from low-born families are unable to remain firm in the Dispensation (Sāsana) due to the instability of their lineage. However, the sons of householders, having plowed the earth until sweat poured from their armpits and salt crystals formed on their backs, lack such pride and have abandoned arrogance and conceit. After going forth, without being arrogant or conceited, they learn the Word of the Buddha according to their ability, and by practicing Vipassanā, they are able to become established in Arahantship. Furthermore, those who go forth from other classes are not many; it is mostly householders who do so. Thus, because they have abandoned pride and are numerous, the householder is mentioned first.

'Aññatarasmiṃ vā' means in any one of the other classes. 'Paccājāto' refers to one who is born. 'Tathāgate saddhaṃ paṭilabhati' means that upon hearing the pure Dhamma, one acquires faith in the Tathāgata, the Lord of Dhamma, thinking, 'The Blessed One is indeed the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha).' 'Iti paṭisañcikkhati' means he reflects in this way. 'Sambādho gharāvāso' means that even if a husband and wife live in a house sixty cubits wide or even a hundred yojanas apart, household life is still 'crowded' (confined) for them because of the nature of having possessions and worries. 'Rajāpatho' is stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā as the place where the dust of passion (rāga) and so forth arises. It can also be called the 'path of arrival.' 'Abbhokāso viya' means being like the open air because of the nature of non-attachment. A monk, even when living in a gabled mansion, a jewel palace, or a celestial mansion with closed doors and windows, does not cling, is not attached, and is not bound. Therefore, it is said, 'Going forth is like the open air.' Alternatively, household life is crowded because there is no opportunity to perform wholesome deeds as one pleases. It is called 'rajāpatho' because it is a place where the dust of defilements accumulates, like a place where unswept rubbish gathers. Going forth is like the open air because there is the opportunity to perform wholesome deeds as one pleases.

In the passage 'Nayidaṃ sukaraṃ ... pabbajeyya,' the brief explanation is: there is this holy life (brahmacariya) consisting of the three trainings (sikkhā). Because it must be brought to the final moment of death (cuti-citta) without being broken for even a single day, it is absolutely complete. Without letting it be stained by the defilement of impurities for even a single day...
375:
...because it must be brought to the final moment of death (cuti-citta), it is perfectly pure, and should be practiced like a polished conch shell (saṅkhalikhitaṃ). It is not easy for one living in a house, one dwelling in the midst of a home, to practice this [holy life] in its complete perfection. 'If only I were to shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness.' Here, the work of the home, such as farming and trade, is called 'āgāriya' (of the home). Since such work does not exist in the state of a monk, the state of a monk is known as 'anagāriya' (homelessness). 'Pabbajeyya' means one should go forth.

'Appaṃ vā' means a mass of wealth below a thousand is called 'small'; from a thousand upwards, it is called 'large.' Because of the nature of binding, only relatives are called the 'circle of relatives' (ñātiparivaṭṭo). That circle of relatives is called 'small' if below twenty, and 'large' from twenty upwards. 'Bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno' means attaining by way of fulfillment both the training (sikkhā) known as the higher virtue (adhisīla) of monks, and the livelihood (sājīva) known as the training rules (sikkhāpada) prescribed by the Blessed One, in which they live together with a common livelihood. 'Samāpanna' means having reached both of these by fulfilling the training and not transgressing the livelihood.

'Pāṇātipātaṃ pahāya' and so forth have the meanings already stated. 'Imesaṃ bhedāya' means for the sake of dividing those from whom one has heard words. 'Bhinnānaṃ vā sandhātā' means a reconciler of friends who are divided, or of those with the same preceptor (upajjhāya) who are divided for some reason, by approaching each one and saying, 'It is not proper for people like you, born of such families and so learned, to be divided in this way.' 'Anuppadātā' means one who gives the state of reconciliation. Seeing two people in harmony, he is one who strengthens it by saying, 'It is appropriate for those born in such families and endowed with such qualities to be in harmony like this.' Because that monk delights in harmony, he is called 'samaggārāmo.' It means he does not even wish to live in a place where there are no harmonious people. There is also the Pali 'samaggarāmo,' which has the same meaning. 'Samaggarato' means one who delights in those who are harmonious; he does not wish to leave them and go elsewhere. Because he rejoices when seeing or hearing of those in harmony, he is called 'samagganandī.' Because he speaks words that create harmony...
376:
Whatever speech unites beings, he speaks only such speech that illustrates the virtue of harmony, and not otherwise. 'Nelā' means fault. Because that speech has no fault, it is called 'nelā', meaning faultless speech. It is like the word 'nela' mentioned in the passage 'nelango setapacchādo' (Udāna 65). Because it is sweet in its phrasing (byañjana-madhura), it is pleasant to the ears, thus it is called 'kaṇṇasukhā'. It does not cause pain to the ear like the piercing of a needle. Because it is sweet in its meaning (attha-madhura), it does not cause anger in the whole body but generates love, thus it is called 'pemanīyā'. Because it enters the mind easily without obstruction, it is called 'hadayaṅgamā'. Because it is full of virtues, it is speech of the city (urbane), thus it is called 'porī'. It is also called 'porī' because it is delicate like a woman raised in the city, or because it is the speech of city-dwellers. Indeed, city-dwellers have appropriate speech; they call one who is like a father 'father', and one who is like a brother 'brother'. Such speech is beloved by many people, thus it is called 'bahujanakantā'. Because it is beloved, it gladdens and develops the minds of many people, thus it is called 'bahujanamanāpā'.

Because he speaks after noting the appropriate time to speak, he is called 'kālavādī'. Because he speaks only what is real and true, he is called 'bhūtavādī'. Because he speaks based on the benefits of the present life and the future life, he is called 'atthavādī'. Because he speaks based on the nine supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma), he is called 'dhammavādī'. Because he speaks based on the discipline of restraint (saṃvara-vinaya) and the discipline of abandonment (pahāna-vinaya), he is called 'vinayavādī'. A place of storage is called 'nidhāna'. Because he speaks speech that is worthy of being stored in the heart, he is called 'nidhānavatī'. Even when speaking such speech, he does not speak at an improper time, thinking 'I will speak speech worth treasuring', but speaks only after considering the appropriate time. Because it is accompanied by illustrations and reasons, it is called 'sapadessaṃ'. Because he speaks by showing the limits clearly so that the boundaries are understood, it is called 'pariyantavatī'. He speaks speech that is full of benefit, which cannot be exhausted even when analyzed in various ways. Or, because that speaker of benefit (atthavādī) speaks speech that is connected with the benefit he mentions, it is called 'atthasaṃhitaṃ'. It means he does not discard one benefit to speak another useless thing.
377:
Regarding 'bījagāma-bhūtagāma-samārambhā', it means abstaining from destroying the five kinds of seed-groups (bījagāma)—namely, root-seeds, trunk-seeds, joint-seeds, bud-seeds, and grain-seeds—and the plant-groups (bhūtagāma) such as green grass and trees, by means of cutting, breaking, cooking, and so forth.

In the term 'ekabhattiko', there are two meals: the morning meal and the evening meal. Of these two, the morning meal is defined as being within midday, and the other is defined as being from after midday until before dawn. Therefore, even if one eats ten times within midday, one is still 'one who has a single meal' (ekabhattiko). It is in reference to eating within midday that 'ekabhattiko' is said. One who abstains from eating at night is called 'rattūparato'. Eating from after midday until sunset is called 'vikālabhojana' (untimely eating), and because of abstaining from such eating, one is called 'virato vikālabhojanā'.

'Jātarūpa' means gold. 'Rajata' refers to the currencies used in the world, such as kahāpaṇa, bronze coins, lac coins, and wooden coins. One who abstains from accepting both of these means he does not take it himself, does not have others take it, and does not consent to it being kept for him nearby.

'Āmakadhañña-paṭiggahaṇā' means abstaining from accepting the seven kinds of raw grains, namely: sāli rice, paddy, barley, wheat, millet, beans, and kudrūsa grain. Not only is accepting these grains improper for monks, but even touching them is not allowable. In the context of 'āmakamaṃsa-paṭiggahaṇā', except for what is specifically allowed, accepting raw meat and raw fish is improper for monks, but it does not mean that touching them is not improper.

In the context of 'itthikumārika-paṭiggahaṇā', 'itthi' refers to a woman who has a husband, and 'kumārikā' refers to a young girl. Both accepting and touching them is unallowable. In the context of 'dāsidāsa-paṭiggahaṇā', accepting them as female and male slaves is improper; however, if they are offered by saying, 'I give a kappiyakāraka (attendant)' or 'I give a monastery-guard (ārāmika)', then it is allowable. From goats and sheep up to fields and sites, the method of what is allowable (kappiya) and unallowable (akappiya) should be examined according to the Vinaya. Therein, 'khetta' (field) is the land where 'pubbaṇṇa' (staple crops like rice and grain) grows. 'Vatthu' (site) is the land where 'aparaṇṇa' (subsidiary crops like beans and maize) grows. Or, where both grow is called 'khetta', and the uncultivated land intended for those crops is called 'vatthu'. By the heading 'khettavatthu', irrigation works, tanks, and ponds are also included.
378:
The work of a messenger, which involves taking letters or messages from people (or kings) and traveling to various places, is called dūteyya. The minor errands of one sent from house to house are called pahiṇagamana. Anuyoga refers to the performance of both of these. Therefore, in this context, the meaning of 'anuyoga of dūteyya and pahiṇagamana' should be understood as repeatedly exerting effort in these tasks. Kayavikkaya means buying and selling.

In terms of tulākūṭa (cheating with scales) and so on, kūṭa means deception (fraud). Tulākūṭa is of four types: rūpakūṭa, aṅgakūṭa, gahaṇakūṭa, and paṭicchannakūṭa. Among these, rūpakūṭa means making two scales of similar appearance, using the large one when buying and the small one when giving (selling). Aṅgakūṭa means pressing the back of the scale with the hand when buying, and pressing the front when giving. Gahaṇakūṭa means holding the base of the scale-string when buying, and holding the tip when giving.
