Paṭicchannakūṭa means making the scale-arm hollow and filling it with iron filings, making the filings move to the back when buying and to the front when giving.

A gold bowl is called kaṃsa; deception using such a bowl is kaṃsakūṭa. How? One makes one genuine gold bowl and two or three other bronze bowls that look like gold. Then, going to the countryside and entering a wealthy family's house, one says, "Buy these gold bowls." When asked the price, they want to give a fair price. Then, when they ask, "How can we know if these are real gold?", the person says, "Test them and take them," rubs the real gold bowl on a stone to show them, gives all the bowls, and leaves.

Mānakūṭa (cheating by measure) is of three types: hadayabheda, sikhabheda, and rajjubheda. Among these, hadayabheda is found when measuring ghee, oil, and so on. When buying these, using a measuring vessel with a hole at the bottom, one says, "Pour slowly," and lets much of it leak into one's own container. When giving, one plugs the hole, fills it quickly, and gives it. Sikhabheda is found when measuring sesame, rice, and so on. When buying these, one slowly lets the heap (peak) rise. When giving, one fills it quickly and cuts off the peak. Rajjubheda is found when measuring fields and lands. Those who do not receive a bribe measure the field as large even if it is not.

In ukkoṭana and so on, ukkoṭana means taking bribes to make owners into non-owners. Vañcana means deceiving others through various means. Regarding this deception, there is this story:
379:
Story—It is traditionally heard that a hunter caught a large deer and a young deer and was coming along. A clever man asked the hunter, "Friend, how much is the large deer worth, and how much is the young deer worth?" When told, "The large deer is worth two kahāpaṇas, and the young deer is worth one," the clever man gave one kahāpaṇa, took the young deer, went a little way, and then turned back, saying, "Friend, I no longer want the young deer; give me the large deer instead." The hunter said, "Then give me two kahāpaṇas." The man said, "Friend, did I not already give you one kahāpaṇa first?" The hunter admitted, "Yes, you did." The man said, "Take this young deer as well; thus, that (already given) one kahāpaṇa and this young deer worth one kahāpaṇa, these two together make two kahāpaṇas." The hunter, thinking "He is speaking with sound reason," took back the young deer and gave him the large deer. Nikati means deception by using a counterfeit, such as making something that is not a head-ornament appear as one, or making a non-gem appear as a gem, or non-gold appear as gold, through effort or trickery (māyā). Sāciyoga means a crooked scheme. It is another name for ukkoṭana (bribery) and so on. Therefore, in this context, the meanings should be understood as ukkoṭanasāciyoga, vañcanasāciyoga, and nikatisāciyoga. Some teachers say that showing one thing and exchanging it for another is sāciyoga; however, that is included within vañcana (deception).

Among the terms chedana and so on, chedana means cutting off hands and so on. Vadha means killing. Bandha means binding with ropes and so on. Viparāmosa is of two types: himaviparāmosa and gumbaviparāmosa. Robbing travelers by hiding in the mist or snow when it falls is called himaviparāmosa. Robbing by hiding in bushes and so on is called gumbaviparāmosa. Plundering and destroying villages, market towns, and so on is called ālopa. Sahasākāra means acts of violence; entering a house, placing a weapon at people's chests, and taking the desired goods. In this way, one is a refrainer from chedana... (etc.) ...sahasākāra.

"That monk is content" means that the monk is endowed with contentment regarding the four requisites in twelve ways as mentioned above, being satisfied with whatever is available. For a monk endowed with such twelve-fold contentment with whatever is available, the eight requisites are allowable. They are: three robes, an alms-bowl, a small axe for cutting tooth-sticks, a needle, a waist-belt, and a water filter. It is also said:

Three robes, an alms-bowl, a small axe, a needle, a waist-belt,
And a water filter—these eight items are allowable for a monk who exerts effort.

All these eight requisites should be carried without being separated from the body...
380:
“The three robes, the bowl, the adze, the needle, the waistband, and the water-filter—these eight requisites are suitable for a monk who is diligent in his efforts.” All these requisites are both for the maintenance of the body and for the maintenance of the stomach. How? Firstly, the three robes are for the maintenance of the body because they support and nourish the body when worn and wrapped while wandering. They are for the maintenance of the stomach when used to filter water with the hem of the robe for drinking, or when used to carry various large and small fruits; thus, they support and nourish the stomach. The bowl is for the maintenance of the body when used to draw water for bathing or when used in repairing the hut; it is for the maintenance of the stomach when used to receive and consume food. The adze is for the maintenance of the body when used for cutting tooth-sticks or when preparing parts of couches and stools, legs, robe-racks, and posts for the hut; it is for the maintenance of the stomach when used for cutting sugarcane, coconuts, and the like. The needle is for the maintenance of the body when used for sewing robes; it is for the maintenance of the stomach when used to pierce cakes or fruits for eating. The waistband is for the maintenance of the body when tied while wandering; it is for the maintenance of the stomach when used to bind and carry sugarcane and the like. The water-filter is for the maintenance of the body when used to filter water for bathing or when repairing the lodgings; it is for the maintenance of the stomach when used to filter drinking water or juices, or when used to carry sesame, rice, flattened rice, and so forth for eating. This is the extent of the requisites for a monk who carries the eight requisites.

For a monk who carries nine requisites, a bedspread or a key is also suitable when entering the sleeping quarters. For a monk who carries ten requisites, a sitting cloth or a piece of skin is suitable. For a monk who carries eleven requisites, a walking stick or an oil tube is suitable. For a monk who carries twelve requisites, an umbrella or sandals are suitable. Among these, it should not be said that only the monk with eight requisites is content, while the others are discontented, greedy, or heavily burdened. They too are of few wishes, content, easy to support, and lead a life of lightness. However, the Blessed One did not teach this sutta with reference to them, but with reference to the monk who carries eight requisites. This is because such a monk can put the small adze and needle into the water-filter, place them inside the bowl, hang the bowl on his shoulder, and, with the three robes inseparable from his body, go happily wherever he wishes; there is no requisite he must turn back to retrieve. Thus, for this monk...
381:
The Blessed One, wishing to show the monk’s lightness of living, said: “He is content with robes for the protection of the body,” and so forth.

In that passage, “kāyaparihārika” means just enough for the maintenance of the body. “Kucchiparihārika” means just enough for the maintenance of the stomach. “He goes taking [them] with him” means he goes taking all those eight requisites, making them inseparable from his body. For him, there is no attachment or bond such as “my monastery, my precinct, my attendant.” He is like an arrow released from a bowstring, or like a rutting elephant that has left the herd; he stays alone, sits alone, and is solitary without a companion in all postures, making use of whatever lodgings, forest groves, foot of trees, or mountain clefts he desires.

“He can go to the four quarters and is without hostility,
Contented with whatever he receives,
Enduring dangers, undaunted,
He should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.”

In this way, he attains the state of wandering like a rhinoceros horn as praised.

Now, wishing to establish that meaning with a simile, the Blessed One said: “Just as,” and so forth. In that passage, “pakkhī sakuṇo” means a winged bird. “Ḍeti” means it flies up. The summary of the meaning here is: Birds, knowing that “the trees in such a place have ripe fruit,” come from various directions and eat those fruits, piercing them or shaking them with their claws, wings, and beaks. They do not have the thought, “This is for today, this is for tomorrow.” When the fruit is exhausted, they do not keep guard over the tree, nor do they leave behind a wing, a feather, a claw, or a beak. Rather, being without concern for that tree, whichever bird wishes to go to whichever direction, it flies away taking only the burden of its own wings.

In the same way, this monk goes without attachment and without concern; he goes taking [his requisites] with him. “Ariyena” means faultless or noble. “Ajjhattaṃ” means within his own person. “Anavajjasukhaṃ” means blameless happiness.

“Having seen a form with the eye” means that this monk, endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, having seen a form with eye-consciousness...
382:
I have already stated everything that should be said regarding the remaining terms in the Visuddhimagga. The bliss untainted (abyāsekasukha) is the happiness that is not smeared by defilements; it is also called unmixed bliss (avikiṇṇasukha). Indeed, the bliss arising from the restraint of the sense faculties is unmixed because it occurs by the power of merely seeing and so forth regarding visible objects and other sense data.

"In moving forward and backward" (so abhikkante paṭikkante): This means that the monk, endowed with the restraint of the sense faculties—with the mind as the sixth—is one who acts with clear comprehension by the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension in these seven instances, such as moving forward and backward. Among these, moving forward (abhikkanta) means going ahead, and moving backward (paṭikkanta) means returning.

"He is one who acts with clear comprehension" (sampajānākārī hoti): This means that by the power of the four types of clear comprehension associated with mindfulness—namely, clear comprehension of purpose (sātthaka-sampajañña), clear comprehension of suitability (sappāya-sampajañña), clear comprehension of the resort (gocara-sampajañña), and clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña)—he performs those acts of moving forward and backward only after establishing mindfulness and discerning with wisdom. The same method applies to the remaining terms. This is a brief explanation here; for a detailed account, one who desires it should take it from the commentary on the Sāmaññaphala Sutta in the Dīgha Nikāya or from the commentary on the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta in the Majjhima Nikāya.

What does he show by the words "And he, by this..." (so iminā ca)? He shows the fulfillment of the conditions for forest dwelling. Indeed, if a monk does not possess these four factors, his forest dwelling will not be successful; he would end up living with animals or with hunters who roam the forest. Deities residing in the forest would make terrifying sounds, thinking, "What benefit is there for such a wicked monk to live in the forest?" They would strike his head with their hands and make him flee. The ill-repute that "such-and-such a monk entered the forest and committed such-and-such an evil deed" would spread. However, if a monk possesses these four factors, his forest dwelling is successful. When he reflects on his own virtue (sīla) and sees no coarse fault like a black mole or subtle fault like a freckle, he gives rise to joy (pīti). By contemplating that joy in terms of its passing away and vanishing, he enters the Noble ground (ariyabhūmi). Deities residing in the forest, being pleased, speak of his virtues. Thus, his fame spreads like a drop of oil cast upon water.

In that text, "secluded" (vivittaṃ) means empty, quiet, and without the noise of shouting. Referring to a place without the sound of people, it is stated in the Vibhaṅga: "Secluded means that even if a lodging is nearby, if it is not crowded with householders and monastics, it is called secluded." Because one sleeps (seti) and sits (āsati) there, it is called a lodging (senāsana). This is a designation for beds and chairs. Therefore, it is said—
383:
"Lodging (senāsana) means a bed is a lodging, a chair is also a lodging, a bolster, a pillow, a monastery, a lean-to, a long house, a mansion, a cave, a watch-tower, an attic, a cell, a bamboo thicket, the foot of a tree, and a pavilion are also lodgings. Wherever monks resort to, all that is called a lodging"—thus it is stated in the Vibhaṅga. Furthermore, the group consisting of a monastery (vihāra), a lean-to (aḍḍhayoga), a long house (pāsāda), a mansion (hammiya), and a cave (guhā) is called 'monastery-lodging' (vihāra-senāsana). The group consisting of a bed (mañca), a chair (pīṭha), a bolster (bhisi), and a pillow (bimbohana) is called 'bed-and-chair-lodging' (mañcapīṭha-senāsana). The group consisting of a bedspread (cimilikā), a hide (cammakhaṇḍa), a grass mat (tiṇasanthāra), and a leaf mat (paṇṇasanthāra) is called 'spread-lodging' (santhata-senāsana). Wherever monks resort to, that place is called 'space-lodging' (okāsa-senāsana). Thus, there are four kinds of lodgings. All of them are included under the term 'lodging'.

To show the lodging suitable for this monk who is like a bird and belongs to the four directions, the Buddha said "a forest, the foot of a tree" (araññaṃ rukkhamūlaṃ) and so forth. In that context, "forest" (arañña) defined as "everything outside the threshold is the forest" is the meaning of forest that comes in the context of bhikkhunīs. However, the statement "an aranyaka lodging is at least five hundred bow-lengths away" is the forest suitable for this monk. Its characteristics are stated in the description of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅganiddesa) in the Visuddhimagga. "Foot of a tree" (rukkhamūla) means any secluded foot of a tree with cool shade. "Mountain" (pabbata) means a rocky mountain. For, when a monk has performed his water duties at the mountain pools and sits in the cool shade of a tree, as the various directions become clear and he is fanned by the cool breeze, his mind becomes concentrated.

In the word "glen" (kandara), "ka" means water; it refers to a mountain region split or broken by water, which is also called a mountain slope or a river-cleft. In such a river-cleft, there is sand like silver plates. Above, there is a forest thicket like a jeweled canopy. Water like a mass of beryl flows. Having descended into such a glen, drunk the water, cooled his body, gathered the sand, spread his rag-robe, and sat down to perform the recluse's duties, the monk's mind becomes concentrated. "Mountain cave" (giriguhā) means the space between two mountains, or a large cave like a tunnel within a single mountain. The characteristics of a cemetery (susāna) are stated in the Visuddhimagga. "Woodland haunt" (vanapattha) means a place beyond the vicinity of a village, not frequented by people, where there is no plowing or sowing. Therefore, it is said: "Woodland haunt is a designation for distant lodgings." "Open air" (abbhokāsa) means an uncovered place. If he so desires, a monk may live there by making a robe-hut (cīvarakuṭi). "Straw heap" (palālapuñja) means a pile of straw.
384:
A straw heap (palālapuñja) refers to a pile of straw. From a large heap of straw, they pull out straw to create spaces resembling mountain caves. They also place straw over bushes and thickets and, sitting underneath, practice the Dhamma of a recluse. It is in reference to such a straw heap that this is said.

'After the meal' (pacchābhatta) refers to the time after eating. 'Returned from the alms round' (piṇḍapātapāṭikkanta) means having departed from the search for alms-food. Sitting with the legs interlocked from all sides is called 'cross-legged' (pallaṅka). 'Having folded' (ābhujitvā) means having bound.

'Keeping the body erect' (ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya) means keeping the upper body straight, aligning the eighteen vertebrae of the spine end to end. For a monk sitting in this manner, the skin, flesh, and sinews do not bend. Because they do not bend, the pains that would arise moment by moment due to the bending of skin, flesh, and sinews do not occur. When those pains do not arise, the mind becomes concentrated and calm; the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) does not fail but reaches growth and increase.

'Setting up mindfulness in front' (parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā) means setting up mindfulness directed towards the meditation subject, or it means placing it near the face (the tip of the nose). Therefore, it is said in the Vibhaṅga: "This mindfulness is established, well-established at the tip of the nose or at the sign of the mouth. Therefore, it is said 'setting up mindfulness in front'."

Alternatively, 'pari' has the sense of embracing, 'mukha' has the sense of leading out (from defilements), and 'sati' has the sense of establishing. Therefore, it is called 'parimukhaṃ satiṃ'. The meaning should be understood according to the method described in the Paṭisambhidāmagga. The summary of that meaning is: "Having established mindfulness that is all-embracing and leads to liberation."

In the phrase 'covetousness in the world' (abhijjhaṃ loke), the 'world' refers to the five aggregates of clinging because they have the nature of breaking up and crumbling. Therefore, the meaning here is: having abandoned lust for the five aggregates of clinging and having removed sensual desire (kāmacchanda).

'With covetousness gone' (vigatābhijjena) means dwelling with a mind free from covetousness because it has been removed (by suppression/vikkhambhana); it does not mean a mind like eye-consciousness. 'He purifies the mind from covetousness' (abhijjhāya cittaṃ parisodheti) means liberating the mind from covetousness. It means acting in such a way that covetousness releases the mind and, once released, does not overwhelm it again.

The same method should be applied to phrases like 'having abandoned ill-will and malevolence' (byāpāda-padosa). Because of this [anger], the mind becomes corrupted; it abandons its original nature like rotten barley flour, hence it is called 'byāpāda'. Because it becomes corrupted through transformation and perishes, or because it destroys others, it is called 'padosa'. Both are synonyms for anger (kodha).

Sickness of the mind is 'thina' (sloth); sickness of the mental factors is 'middha' (torpor). The two together are called 'thinamiddha'. 'Perceiving light' (ālokasaññī) means with a perception that is capable of perceiving light seen by day or night, free from hindrances, and pure...
385:
...endowed with. 'Mindful and clearly comprehending' (sato sampajāno) means endowed with mindfulness and wisdom. These two are mentioned because they are helpful for the perception of light (ālokasaññā). Restlessness and remorse together are called 'uddhaccakukkucca'. 'One who has crossed over doubt' (tiṇṇavicikiccho) means one who stands having crossed over and transcended doubt. 'One who is free from "how is this?"' (akathaṃkathī) is so called because he does not proceed in the manner of "How is this? How is that?". 'In wholesome states' means in blameless states. It means he does not doubt or hesitate, thinking "Are these states wholesome? Why are these states wholesome?". This is the summary here. Regarding these hindrances (nīvaraṇa), what should be said concerning the distinction of word-definitions, characteristics, etc., has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga.

'Factors that weaken wisdom' means that when these five hindrances arise, they do not allow unarisen mundane or supramundane wisdom to arise, and they cut off and destroy the eight attainments or five higher powers that have already arisen. Therefore, they are called 'factors that weaken wisdom'. The phrases beginning with 'Quite secluded from sensual pleasures' (vivicceva kāmehi) are explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga.

The phrase 'These taints' (ime āsavā) etc., is spoken for the purpose of explaining the Four Noble Truths by another method. By the statement 'He knows: there is no more of this state' (nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānāti), the fruitlessness of external systems is shown by the first three factors, and the profundity of his own Dispensation (Sāsana) is revealed by the fourth factor, reaching the pinnacle of the teaching with Arhatship. Now, wishing to conclude the teaching, he said 'Thus, monks,' and so on.

## 9. Taṇhā Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the ninth sutta, 'jālinī' (the ensnarer) refers to craving which is like a net. Just as a net is sewn all around and is tangled and confused, craving is also called 'jālinī' because it is like a net. Or, because that craving, which stands overwhelming the three realms of existence, has a net that is its own part in various births, it is called 'jālinī'. 'Saritaṃ' means running and wandering repeatedly in various births. 'Visaṭaṃ' means spread out, expanded in various ways. 'Visattikaṃ' means spread out and clinging in various births. Alternatively, the meaning of this term should be understood by the method: 'Visattikā because it has a poison-like root; Visattikā because it has a poison-like fruit,' etc.

'Uddhasto' means destroyed above. 'Pariyōnaddho' means enveloped all around. 'Tantākulakajāto' means become tangled like a weaver's thread. For example, a weaver's thread that is poorly kept and bitten by mice becomes tangled here and there, making it difficult to match end to end or root to root, saying 'This is the end, this is the root.' Similarly, beings by this craving...
386:
Beings, being enveloped and overwhelmed by craving, are so entangled that they are unable to straighten the path leading to their escape from the suffering of the round of rebirths. "Gulāguṇṭhikajāta" means that the ball of thread used by weavers is called gulāguṇṭhika. Some teachers say that gulā refers to a small weaver bird, and its nest is called gulāguṇṭhika. Just as both of these are so entangled that it is difficult to align end with end or base with base, this should be understood and applied in the same manner as previously mentioned.

"Muñjapabbajabhūta" means having become like muñja grass and pabbajja grass. When a rope made by pounding these grasses becomes rotten and falls somewhere, it is extremely difficult to pick it up and align end with end or base with base, saying, "This is the end, this is the base." While it might be possible for humans through their own effort to straighten the ends of the grass in that rotten rope, there is no being—except for Bodhisattas—who is capable of tearing through the web of craving by their own nature and straightening the path of their own escape from the round of rebirths. Thus, this world of beings, being enveloped by the web of craving, cannot transcend the states of deprivation (apāya), the unhappy destinations (duggati), ruin (vinipāta), and the suffering of the round of rebirths (saṃsāra).

In that context, "apāya" refers to hell, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts (peta), and the host of asuras. Indeed, all these are called apāya because they lack the benefit known as prosperity. Likewise, they are called "duggati" because they are the destination of suffering. They are called "vinipāta" because they involve falling away from all forms of happiness. As for the other term, saṃsāra:

The continuity of the aggregates,
And of the elements and sense bases,
Proceeding without interruption,
Is specifically called "saṃsāra."

Unable to transcend all those states of deprivation and the round of rebirths, beings indeed merely revolve—taking up repeated births and deaths from death to rebirth and from rebirth to death—within the three realms of existence, the four modes of birth, the five destinations, the seven stations of consciousness, and the nine abodes of beings, like a ship tossed by the wind in the great ocean or like an ox yoked to a mill.

"Ajjhattikassa upādāya" means clinging to the group of five aggregates that occur internally. Here, the genitive case in "ajjhattikassa" carries the meaning of the accusative case. "Bāhirassa upādāya" likewise means clinging to the group of five aggregates that occur externally; this also uses the genitive case in the sense of the accusative. "Asmīti, bhikkhave, sati" means: O monks, when there is the clinging to the five internal aggregates as a whole through the power of craving, conceit, and views, the thought "I am" arises; it means "when such grasping exists." "I am" is the meaning. In the phrases beginning with "itthasmīti hoti," when there is such grasping as a whole as "I am" by this aforementioned method, there are two types: grasping without comparison and grasping with comparison.
387:
Grasping occurs in two ways: without comparison (apanidhāya) and with comparison (upanidhāya). Of these two, grasping without comparison means the occurrence of "I am of such a nature" by taking only one's own nature as the object without approaching any other state. It means that among kings and so forth, the thought "I am of this sort" occurs through the power of craving, conceit, and views. This is first: grasping without comparison.

Grasping with comparison is of two types: as an equal and as an unequal. To show these two, it is said: "I am thus" (evaṃsmi) and "I am otherwise" (aññathāsmi). Between these two, "I am thus" is grasping with comparison as an equal. It means: "Just as this person is a king, just as this person is a brahmin, so too am I."

"I am otherwise" is grasping as an unequal. It means: "This person is a king, this person is a brahmin; I am different from them, whether inferior or superior." These are first the four modes of craving (taṇhā-vicarita) occurring by way of the present.

Regarding the two, "I exist" (asasmī) and "I am sinking" (satasmī): because it is said "I exist," it is called "asa"; this is a designation for the permanent (nicca). Because it is said "I sink/perish," it is called "sata"; this is a designation for the impermanent (anicca). Therefore, they should be understood as being spoken by way of the eternalist view and the annihilationist view. The four beginning with "santi" (I might be) that follow these are spoken by way of doubtful reflection. In the phrases beginning with "santi hoti," the meaning should be understood as the occurrence of "I might be." The intention here should be taken in the same manner as mentioned in the first tetrad.

The four beginning with "apiham santi" are spoken by way of longing and imagination, as in "Would that I were!" These four should also be understood in the same manner as mentioned in the first tetrad. The four beginning with "bhavissanti" are spoken by way of the future. Their meaning should also be understood in the same manner as mentioned in the first tetrad. Thus:

Two headed by views, four others that are purely heads,
And those that are rooted in the heads in groups of three;
These eighteen modes of craving,
Should be clearly explained.

Among those modes of craving, these two, "asasmī" and "satasmī," are called "diṭṭhisīsā" (view-headed). These four, "asmi," "santi," "apiham santi," and "bhavissanti," are purely heads, called "suddhasīsā." The twelve in groups of three beginning with "itthasmi" are called "sīsamūlakā" (head-rooted). Thus, one should understand the eighteen modes of craving known as two view-headed, four pure-headed, and twelve head-rooted. These are first the eighteen modes of craving that occur based on the internal. Regarding the modes of craving that occur based on the external...
388: This method is the same as the previous one. 'By this' means by this aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) ... etc. ... by the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha); thus the distinction should be understood. The remaining wording is similar to the craving-explorations (taṇhā-vicarita) based on the collection of the five aggregates occurring within that individual's own continuity. These thirty-six that are past means that for each individual, there are thirty-six craving-explorations in the past duration. Thirty-six that are future means that for each individual, there are thirty-six craving-explorations in the future duration. Thirty-six that are present means that for one individual or for many individuals, as is appropriate, there are only thirty-six in the present duration. However, for all beings, by rule, there are thirty-six in the past duration, thirty-six in the future duration, and thirty-six in the present duration. Indeed, beings with various types of craving, conceit, and views are infinite. In the passage 'there are one hundred and eight craving-explorations,' the meaning should be understood as: there is the mental exploration of craving known as the one hundred and eight. ## 10. Pemasutta-vaṇṇanā In the tenth sutta, 'na usseneti' (does not uplift) means one does not uplift through the power of views (diṭṭhi). 'na paṭiseneti' (does not retaliate) means one does not uplift through the power of quarrels and disputes by being antagonistic. 'na dhūpāyati' (does not fume) means one does not fume through the power of craving-explorations based on the internal. 'na pajjhalati' (does not blaze) means one does not blaze through the power of craving-explorations based on the external. 'na sampajjhāyati' (does not brood) means one does not brood through the power of the conceit 'I am' (asmimāna). The rest should be understood according to the method of the Pali text. In this sutta, the round of suffering (vaṭṭa) and the liberation from the round (vivaṭṭa) are taught. ## Mahāvagga, the Fifth. ## The Fourth Paṇṇāsaka is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Soṇakāyana Sutta
In the third sutta, 'Sikhā-Moggallāna' refers to a Brahmin of the Moggallāna clan who possessed a large topknot (sikhā) in the middle of his head. 'Former ones' (purimāni) refers to the days prior to the immediately preceding day, and 'even earlier ones' (purimatarāni) refers to those starting from the second day back, etc. 'Soṇakāyana' is the pupil of that same Sikhā-Moggallāna. 'Sir, this world is of the nature of kamma' means, 'Sir, this world exists according to the nature of kamma'. 'Persists through the undertaking of kamma' (kamma-samārambha-ṭṭhāyī) means it exists by the undertaking of kamma. It shows the meaning that as long as one accumulates kamma, it persists; if one does not accumulate, it is cut off. The rest is as explained below.

## 4-9. Commentary on the Sikkhāpada Sutta, etc.
The fourth and subsequent suttas also have clear meanings. Regarding the path factors (magganga), because one establishes [the object] with mindfulness (sati) and then discerns it with wisdom (paññā), both of these alone are called 'kamma'. It is said that the remaining factors are merely factors, not kamma. The same method applies to the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga). In the Abhidhamma, however, all these are described without distinction as kamma associated with volition (cetanā).

## 10. Commentary on the Samaṇa Sutta
In the tenth sutta, 'only here' (idheva) means only in this Dispensation (sāsana). This restriction should also be understood in the remaining terms. For the second and subsequent types of ascetics (samaṇa) are also found only here, and not elsewhere among other sects. 'Void' (suññā) means empty or hollow. 'Doctrines of others' (parappavādā) refers to the four doctrines of eternalism, four of partial eternalism, four of finitism and infinitism, four of eel-wriggling, two of fortuitous origination, sixteen of percipient after-death, eight of non-percipient after-death, eight of neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient after-death, seven of annihilationism, and five of Nibbāna in this life. All these sixty-two wrong views mentioned in the Brahmajāla Sutta are called 'doctrines of others' because they are the doctrines of those outside this Dispensation. 

All those doctrines are void of the four types of ascetics who stand in the fruits (phalattha-samaṇa). This is because those ascetics do not exist in those external sects. Not only are they void of these four, but they are also void of the four types of ascetics who stand in the paths (maggaṭṭha-samaṇa), and also of those practicing insight (vipassaka) for the sake of the four paths. Thus, they are void of all twelve types of ascetics. With this meaning in mind, the Blessed One said in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta: 'Subhadda, when I was twenty-nine years of age, I went forth as a seeker of the wholesome [Omniscient Knowledge]. Subhadda, from the time I went forth...'
393:
Subhadda, I was twenty-nine years of age when I went forth seeking what is wholesome. Subhadda, more than fifty years have passed since I went forth. A monk who stands in insight (vipassanā), which is a part of the Noble Path that knows the Four Noble Truths, does not exist in any other teaching outside this dispensation.

"There is no second monk, no third monk, no fourth monk; other doctrines of others are empty of noble monks," he said. Here, 'padesavattī' refers to a person currently practicing insight (āraddhavipassaka). Therefore, by grouping together the person practicing insight for the path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga), the one standing in the Path, and the one standing in the Fruit, these three together, he said, "a monk does not exist [elsewhere]." By grouping together the person practicing insight for the path of Once-returner (Sakadāgāmi-magga), the one standing in the Path, and the one standing in the Fruit, these three together, he said, "there is no second monk." The same method applies to the remaining two [stages]. The eleventh sutta has a clear meaning.

## 1. Saṅghabhedaka Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the first sutta of the fifth vagga, "Ananda, that legal issue..." means that one of the legal issues, such as a legal issue arising from a dispute (vivādādhikaraṇa), arose among the Saṅgha of monks; the Teacher said this wishing to ask whether that legal issue had been settled. "Voyuñjati" means he strives, he applies himself repeatedly. "Atthavase" means by way of cause. "Nāsessanti" means they will expel him, not allowing him to attend the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā. The remaining words should be understood according to the Pali.

## 2. Āpattibhaya Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the second sutta, "khuramuṇḍaṃ karitvā" means making the head bald with a razor, leaving five tufts of hair. "Kharassarena" means with a harsh voice. "Paṇavena" means with the drum beaten for one to be executed. "Thalaṭṭhassa" means to one standing on one side. "Sīsacchejjaṃ" means an offense deserving decapitation. "Mosallaṃ" means a punishment deserving being beaten with a pestle. "Yathādhammaṃ" here means a monk who emerges from a Saṅghādisesa offense and stands in the part of purity is said to act according to the Dhamma. "Bhasmapuṭaṃ" means a bag of ashes. "Gārayhaṃ bhasmapuṭaṃ" means a punishment deserving being struck on the head with a contemptible bag of ashes. "Yathādhammaṃ" here means curing the offense according to the Dhamma by confessing the offense. "Upavajjaṃ" means a blameworthy fault. "Pāṭidesanīyesu" means in the offenses to be confessed. ## 3. Sikkhanisaṃsa Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, it is called "sikkhanisaṃsa" because the training (sikkhā) is beneficial. It is called "paññuttara" because wisdom (paññā) is supreme. It is called "vimuttisāra" because liberation (vimutti) is the essence. It is called "satādhipateyya" because mindfulness (sati) is the governing factor. It means one should live for the sake of these benefits such as training, etc. "Ābhisamācārikā" means noble conduct. It is a name for the virtue (sīla) prescribed by way of duties (vatta). "Tathā tathā so tassā sikkhāya" means that monk who desires training practices in that training rule in such and such a way.

"Ādibrahmacariyikā" is a name for the four great virtues that are the beginning of the noble life of the Path. "Sabbaso" means in every way. "Dhammā" means the Four Noble Truths. "Paññāya samavekkhitā honti" means they are well-seen by Path-wisdom along with insight (vipassanā). "Vimuttiyā phusitā honti" means they are touched by the touch of knowledge through the liberation of the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala-vimutti). "Ajjhattaṃyeva sati sūpaṭṭhitā hoti" means mindfulness is well-established only within oneself. "Paññāya anuggahessāmi" means "I will support with insight-wisdom..."
395:
I will support with insight wisdom. In the phrase "I will clearly contemplate with wisdom," insight wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) is also intended. However, in the phrase "I will support the experienced Dhamma therein with wisdom," only path wisdom (magga-paññā) is intended.

## 4. Seyyāsutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fourth sutta, "peta" refers to those who have passed away. They mostly lie on their backs. Alternatively, those born in the realm of petas are called petas; because they have very little flesh and blood and are entangled with a mass of bones, they are unable to lie on one side and lie only on their backs.

In the phrase "he becomes displeased," the lion, the king of beasts, because of his sharp power, sleeps by placing his two front paws in one spot and his two hind paws in another spot, tucking his tail between his thighs, marking the positions where the front paws, hind paws, and tail are placed, and then resting his head on top of the two front paws. Having slept the whole day, when he wakes up, he wakes without being startled. Lifting his head, he observes the positions of the front paws and so on; if he has moved even slightly from the original position, he becomes displeased, thinking, "This is not worthy of your birth, nor is it suitable for your courage," and he sleeps again in that very spot, not going out for food. It is with reference to this displeasure that it is said, "he becomes displeased."

If he remains in the original position without moving, he becomes joyful and satisfied, thinking, "This is suitable for your birth and your courage." He then stands up, stretches in the manner of lions, shakes his mane, roars the lion's roar three times, and departs to search for food. Therefore, it is said, "he becomes pleased and joyful."

## 5. Thūpārahasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fifth sutta, regarding the term "Cakkavatti King," why did the Blessed One allow the construction of a stupa for a Cakkavatti king who died while living in the household life, but did not allow it for a virtuous worldling monk (puthujjana-bhikkhu)? It is because it would not be extraordinary. If stupas for worldling monks were allowed, there would be no space left for stupas even in the island of Tambapaṇṇi (Sri Lanka), and likewise in other places. Therefore, considering that "those stupas will not be extraordinary," he did not allow it.

A Cakkavatti king appears only one at a time; therefore, his stupa is extraordinary. However, for a virtuous worldling monk, it is indeed proper to perform great honor just as for a monk who has attained Parinibbāna. The sixth and seventh suttas have meanings that are clear and obvious.

## 4. Mālukyaputtasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fourth sutta, "Mālukyaputto" is the son of the Brahmin lady named Mālukyā. "Ettha" (here) means in this request of yours for instruction. With these words "Mālukyaputta," the Buddha both rebukes and encourages the Elder. How? It is said that this Elder, when he was young, was attached to the four requisites, and later, when he was old, he desired to live in the forest and requested a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). Then the Blessed One, speaking with the intention: "What shall we say to the young monks here regarding this request of yours for instruction? Will you all, like Mālukyaputta, be attached to requisites when young and only enter the forest to practice the Dhamma of a recluse (samaṇadhamma) when old?"—is said to rebuke the Elder. However, because the Elder desires to enter the forest and practice the Dhamma of a recluse even in his old age, the Blessed One, saying: "What shall we say to the young monks here regarding this request of yours for instruction? This Mālukyaputta of ours, even in his old age, desires to enter the forest and practice the Dhamma of a recluse...
397:
...and requests a meditation subject. You, however, do not make an effort even in your youth"—speaking with this intention, he is said to encourage the Elder. This is how the connection should be understood.
